Reply of the Government
 
5.         To ensure that developmental activities would take place in the North East along with rest of the country, there is a stipulation to spend 10% of budgetary allocation
for planned activities for the North East. It provides that if the Ministry/ Department is not able to spend 10% of the funds in the North East, the difference would be
transferred to the non-lapsable pool which can be utilized by different Department/ Ministry for taking up activities in the North East subsequently. It cannot, therefore, be
stated that the funds remain un-utilized, as these funds are especially earmarked for the North East and will be utilized for projects taken up there
 
6.         So far as CRR Scheme is concerned, number of VRS optees is limited in the North Eastern States. When those who opt for VRS from CPSEs located in the North
East, many of them return back to their States of domicile on retirement. In many cases, it may also be true that these VRS optees who have come back from the North East
are taking advantage of this Scheme within their State of domicile. DPE is, however, making all out efforts to reach the VRS optees of the North East. More nodal agencies
have been identified for north eastern region, particularly in Assam.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
            The Committee does not propose to pursue the issue for now in view of the constraints as suggested in the reply of the Government. However, the
Committee considers that non-utilisation of scares resources. The Committee may be informed if such un-utilised funds are assigned to non-lapsable pool meant of
North - Eastern region.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CHAPTER - III
Recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
1.         The Committee observes that maximum PSEs for which revival has been recommended by the BRPSE belonged to the capital goods sector under
Department of Heavy Industries followed by the chemicals and fertilizer sector.  The Committee expresses serious concern over the costly revivals that largely
entail waivers and conversions of the secured loans and interest dues towards Government of India. The Committee notes that as per the revival plan, the revived
units are likely to earn meager profits by the 2009-10.  The Committee seeks information from the DPE that of the fresh cash infusions how much would be in the
form of secured loans, unsecured equity and grants respectively.   The Committee also seeks information regarding the steps taken to secure the government loans
and interest there on.
(Para 4.6)
 
Reply of the Government
 
2.         Government has so far approved revival proposals of 26 PSEs pertaining to different administrative ministries/departments. Out of these 26 cases of the proposals

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/205threport.htm[04-07-2016 13:16:21]
approved for revival, there is cash infusion in 16 cases from GOI involving an amount of Rs.1941.30 crores. The cash infusion comprises of Rs.636.08 crores in the form of
loans, Rs.354.32 crores in the form of equity share capital, Rs.756.00 crores in the form of redeemable preference share capital and the balance of Rs.194.90 crores in the
form of grant.
 
 3.        The loans that are sanctioned for PSEs by the Government are generally unsecured loans since the entire /majority of the holding or ownership of the PSEs is held by
the Government. The competent authority while granting reliefs and concessions in the form of waivers/conversion of loans/interest takes into account the need of the PSE,
the quantum of accumulated losses, net worth position, debt equity ratio, and liquidity position and the capacity of the sick PSE to pay the loans/interest and decides, case by
case, the infusion of funds in the form of equity, loan, grant or a mix of them. The PSEs are expected to turn around and post net profit (profit after meeting interest and other
liabilities) after implementation of the revival package. The loans are to be repaid by the PSE  as per revival package approved.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
4.         The Committee underscores that out of the cash infusion of Rs.1941.30 crores approved for 16 PSUs, only Rs. 636.08 are in form of loans, 194.30 are in
terms of Grants, remaining amount is insecure share capital.  Even the Loans are unsecure. The Committee finds the logic untenable that the loans given by the
Government out of Budget, should have been unsecure as the majority of holding in a PSE, were held by the Government.  The Committee wonders if it is a fair
and prudent practice even when the  PSEs are loosing money and have not been found credit worthy enough by the market.  In any case there have been recurring
instances where the loans are eventually   converted into equity.    The Committee would also like to know the strategic difference between equity share capital and
preferential share capital. How does such a difference make a PSE financially sound and Government’s investment more secure?
 
5.         The Committee is of the view that Government should secure its loans and large part of cash infusion should be done through loans from the market
against surplus assets or Government’s guarantee instead of unsecure equities. 
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
6.         The Committee also observes among the administrative Ministries, the practice of using the recommendations of the BRPSE as the alibi without actually
justifying the revival package.  The Committee recommends that once a revival package is approved by the competent authority, the onus of justifying the revival
package must be on the administrative Ministries.   The NCMP states “While every effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick public sector companies
and revive sick industry, chronically loss-making companies will either be sold-off, or  closed, after all workers have got their legitimate dues and compensation”. 
However, the Committee observes that the revival plans have been largely confined to the manpower rationalization, cutting the wage cost and liquidating the
liabilities for the accounting adjustments.  The Committee wonders that after such accounting adjustments the PSEs will be earning only the notional profits or the
actual profit.  Taking lesson from the earlier failed attempts of revival such as HMT etc. it is evident that such window dressing of accounts will result only in
notional revival that may not be sustainable in longer run.  The Committee wonders if measures to secure Government investments are built in the revival
package.  The BRPSE must suggest measures to secure Government’s investments as a substantial part of Government’s investments are in form of unsecured
equity.  The Committee suggests that instead of waiving the loans and interests dues towards Government, they can be deferred till a prescribed period till such
time PSE should attain profitability.
(Para 4.7)
 
Reply of the Government
 
7.         The National Common Minimum Programme states that “while every effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick public sector companies and revive sick
industry, chronically loss-making companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have got their legitimate dues and compensation”.      The administrative
Ministries / Departments prepare a comprehensive package for revival/rehabilitation /closure of loss making PSEs after due consultations with all stakeholders. The reasons
for sickness/losses in PSEs are manifold and may vary from unit to unit. The revival plan prepared for sick PSEs looks into the ways and means to address the suboptimal
performance of PSE which inter alia includes manpower rationalization, reducing the manpower cost, liquidating the liabilities, technological up-gradation, modernization,
diversification, capital restructure etc. The competent authority also takes into account the accumulated losses, net worth position, debt equity ratio, liquidity position and
working capital requirements of the PSE, while drawing the revival plan. The Board may, after consultation with all relevant authorities including Ministry of Finance, and
Labour, Banking and other Financial Institutions and State Government(s),as may be necessary, in each case, recommend concessions as considered appropriate for
revival/restructuring of the PSE. Deferment of loans and interest dues towards Government till a prescribed period till such time PSE should attain profitability as suggested
by the Committee instead of waiving these loans and interest will keep the accumulated losses, negative net worth, high debt etc will remain in books which may pre-empt
the prospects of revival of sick PSE. Waivers of loans, interest etc. are included to clean the balance sheet, make the net worth positive and to improve profitability in future.

It also enables the PSE to get working capital requirements funded from Banks FIs etc.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
8.         The Committee does not accept the argument of massive waivers to acquire only notional profitability through book manipulations.  The fact remains that
such packages do not make any fundamental change in corporate prospects and management or technological modernisation of the Company. It has been
observed that while budgetary sources are used for clearing the balance sheets, for the capital investments the PSEs have to look for strategic partners. The
Committee would like to know that of the revival packages approved for PSEs how much is allocated for capital expenditure in each case and also give the detail of
such capital expenses.
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
9.         The Committee is constrained to note the tardy progress made after passage of two years. The Secretary, M/O HRD has not even responded to the DPE’s
reminder, whereas the DG, ICPE has not followed up on the advice to contact the CSIR. The Committee recommends that India as the prominent contributor and
founder member of the ICPE, must persuade the ICPE for such academic cooperation between CSIR and ICPE. The Committee strongly disapproves the
lackadaisical approach of the M/O HRD. DPE must secure an early and elaborate response from the M/O HRD in this respect.
(Para No. 5.8)
Reply of the Government
 
10.       The matter was taken up with CSIR and Ministry of HRD for utilizing the expertise of Indian Management Institutes and Institutes of Technology to impart training
to the participants of member countries of ICPE. The response from HRD is still awaited whereas CSIR has given its positive response. ICPE is being reminded with
reference to response received from CSIR. Ministry of Human Resource Development is also being reminded.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
           
11.       The Committee takes serious view of inaction by various Departments of the Government and failure of DPE to follow up with ICPE.   The response
indicates             lack of earnestness. The Committee desires the DPE to pursue the issue with greater earnestness than its defence for the retention of membership
of ICPE.
CHAPTER – IV
Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been received
 
Observation of the Committee
 
1.         In its interaction with the respective Ministries over the compliance of certain guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), the
Committee is constrained to observe recurrent violations. The Committee therefore reiterates its recommendation that the DPE must also be proactive and
persuasive in collecting, collating and monitoring the performance and progress of the guidelines for PSE. In this regard the Committee further recommends that
the DPE must undertake thematic consultancies and studies, seminars and workshop on the issues concerning PSEs more regularly. And that the Planning
Commission should be approached to allocate more funds for this purpose. The DPE must also conduct annual survey of allocate more funds for this purpose. The
DPE must also conduct annual survey of the State PSEs with the help of Institute of Public Enterprises, Hyderabad. The Committee also recommends that
Institute of Public Enterprises, Central Manufacturing Technology Institute, Bangalore should be brought under the administrative control of Ministry of HI &
PE. The Department must also contribute funds to the National Foundation for Corporate Governance. The Committee also recommends that DPE must be
represented on the Boards of Governors of the premier management institutes in consonance with the autonomy of these institutes. The Committee believes that
greater interaction with the professional academia will help the DPE to evolve modern management practices for the PSEs. The Committee suggests that DPE
should contact these institutions to conduct periodic surveys on the constraints faced by the PSEs and bring out recommendations that could become a useful input
for the BRPSE.
             (Para No. 1.4)

Reply of the Government
 
2.         DPE is nodal Department in respect of CPSEs for issuing non-financial guidelines.   DPE  guidelines  are advisory in nature whereas presidential directives are in the
nature of mandatory. DPE has also submitted a proposal to Planning Commission for providing funds for undertaking thematic consultancies and studies, seminars and
workshop on the generic issues. The proposal also includes requirements on account of annual survey of state PSEs to be conducted by Institute of Public Enterprises,
Hyderabad. DPE has already taken up the matter with Ministry of Human Resource Development for transfer of IPE, Hyderabad. to this Department.. With regard to
contribution to National Foundation for Corporate Governance, DPE had taken up the matter with Planning Commission. They have informed that a corpus amount of Rs.10
crore has already been sanctioned through Ministry of Company Affairs when it was set up. Further the matter is being taken up with the Department of Industrial Policy &
Promotion for transfer of Central Manufacturing Technology Institute, Bangalore  under the administrative control of Ministry of HI&PE. DPE has already taken up the
matter with the Ministry of HRD for inducting a nominee of DPE on the Board of Governors of Indian Institutes of Management. Secretary(HI&PE) has already been
inducted on the Board of Governors of IIM Kolkata.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
3.         The Committee considers that DPE’s guidelines must have the force of a Government’s policy and not remain only an advisory where implementation is
voluntary.   The DPE must therefore jointly monitor the implementation and performance of its guidelines with the administrative Ministries/Departments and
collect and analyze the data accordingly. Without regular monitoring such guidelines will remain as ineffective.
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
 
4.         In view of absence of Department’s specific reply on the query regarding the impact of costly courses of ICPE and also considering the depleting
membership of the ICPE, the Committee feels if the erstwhile members of ICPE did not consider the organization as worthwhile, the rationale for continuing with
the costly contribution should be more robust than were survival of a moribund organization. The Committee therefore, desires DPE to review its stand on ICPE
and inform the Committee the outcome thereof.
(Para No.5.3)
Reply of the Government
 
5.         International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE) was founded in 1974 on the initiative of the UN for promoting public enterprises in developing countries. It
is an inter-governmental organization of developing countries for improving the performance of their public enterprises, a strategic instrument of economy and social
development. The ICPE has now been mandated to promote and support enterprises development in the developing and transitional economies with a view of fostering their
economic development in the regional and global context. India is a founder Member Country and it gives contribution to this organization as a member country. The
financial position of ICPE has deteriorated mainly on account of non-payment of annual contribution by the Member Countries and depletion of its membership. The new
Director General has attempted to revamp the organizational set up of ICPE. A drive has been launched to vigorously follow up with the defaulting Member Countries for
payment of their membership fee. After restructuring activities of ICPE, the Standing Committee of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) of operation of this organization has been
enlarged and it is now focusing more on transitional economies and enterprises in both public as well as private sector. The Ambassador of India for Slovenia  strongly
advocated for the strengthening of the financial position of ICPE. The strengthening of the organization will provide a link between Slovenia/European Union and South
Eastern Europe with India and South Asia in particular and developing countries in general. The Slovenian experience of economic reforms and transmission to market
economy has considerable relevance for  countries of EU and other European countries that are seeking membership. The importance of Slovenia has considerably enhanced
as it would be tipped of for the President of EU in 2008. In view of this it has been decided to continue with the membership of ICPE for the time being. However, a matter
could be reviewed after next General Assembly & Council Meeting of ICPE likely to be held in November 2007.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
6.         The Committee considers that the Indo-Slovenia or Indo-EU relations are at different bilateral plains whereas ICPE is a multilateral institution.    The
argument that a costly membership of the ICPE was significant to sustain and strengthen the essentially bilateral relations with   EU, whose Chairmanship were to
be assumed by Slovenia, is facile and far fetched.  Keeping in view the depleting membership of ICPE, the Committee does not find Ministry’s reply convincing.

The Committee desires that the outcome of November meeting of General Assembly and Council of ICPE may be informed it.
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
 
7.         The Committee observes that over and above annual contribution an amount of Euros 15450 (about Rs. 8 lakhs per candidate) is spent on every candidate.
The Committee feels that performance of the Company must justify this expenditure. However no assessment based on tangible benchmarks regarding the impact
of such courses was given to the Committee. The Committee considers such cost-benefit assessment is essential given the financial stakes involved in such training.
The DPE may inform the Committee if such an assessment has at all been formulated. The DPE must initiate a survey of the efficacy of ICPE training.
(Para No. 5.5)
 
Reply of the Government
 
8.         The ICPE designs, develops and imparts tailor made and standardized programmes to meet the requirements of Managers and Administrators. These programmes are
offered to Civil Servants, Executives and Entrepreneurs in the Public and Private Sector. India is a founder member country. Besides, in the field of management
development and training, ICPE regularly conducts an International one year MBA programme  for practicing managers and policy makers of organizations from various
countries in which India has been taking an active part. So far, about 250 executives from PSEs, Government of India and other organizations in India have availed the
benefits of this programme . Training is a part of carrier of Executives of CPSEs. DPE has requested Chief Executives of CPSEs who had sent their executives for MBA
programmes to ICPE to indicate the efficacy of the programme.
 
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
9.         The reply does not respond to the Committee’s query about a cost benefit assessment of such courses given the high financial stakes involved in training.
The Committee reiterates that such analysis is essential for the continuance of such programme.   The Committee should be informed of the basis of such an
anlysis.
 
Observation of the Committee
 
10.       The Committee finds the reply too general without any specific information. Given the up gradation of tools and machines and increasing computer-based
automation it is necessary that the supervisory and lower levels of workers must be trained to align their skill sets with new modifications on floor shops and in
production processes. Absence of such skill upgradation will seriously jeopardize the redeployability of the workers and may cause redundancies leading to
possible protest against modernization, which in itself is essential for retaining competitive edge in the open market. The Committee is constrained to note that
while  DPE and concerned PSEs facilitate expensive trainings for middle and higher management levels, the lower cadre remains vulnerable to changes in
company structures and modernization in technology due to lack of regular training. A fact glaringly borne out by the number of rationalized employees in these
cadres and low redeployment rate of employees even after CRR Scheme. The Committee finds such large redundancies a telling example of poor HR management
practices and lack of sufficient emphasis on training/skill upgradation and therefore recommends a more structured approach to this issue. The DPE should
formulate comprehensive guidelines in this respect in consultation with the stakeholders and independent resource agencies. The Committee feels that HR
management should be held accountable for large redundancies in the PSEs resulting in large liability towards VRS/VSS cases.
(Para No. 6.3)
 
Reply of the Government
 
11.       The Department of Public Enterprises conducts Executive Development Programme relating to issues of CPSEs in collaboration with Premier Management
Institutions in the country. Training is being conducted by respective CPSEs for various categories of employees keeping in view of the requirement of technology. Based on
the recommendation of the Committee, the management of CPSEs was advised to take immediate action for the training of their employees. CPSEs have informed this
Department about the steps taken by them in this regard. They conduct training programmes  as per their requirements. In the competitive environment up gradation of
technology is single important factor which can not be ignored by any enterprise. Technology up gradation necessitates training in shop-floors. SCOPE being an apex body

of CPSEs  is being consulted to formulate  comprehensive guidelines for Skill Development / training programmes  specially for shopfloor employees of CPSEs, supervisors
and workmen.
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
12.       Committee may be informed of the outcome of consultations with SCOPE on formulating comprehensive guidelines of Skill Development/ training
programme for shop-floor    employees, supervisors and workmen. 
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
13.       The Committee recommends that DPE must collect full information as sought by it to give a complete picture of the redundancies and its social cost. The
DPE must maintain dis-aggregated information regarding VRS optess and monitor the trend. Such high redundancies are indeed a telling remark of the poor HR
management in the PSEs. On one hand the PSEs have to borrow from the Government and open market to liquidate the costly VRS and statutory dues of the VRS
optees on the other hand further money is spent on their training under CRR which in any case does not result in redeployment. However, no apparent efforts
have been made to upgrade the skill sets of these workers. The Committee observes that the DPE, concerned PSEs and the administrative Ministries have been
rather insensitive towards redeployability of VRS/VSS optees and corrective measures have to be taken in this regard.
 
(Para No.7.4)
 
Reply of the Government
 
14.       Manpower restructuring in CPSEs is a continuing process. Therefore, VRS in CPSEs is to continue in future. Under the CRR Scheme training on skill development
and entrepreneurship development is imparted to VRS optees. It is to be kept in view that CRR Scheme basically deals with negative consequences of manpower
rationalization and aims at rehabilitation of VRS optees of CPSEs. Under the Scheme VRS optees upto 58 years of age are covered. At the fag end of the career it is difficult
for the individuals to get finance from banks in absence of collateral guarantee and start a business or take up a new employment and support the family. As such, the
existing average rate of redeployment of around 42% should be considered satisfactory. V.V. Giri Institute which evaluated the Scheme in the year 2004 has also mentioned
that the rate of redeployment is quite commendable. Dependants of VRS optees are proposed to be included in the CRR Scheme. Belonging to a younger age group they
would be more keen and capable to go through intensive skill development or entrepreneurship development training to engage themselves in self-employment activities.
The CRR Scheme is being reviewed in 11
th Plan for bringing out further improvements.
 
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations -IV
 
15.       Committee may be informed of the final outcome of the  proposal to  include younger  dependents of VRS optees.            The Committee may be provided a
tabular presentation of the age wise  break up of the VRS optees  vis a vis CRR trainees so as to indicate their redeployment.   The Committee has also taken note
of the fact that since 2002-03 VRS incidents in Non-executive cadre is much higher then Executive and Supervisory  cadres combined.
 
16.       It has also been observed that VRS among Executives has been highest in Schedule A and B as compared to Schedule C and D Company.  The Committee
would like to have DPE’s view over such a trend.    Similarly the VR has been highest from the PSEs in sunrise areas like petroleum, telecom, Coal, Steel which are
opening up for private players.  Some of such PSEs are profit earning.     In case of NTC the incidence of VR in the maximum, the gap between Executives and Non
Executive Cadre is the maximum.  Considering that textile sector is a labour intensive sector, such trends  reaffirm the view that manpower rationalizations has
taken place at the peril of semi skilled and skill non executive workers of PSEs.
 
 
Observation of the Committee
 
 
17.       Despite an elaborate monitoring mechanism to review the performance of CRR Scheme, the Committee observes the gap between the VRS optees and the
CRR trainees and the redeployed employees. With less than half employees trained getting redeployed, the performance of the Scheme is indeed doubtful and
corrective measures need to be taken thereon.

(Para No. 7.8)
 
Reply of the Government
 
18.       The position in regard to redeployment of VRS optees has been explained in reply to para 7.4.  above. Based on suggestions of Planning Commission, further
modifications have been proposed in the CRR Scheme. The modified proposal is being considered by the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC).
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
19.       The Committee may be informed of the decision of the Expenditure Finance Committee on such modifications.
 
Observation of the Committee
 
20        Keeping in view the importance of retraining and redeployment of the VRS optees to avoid any financial hardship due to manpower rationalization, and
that most of the nodal agencies are Government run, the Committee feels that real test of  the efficacy of this lies in the  redeployment of the trained employees.
Lack of efficacy of the Scheme is brone out by the fact that none of some 1100 trainees of four nodal agencies namely CDAC, Mohali; CIPET, Guwahati; SISI,
Chennai and SISI , Indore could be redeployed. The performance of most of the nodal agencies has remained indifferent despite significant allocations by DPE
under the CRR Scheme. The Committee recommends that DPE should redesign the scheme commensurate with the requirements of the job market. The
Committee also directs the DPE to extend the coverage and scope of the Scheme to include one of the dependent of the VRS optee. Further the DPE must ensure a
better performance from nodal agencies in redeployment and link the allocation with the performance.
(Para No.7.19)
 
Reply of the Government
 
21.       The proposed modifications in CRR Scheme lay greater emphasis on redeployment.   The separated VRS optees and their dependants if combined together would
have higher level of skill which will yield more productivity as well as adaptability in the changing environment. More market oriented trades would be pursued and
inclusion of unemployed spouses and family members of VRS optees is likely to result in higher redeployment.
 
Observation of the Committee
 
22.       The Committee is of view that the Planning Commission should have given adequate reasons for reducing the funds  from the CRR Scheme which is important to
fulfill the Government’s commitment with the VRS optees. In its previous reports the Committee has been recommending to expand the scope of the CRR Scheme to cover
the families of the VRS optees to raise the family income, instead the Planning Commission has even reduced the allocation. The Committee finds the reduction
unacceptable. Instead the Committee recommends that the Scheme should be accordingly redesigned to increase its coverage and scope.
(Para No. 7.20)
 
Reply of the Government
 
23.       Planning Commission have provided budget allocation of Rs. 10 crore for CRR Scheme for the year 2007-08. CRR Scheme is under review for the 11 th Plan period.
The Scheme is to be reviewed by the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC). After review by EFC, allocation for 11th Plan will be approved.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
24.       Committee may be informed of the outcome of review by EFC and Planning Commission.  The Committee also recommends that the performance of the
Nodal Agencies in producing the redeployment to the trainees, be reviewed.
 
 
Observation of the Committee

25.       The Committee recommends that the PSEs should impart on-job or in-campus training for skill upgradation  or vocational training to its employees to facilitate a
smoother transition to new vocation. The Committee further recommends that the HR Department of the concerned PSE should be made accountable and responsible for the
VRS optees not availing the CRR Scheme. The gap between VRS optees and CRR trainees and their redeployment suggest that the PSEs are seriously lacking in their
efforts. The Committee recommends that beyond customary communication with the PSEs and the Ministries, the DPE must make pro-active efforts to persuade the PSEs
about CRR Scheme.
(Para No. 7.21)
 
Reply of the Government
 
26.       PSEs have been advised to counsel VRS optees even before they actually quit the organisation. Some of CPSEs have taken initiative to get the counselling session
conducted within the premises of the company itself. However, wherever there is sporadic voluntary retirement, the optees sometimes contact the Nodal Agency directly also
and take advantage of the Scheme. It has also been seen that all those who are counselled  do not take up training as it might not suit the temperament of all the VRS optees.
Hence, there is a gap between the number of VRS optees and number of CRR trainees.
 
27.       As regards redeployment, it may be emphasized that short duration training towards the fag end of the career may not be expected to achieve 100% redeployment.
Only the enterprising among the VRS optees really take advantage of the Scheme, the training imparted by the Nodal Agency and set up a self employment unit or takes up
wage employment. It must be kept in mind that VRS optees are generally 50 years and above and sometimes it may be difficult for them to start a new unit.  DPE is making
efforts to sensitize CPSEs towards the need to counsel and train the VRS optees. The modifications in the existing Scheme and newly introduced interactive web enabled
software will have a positive effect on the VRS optees.
 
Committee’s Further Recommendations
 
28.       The Committee takes note that DPE by its own admission is not optimistic about the efficacy of the CRR Scheme.  Considering the fact that number of non
executive VR is much higher than the Executives, it must be assessed if executives too opt for CRR Schemes and if so what is the rate of their redeployment.  It is
disturbing that the skilled and semi-skilled non-executive cadre of the PSEs are not able to deploy their skills in open market.

upgradation, conservation of resources etc. (through exposure visits, training programmes , seminars, delegation to domestic and international trade exhibitions, technology

15.       The Committee also desires to know the background behind the revamping of Jamnalal Bajaj Central Research Institute (JBCRI) (now known
as Mahatma Gandhi Institute For Rural Industrialization).
(Para 6.5)
16.       The JBCRI had its roots in the All India Village Industries Association set up by Mahatma Gandhi in 1934 in the same campus, where he stayed for two
years before shifting to Sewagram. It was re-christened as JBCRI in 1955 with the objectives of conducting research, extension, training programme, etc., for
village industries units such as oil, pottery, handmade paper, etc., and to solve their problems relating to technology, productivity, etc. The JBCRI was expected
to serve as a link between national laboratories and small research institutes in the KVI sector. No major R&D project was undertaken at the institute after 1976
and, therefore, KVIC in 1976 decided to close the activities of JBCRI.  Some staff were also retrenched and the remaining activities were taken up by the
relevant Industry Directorates of KVIC under its S&T schemes. Some of the staff also left in between when they got better options in other organisations. 
However, some training activities were continued at JBCRI, Wardha to utilise the available infrastructure. Several Committees were constituted to look into the
working of the JBCRI. The Bhagwat Saboo Committee (1994) recommended the setting up of an independent autonomous body with the Minister-in-charge of
Village Industries of Government of India as Chairman of the body.

17.            Accordingly, in 1999, the KVIC decided to revamp the JBCRI, convert it into a society (autonomous body) registered under the Societies Act, 1860 and re-name it as the National
Institute for Rural Industrialization (NIRI).  The proposal for creation of autonomous body could not be pursued further at that point of time (September 2000) due to ban on creation of any new
autonomous body in that financial year.  However, the Standing Finance Committee (SFC) under the Chairmanship of Secretary (SSI&ARI), at its meeting held on 30 October, 2000, approved the
revamping of JBCRI with professional back-up of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), New Delhi at a cost of Rs. 8.35 crore on 29 March 2001.  The IIT, Delhi was engaged for this purpose on
a turn-key basis for a period of 3 years, starting May 2001.

20.       The Committee is also not sure whether the Coir Relations Committee  constituted to   assess   and  review the   ground realities did  something
to address the problems.  The Committee may be apprised of the measures taken by this Committee alongwith the  outcome thereof.
 (Para 8.5)
 
 21.      The Coir Relations Committee was constituted as per the request of the coir trade associations representing various sectors of the traditional export
oriented coir product manufacturers.   On the implementation of liberalisation policies by Govt. of India, the Minimum Export Price and Purchase Price
Enforcement scheme that had been in operation in the coir industry was withdrawn.  The exporters engaged in the export of coir and coir products had been
sourcing their requirements for export from the small scale producers at the Purchase Price fixed by Coir Board.  On the suspension of the Purchase Price, the
procurement prices were slashed by the exporters to such a level that it became no longer remunerative for the small scale producers.  This led to the creation of
a non congenial atmosphere in the sector leading to frequent agitations. In this juncture, as per the request of the small scale producers and exporters, Coir
Board constituted a Coir Relations Committee with the representatives from Exporters' Associations and Small Scale Producers and Trade Unions to negotiate
and fix a fair price for the materials procured by the exporters from the small scale producers.  The meetings of the Coir Relations Committee were convened at
regular intervals for resolving the problems related to the traditional export oriented coir sector. The problems were discussed across the table in the presence of
the Chairman, Coir Board and decisions were taken which were binding on both the parties.   Prices are being revised in accordance with the production cost,
raw material price etc. and the last revision was made during the month of July, 2006.  The Committee acted as a forum to discuss and resolve the problems
faced by all the stake holders engaged in the export oriented production sector and this resulted in the creation of a harmonious atmosphere in the Industry. The
frequent agitations by the small scale producers and coir workers in the sector could be averted as a result of the involvement of this Committee and
consequently the export sector were be made free from any threat for meeting their commitments.   The handloom mats, being the largest item of export, both in
terms of quantity and value have been increasing during the last five years only due to this intervention promoted by the Coir Board. 
 
22.            The Committee notes that this year the targets for export has been raised by more than 20% in terms of value.  The Committee desires to know to what extent it would benefit
the coir producers.
(Para 8.7)
23.       During the year 2006-07, the actual export of coir and coir goods was 1,68,755 tones  valued at Rs.605.17 crore against a target of Rs.572 crore. This
represented an increase of 24 per cent in quantity and 19 per cent in terms of value over the exports achieved during 2005-06. Export of more coir and coir
products result in demand of the products to go up and lead to in small scale manufacturers getting more orders from exporters. Exporters' turnover and profit
will also go up.  Ultimately, the workers get more employment. At present, the employment available in the coir sector is only around 100 to 150 days
annually.  As a result of increase in the export, the workers would be getting more days of work besides enabling more workers getting absorbed by the
industry. More than 80 per cent of the workforce in the industry are women. Added profit to exporters and manufactures lead to reinvestment of the same in the
coir industry and this in turn leads to additional utilisation of the basic raw material - coconut husk.

34.       While communicating the annual targets to the States/UTs and RBI, a quarterly schedule is also circulated for sanctions and disbursements under
PMRY.  In a few cases, the disbursement spills over the next programme year and the cut off date is extended on the request of certain States/UTs
Governments. The reasons for spill over are non completion of full disbursements for formalities by the applicant, change of activity by the applicant after
recommendation by the Task Force and lack of infrastructural facilities, etc. In a recent communiqué to all State/UT Governments, Secretary (MSME) has
instructed that all the members of the Task Force Committee would collectively be responsible for selection of beneficiaries. This would ensure that the Bank
Manager alone shall not be responsible for the Non Performing Assets (NPAs) if any and thus it is expected that disbursements would be done timely.

and RBI to avoid spill over of disbursements by planning and monitoring the implementation process more diligently and sufficiently in advance from 2007-08.

institutions working in the North-Eastern Zone, which is less than 2% of the total number of all India institutions in the khadi field. Therefore, there is
an imminent need to establish new KVI institutions in the North-Eastern region. The Committee accordingly, recommends for a special drive for
developing new KVI institutions in the North-Eastern region. Secondly in order to bring effective management and organization in the khadi field in
the North East region, reputed khadi institutions from other parts of the country like Bihar, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh etc., requires to be
encouraged to bring in their managerial cadre/Khadi Karyakartas, who will train the local artisans in khadi work and also provide help in marketing
of khadi etc., if require, some special grants can be earmarked for this purpose.
 
(Para 5.14)
 
2.          As stated in paragraph No. 5.10 above, there are 65 khadi institutions registered with KVIC and State KVIBs in the NE Region. To improve the khadi
activities in the NER, a   Zonal   Level Committee under the Chairmanship of Member, KVIC, North Eastern Zone (as per the KVIC (amended) Act, 1956) has
been constituted to review and monitor the implementation of schemes/programme and to provide feedback to the Commission on the problems and difficulties
faced and suggestions made by banks, voluntary agencies, artisans and others engaged in the operation of the programmes of KVIC. Representatives of each
State KVIBs of the States, Zonal Dy. Chief Executive Officer, State Directors of the Zone, Zonal or Regional manager of the lead banks operating in the zone
and representative of an institution of repute working for at least ten years in KVI sector are the members of the Committee.
 
3.         In addition, relaxation on ban of registration of new khadi institutions has been given for the khadi institutions situated in NE Region.
 
4.         Efforts have also been initiated by the KVIC to motivate khadi institutions/ khadi workers from other parts of the country, especially from Bihar, Uttar
Pradesh and West Bengal to depute their expertise for development of khadi activities in NE Region. These will be pursued seriously.
 
 
5.         The Committee welcomes the proposals for the development and promotion of mega clusters in the States of Kerala,Tamil Nadu, Andhra
Pradesh, Karnataka and Orissa.  The Committee desires that similar clusters should also be promoted in other States which are growing coconut like
Gujarat, Tripura and Goa etc. in a time  bound manner.  The Committee impresses upon the Coir Board to ensure that these clusters prove to be
booster  in not only in increasing the production but also improve the quality of products.
 
(Para 10.3)
 
 
Further Recommendation
71.            The Committee further recommends that KVIC should play a key role by pooling the resources of developmental agencies through its vast network of NGO’s by convergence
activities which would definitely give tremendous confidence and better life to the people in N.E. region.

6.         The Board has proposed a new scheme viz. Rejuvenation, Modernisation & Upgradation of Technology in Coir Industry with an outlay of Rs.1654
crores during the 11th Plan period.  Under the Technology Upgradation programmes, six mega clusters are proposed to be implemented in the major coir
producing States of the country inclusive of one in the North-East region.  The Board is also the Nodal Agency for implementing the cluster development
programme "Scheme for Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI)" with an outlay of about Rs.1 crore for each cluster. So far 26 coir clusters
(covering the States of Gujarat, Tripura, Goa, West Bangal, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshdweep, Pondicherry and Assam) have been approved by the Scheme
Steering Committee of SFURTI for their development. Out of these, 01 coir cluster from Gujarat , 01 from Tripura, 01 from Goa.   The scheme is under
implementation.  The cluster development programme includes Development of Production Infrastructure, Common Facility Centres, Market Linkage
interventions etc.  The Common Facility Centres envisaged under the Cluster Development Programme are exclusively for improving the quality of the
products produced by the units functioning in the cluster area.   The market linkage intervention will facilitate exploration of new market avenues for the
products produced by the units which inter-alia improves the production.   Therefore, the mega clusters as well as the clusters under SFURTI are for improving
the production as well as improving the quality of the products produced by the units. 
 
 
7.         As regards the Science & Technology Programme which is a continuing plan programme of the Coir Board, the Committee feels that  
consistent efforts are to be made towards technology upradation, product diversification, introduction of pollution free processing technologies etc. 
The Committee feels Board’s extension service programmes are needed by the Industry.  The Committee therefore, desires the Coir Board  to take the
necessary steps.
(Para 10.4.)
 
 
8.         The Coir Board has got an Extension Service Wing at Central Coir Research Institute (CCRI) and there are three Extension Service Officers positioned.
The 4 Regional Offices of the Board at Bangalore, Pollachi, Rajamundry and Bhubaneswar are also carrying out extension work on the technologies developed
by the CCRI. Laboratories have been set up in the Regional Offices for testing "coirpith" and preparation of "pith plus" to cater to the requirements of the
industry and to demonstrate the process of composting. A programme  is being undertaken  in collaboration  with the Department of Rural Development, Govt.
of  Kerala,   for construction of village  roads using coir geo-textiles in the  State of  Kerala  during  the extension  service  programme in the CCRI.  The CCRI
will also  provide  necessary  assistance   in terms  of technical  advise  for selecting  the  proper  geotextiles for unpaved roads. Collaborative  projects  have
been undertaken  with the Indian  Institute   of Technology,  New Delhi to work on construction of unpaved  roads in the village  of Andhra Pradesh  so as to
popularize  the use of coir geotextiles   in the construction  of village roads. Two more projects   will be undertaken  to construct  such village roads  in Tamil
Nadu and Orissa  in collaboration  with   reputed  institutions.
 
9.         The  demonstration   of composting  of coir pith will be  undertaken in various  parts of the  country  through Regional Offices  and the ‘oil-in-water 
technology’  is being  popularized  in all the coir  producing  states in the country  through the Extension   Service staff  and the Chemistry   Department of
CCRI. A  programme  is being undertaken in collaboration  with National  Research  Development  Corporation, New Delhi to  distribute  necessary equipment 
to 50 Co-operative societies in Kerala so as to popularize  the  Zero Effluent Process preparation of coir fibre for spinning.

7.         The Committee observed that with a huge investment and waivers to the tune of Rs. 3573.44 crores, almost all the PSEs
relapsed into losses within couple of years of  their  revival. The Department of HI informed that the main reasons for the PSEs
relapsing into losses were lack of remunerative orders, working capital shortage, technological obsolescence, erosion in their
competitiveness, excess  manpower etc.
 
8.         The reply of D/O HI indicated that the revival was neither comprehensive enough to improve technological profile and
working capital constraints nor was it able to improve the competitive prospects of the PSEs which continued to rely upon the
Government and its PSEs for orders in a scenario where Government was itself opening up.

9.         During the year 2006-07, the PSEs under DHI recorded a growth of 26.65%.  In the last  year, 2007-08 (upto Feb’08) these
PSEs have clocked a growth of 14.52%.  However Auto Industry in the year 2007-08 had shown a decline of 2.3% in financial
terms.  As regards capital goods, growth in April’07 – Jan’08 has been 18.3% as compared to overall industrial growth of 8.7%.

53.       In addition to presentation and classification of Demands, the Committee has repeatedly observed that the explanatory notes
at the end of Demand did not explain the context and content of the allocation. The explanatory notes on the PSE are prepared
without any reference to the annual budgetary provision.  Previously too, the Committee in its 169
th the Report had raised objection
to such deficient explanatory notes and the Ministry had accepted Committees reservation in its Action Taken Note. Yet the situation
remained unchanged even in the Demands for 2008-09.
 
54.       The Committee also came across several instances of unexplained differences in figures provided in the Statement of Budget
Estimates (SBE) and those provided by the Department in its background notes.
 
55.       The Committee takes very serious note of inexplicable ambiguities in presentation, classification of Demands and
mistakes in the figures provided by the Department. The Committee takes cognisance of the reply presented by the Ministry
of Finance which concedes that while classification on the basis of Capital and Revenue expenditure was a constitutional
requirement adding to it another sub classification of Planned and Non-planned expenditure, just because it has been in
vogue and institutionalised has led arbitrariness, which even the representatives of the Department have found difficult to
elaborate. In absence of a convincing reply from the Department, the Committee gets an impression that the Department
and its relevant wing too could not comprehend the current format of classification. Absence of any standardised definition
of the four hybridised categories obviously has serious consequences and may have resulted in arbitrariness. The Committee
in agreement with the observation made in the Economic Survey regarding Planned and Non-Planned expenditure.  It is the
considered opinion of the Committee that once the Budget is approved by the Cabinet for the presentation to the Parliament,
it is superfluous to indicate in the SBE the approval of Planning Commission or any other expert body to individual
expenditures. The Committee therefore feels that if a classification can not be explained even by the representatives of the
Department and the Planning Commission, it must be done away with. The Committee recommends that in view of the reply
from the Ministry of Finance and the observations made in the Economic Survey,  the Financial Advisor to the Department
must persue with the Ministry of Finance to stop an institutionalised  practice in favour of constitutional requirement.
 
56.       The Committee also recommends that the explanatory notes instead of being generic ones, should be prepared in
context of the allocation to a particular PSE, Scheme/programme.

80.       Cess funds were being used to create necessary infrastructure for the automotive sector.  The infrastructure created includes
facilities for testing of vehicle for the purpose of assessing their conformity to the Central Motor vehicles.   The objectives of the
Cess funded projects range from testing vehicles for roadworthiness, to testing of components and sub-assemblies from the angle of
safety and environmental protection.  Keeping in view these objectives, Cess funds have been utilized over the year to strengthen the

(i)         Silchar : Due to rehabilitation of displaced families the procurement of land at site II got delayed but now it has been

(ii)        Rae Bareilly :  Deliberations with the State Govt. of UP is still on for procurement of land at Rae Bareilly, but till date the

Affairs,  the matter has now been sorted out in a meeting chaired by Secretary, M/O HI&PE.  RLA is has been signed by the
authorized signatory in DHI and the paper possession of the land been taken.
(iv)       Pune : Permission to use the 55.75 ha of forest land for non-forest use for upgradation of ARAI under NATRIP has been
under consideration by the State Govt. of Maharashtra and Ministry of Environment & Forests, GoI.  MoEF had agreed ‘in
principle’ for the diversion of 55.74 Ha of forest land for the proposed purpose in favour of ARAI, Pune, subject to the
fulfillment of certain conditions by the Forest Department, State Govt. of Maharashtra.  It has been learnt now that the State
Govt. have furnished the compliance   report to the MoEF, Govt. of India and now a formal order from MoEF will be
conveyed to the State Govt.
(v)        Indore :  Due to rehabilitation of displaced families, shifting of water pipeline, High Tension Power line etc., the
procurement got delayed.  As of now, most of the land has been transferred to DHI.
(vi)       Chennai : Due to rehabilitation of displaced families, shifting of water pipeline, High Tension Power line etc., the
procurement got delayed.  Land has now been transferred to DHI.

equipment supply about 80% to 90% of the purchase value has to be blocked by way of LC’s the requirement of funds for opening
LC’s for the equipments tendered works out to approximately Rs 289.76 Cr. Similarly for civil works, NATIS would require about
20% of the tender value to be paid upfront as mobilization advance, which works out to Rs. 175.97 crore. Thus if necessary funds of
at least Rs. 450 crore are not budgeted for NATIS in the Annual Plan for 2008-09, the work of supply of the above equipment and
civil works will be delayed. The project implementation schedule will be jeopardized as maximum physical and financial progress is
planned during 2008-09 and 2009-10, as per the DPIR. This will obviously lead to cost escalations. Furthermore, the internal cash
flows from the centres, which were envisaged to contribute Rs. 118 crore to the project cost as per DPIR, will also get adversely
impacted. This will lead to a cascading impact on the project implementation schedule and also the financial estimates made in the
original DPIR.

Coal Gassification Project
 
143.     The Committee sought information about the status of Coal Gasification pilot project and if the BHEL and NTPC been able
to reach to a conclusion despite repeated recommendations of this Committee.  
 
144.     The Department informed the Committee that  Inter-Ministerial Steering Group (IMSG), set up by the Ministry of Power and
chaired by Secretary (Power) met in January 2003, decided that a 100 MW Coal Gasification plant a(IGCC) may be set up by BHEL
at one of the NTPC sites.  It was decided that NTPC will spend Rs.four crore per MW, BHEL will finance to the extent feasible and
the balance funds will be provided by Govt. through DHI as a grant.  The Planning Commission agreed to this as R&D financing.  
The R&D Committee set up by the Principal Scientific Adviser to Govt. of India had endorsed the technical feasibility of the
project.  In the meeting of the IMSG on 15
th Dec., 2005, it was decided that NTPC and BHEL  should come out with Detailed
Project Report (DPR) and funding of IGCC would be undertaken as already decided.   BHEL submitted the DPR in January 2006. 
BHEL’s Board had approved the approach for implementing IGCC project, including BHEL’s contribution of Rs.50 crore.  NTPC’s
expected contribution was Rs.508.6 crore at the rate of Rs.4 crore per MW.  In addition, request for grant of Rs.326.47 crore has
been made to the Government of India.
 
145.     The Committee was informed that in the IMSG meeting taken by Secretary (Power) on 21.2.08, BHEL and DHI reiterated
their commitment to abide by their earlier decision. However, NTPC articulated their stand to pay Rs.4 crore / MW only after
successful demonstration, or alternatively to share the costs on 50:50 basis together with sharing the IPR with BHEL.  BHEL has
developed this technology over the last 25 years and has a number of IPRs. Therefore, this was not agreed to by BHEL and DHI.
 
146.     During the presentation made by the BHEL before the Committee, the Chairman wondered if the present cost of Rs 4 crores
per MW was competitive.
 
147.     The representative of the Company informed the Committee the cost per MW for other IGCC plants being developed world
over ranged between Rs. 9-10 crores per MW. In comparison the technology developed by BHEL was competitive. The Committee
was also informed that the coal gasification technology will become very relevant in future as it addresses environmental issues.
 
148.     The Additional Secretary, Department of HI submitted before the Committee that:
 
149.     “It is an extremely important project for us, because it is the technology of future.  Sir, sooner or later, we are going to have
some kind of environmental convention in which we will be a party and we cannot use coal the way we are doing by having high
pollutants.  Sir, BHEL has invested a lot in the last 30 years for developing this technology.   You are quite right that this is not
commercially established as yet.  We have a long-way to go.  There are 4-5 players in the world who have developed this
technology, but not for our coal given its caloric value as well as sulphur content and other things.  Therefore, it is better that a
domestic player develops this technology, so that they would not lynch us for technology sale.  For this, BHEL required two things. 
Firstly, we want collaboration with the NTPC.  But, somehow or the other, NTPC is not very confident to come with us.  We don’t
mind that.  What we would like the Committee to help us is, all these developmental projects it involves cost and if the Government
can share a part of the cost with BHEL, it is ready to invest.  So, therefore, if NTPC is not coming, we don’t mind.  But the point is,
this technology should be established in the country and I would urge upon the Committee to support us on this’’.
 
150.     The Committee expressed is serious dismay over the delay in settling the issue between the technology developer
BHEL and the technology user NTPC, despite the fact that the technological and commercial feasibility of project has been 
assessed at various competent levels in the Government and the Government itself is ready to provide budgetary support to
the project. The Committee also took in view the competitive cost per MW produced with the technology developed by the
BHEL. Considering that the technology is suited to the quality of domestic coal and that there was a need to develop such
technology indigenously to address the future environmental issues, the Committee was agreeable to the DHI’s proposal that
in absence of NTPC, such project should be funded through budgetary support. The Committee however, expresses its
serious reservations over the intransigence shown by the NTPC for last five years.

Concluding Observations
 
204.     In conclusion the Committee expresses its serious reservation over the performance of the Department in managing
its financial affairs. That significant part of the allocation remains unspent despite seeking higher RE, indicates an avoidable
tendency of hoarding the allocations and this has been the a predominant trend as far as the DHI is concerned.  That bulk of
the  expenditure is spent in last week of the FY indicates the quality of expenditure. Going by the replies given by the
Department in respect of allocations for the revival of PSEs, it appears that entire revival process is so tentative and ad-hoc
which makes even distribution of expenditure through the financial year,  impossible. That there has been a persistent and
serious imbalance in annual Planned and Non-Planned expenditures, with Non-Planned expenditure overshooting the annual
budget estimates every year in contrast to the Planned allocations that have remained unspent in most of the cases, is an
alarming pointer to the quality of revival   of the PSEs and the sustainability of such revival. Such apprehensions of the
Committee are corroborated by the revival packages of individual PSEs. Regardless the directions of the Ministry of Finance
regarding Government’s loans to the PSEs, the revival packages are charters of waivers and concessions without any
provisions to secure the Government’s investments. With such generous waivers and Budgetary support, it was only
expected that the PSEs shall start showing profit. However, the fact is that Order book positions of several of the revivable
PSEs have already started showing decline or stagnation.
 
205.     The performance of the two major Planned schemes namely NATRIP and Modernisation of Capital Goods Sector,
has been rather unsatisfactory. The two schemes have suffered crippling delays due to administrative bottlenecks and
extraneous considerations. The Funds in case of NATRIP have remained unspent, whereas in case of Modernisation of

only undermines the recommendations of the BRPSE.

            Considering the performance of past revival efforts, the Committee is concerned over the security of fresh
Government investments in the revival of PSEs. The reply of the BRPSE does not indicate any mechanism in the revival
package to secure Government’s investment.
(Para 25)
 
 
            However, The Committee also noted that the anticipated aggregate net Profit earned by the PSEs for 2007-08  is Rs
2494.59 crores, which is significantly lower than the target of Rs. 2985.08 crores set for the year. The Committee expresses its
concern over such under achievement by the PSEs which is primarily due to steep rise in the losses earned by the PSEs.
Number of profit-earning PSEs has also come down from 16 to 15. The under performance becomes even more glaring if the
dues to the tune of  Rs 3681.73 crores that have been waived as part of revival too are added to these losses. Despite waiver of

liabilities the PSEs are not able to achieve the targets. In view of such huge waivers annual target of Rs. 3702.76 crores for
08-09 remains only notional. The Committee recommends that the Government should use waivers to benchmark the annual
profits.
(Para 30)
 
            The Committee expresses its dismay that even after the passage of one year of the Prime Minister’s initiative which he
enunciated in his address to the Conference of Chief Executives of Public Enterprises ( 8 th March 2007, New Delhi),
necessary instructions have not yet been formulated. The Committee recommends that detailed instructions on the Prime
Minister’s initiative should be formulated by the Government at the earliest.   And same may be informed to this Committee
in the Action Taken Note of the Department. The Committee also recommends that the listing should become the part of
MoU as revival envisages massive conversions of loan into equity. Such equity can be evaluated only after listing
             (Para 33)
 
 
            However no information is given to calculate the NAV of the converted equity in the unlisted Companies. Without
such information it will be difficult to compare the worth of Government’s equity investments in unlisted Companies.
(Para 36)
 
 
            In view of several PSEs that have been under the BIFR’s reference, the Committee seeks Department’s comments on
such policy option as indicated in the Economic Survey
(Para 39)
 
            The Committee takes very serious note of inexplicable ambiguities in presentation, classification of Demands and
mistakes in the figures provided by the Department. The Committee takes cognisance of the reply presented by the Ministry
of Finance which concedes that while classification on the basis of Capital and Revenue expenditure was a constitutional
requirement adding to it another sub classification of Planned and Non-planned expenditure, just because it has been in
vogue and institutionalised has led arbitrariness, which even the representatives of the Department have found difficult to
elaborate. In absence of a convincing reply from the Department, the Committee gets an impression that the Department
and its relevant wing too could not comprehend the current format of classification. Absence of any standardised definition
of the four hybridised categories obviously has serious consequences and may have resulted in arbitrariness. The Committee
in agreement with the observation made in the Economic Survey regarding Planned and Non-Planned expenditure.  It is the
considered opinion of the Committee that once the Budget is approved by the Cabinet for the presentation to the Parliament,
it is superfluous to indicate in the SBE the approval of Planning Commission or any other expert body to individual
expenditures. The Committee therefore feels that if a classification can not be explained even by the representatives of the
Department and the Planning Commission, it must be done away with. The Committee recommends that in view of the reply
from the Ministry of Finance and the observations made in the Economic Survey,  the Financial Advisor to the Department
must persue with the Ministry of Finance to stop an institutionalised  practice in favour of constitutional requirement.
(Para 55)
 
            The Committee also recommends that the explanatory notes instead of being generic ones, should be prepared in
context of the allocation to a particular PSE, Scheme/programme. 
            (Para 56)
 
            The Committee has observed a rather disturbing trend that most of the actual expenditure is made towards the last
month of the Financial Year. Further the allocations out of lumpsum allocations of Rs 400 crores meant to settle
VRS/Statutory/salary dues are made only in the very last part of the Financial year.
(Para 63)
 
            The Committee underlines that the Non-Planned expenditure is much higher as compared to Planned expenditure.  In
the FY 07-08 the Non Planned allocations have been enhanced during the RE where as the Planned allocations have been
substantially reduced. Moreover the actual expenditure till the last week of FY 07-08 shows substantial Non-Planned
expenditures. Even considering that much of Non-Palnned expenditure did not entail cash out-flow and also taking in view
that much of the Non-Planned expenditure is meant for revival of PSEs, the Committee has observed similar trend during
the previous years too ever since the new revival attempts are being made. This pattern corroborates the Committee’s
apprehensions about the quality of expenditure. Such lopsided expenditure raises questions about the revival plans. Not
withstanding the explanations given by the Department by way of shifting the onus to BRPSE, the fact remains as stark that
revival is largely about settling the liabilities through Budgetary resources instead of enhancing the capabilities of the PSEs.
The Committee cautions that the previous revival attempts made during 1990s too failed within couple of years of clearing
the books of the PSEs.
(Para 64)

            Elsewhere the Department has informed the Committee that the RE 07-08 for the Non-Planned expenditure had
increased by more than double to Rs 1203.65 crores, an increase of Rs 739.57 crores. The Committee takes serious note of

(Para 69)
 
            The Committee observes that the issue of Bonus shares of BHEL to the Government did not entail any cash out-go
nor did it entail even the notional expenditure out of Budget. Yet a Supplementary Demand of Rs. 165.76 crores was sought
that was matched with Capital Receipts. However the SBE does not indicate whether such a transaction entailed any
expenditure. Should not such an entry in the SBE be netted against the Capital receipts?  Does the SBE indicate all the other
capital receipts like Dividends, repayment of loans etc.  The Committee further wonders if a Supplementary Demand was at
all required when there was no expenditure out of Budget?
(Para 70)
 
            Further, no information has been given regarding reduction in Planned expenditure. Despite reduction the DHI could
not spend the Planned expenditure.
(Para 71)
 
 
            The Committee notes that the Planned expenditure meant for PSEs remained under utilised despite reduced RE. The
Committee is of the view that such underutilisation of even reduced allocation does indicate the quality of revival of PSEs.
 
            The Committee reiterates its concern for lack of investment in R&D despite the presence of robust private
participation in the Auto Sector. Earlier too, the Committee has impressed upon the need for private participation in
NATRIP. The Committee is of the view that the Cess fund levied on the sales of automobile can not replace the contribution
from the Auto players who will eventually use these Testing  facilities. The Government may consider greater private
participation in the NATRIP.
 (Para 82)
 
            There is yet another unexplained discrepancy in the figures. The DHI has stated that budgetary support for NATRIP
in 07-08 was Rs 255.10 crores whereas in the SBE and the Outcome Budget it is stated as Rs 200 crores. The DHI has stated
that no money was spent out of Budget allocation during 2007-08, but the table above indicates expenditure of Rs 34.63
crores. The DHI may explain such differences in figures.
(Para 96)
 
            The Committee expresses its reservation over serious under utilisation of funds by the NATRIP.  Against the Total
Plan outlay of Rs. 570.33 crores till 2007-08, only Rs 312.33 crores were actual Budget allocations, out of which only 170.11
crores have been utilised. In initial two years there has been gross under utilisation of funds. It has also been stated that   the
bulk of expenditure on the project was envisaged for 2008-09. In 07-08 too the BE of Rs 200 crores was scaled down to Rs
157 crores in RE. Even the reduced allocation remained un-utilised.  The Committee considers it to be yet another example
of hoarding the scarce funds by the Department of HI and not utilising them.  In view of the past experience with NATRIP
and also taking a view of assertion that the project would seek significant allocations in the Supplementary Demands this
year, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance alongwith Department of HI should scrupulously  follow the
progress of the project and utilisation of funds before committing any further funds in Supplementary Demands.
(Para 97)
 
            However the Committee has not been informed from where the token Supplementary Demand was relocated to
NIDC.   
(Para 101)
 
 
            The Committee expresses its serious disapproval over delay. It notes that earlier the Planning Commission’s approval
was postponed as 2006-07 was last year of the 10 th Plan. Now despite the passage of first year, only an ‘ in principal’
approval for Rs 300 crores as against Rs 860 crores has been given by the Planning Commission to a project   that is likely to
cover sectors which need urgent technological inputs. Annual requirement of Rs 129 crores has been pruned to Rs. 24 crores
with an assurance of enhancing the allocation upon approval from the competent authority. Such approval is yet to be
accorded after the lapse of three years.. Despite the Committee’s observation (7.5) in its 201
st Report regarding the
administrative delay in approval, the Planning Commission has not yet taken a final view.  On the other hand the
performance of the Department too has been lacklustre. Of Rs. 20 crores allocated in BE 07-08 and retained in Revised
Estimates, only Rs 43 lakhs could be spent. Such underutilisation of funds is yet another example of hoarding of scarce funds
by DHI and raises serious apprehensions about the  DHI’s ability to efficiently use the annual allocations. DHI has also not
informed the Committee about the partners who may join the proposed SPV with 50% partnership in this project. The

implementation and monitoring. The Committee also seeks greater information regarding the prospective partners in the
SPV.
(Para 113)
 
 
            The Committee wonders the rationale behind providing Government Loans to settle VRS dues to the same PSEs that
are able to generate Bank Finance even with the Interest Subsidy. The Committee seeks greater details from DGHI in this

  (Para 120)
 
 
            The Committee also noted that as per quarter-wise  information provided by the DHI, waiver of interest was sought
in the First Supplementary Demand in respect of  BYNL, AYCL, NIL and HPC. However, only the interest liability of Rs.
52.62 crores in respect of HPC/NPPC was waived till the February 2008.
(Para 126)
 
            Similarly, waiver of Loans in respect of NIL, BYNL and HPC/NPPC as reflected in RE 07-08 were sought in the first
Supplementary Demand in 2007. Yet as per the quarter-wise information provided by the DHI, only Rs 29.87 crores in
respect of HPC/NPPC were waived till February 2008.
(Para 127)
 
            In view of above the Committee takes strong objection to the practice of seeking Supplementary Demands in the
beginning of a Financial Year without actually utilising the same till the very end of Financial Year. The Committee
observed this recurrent trend in almost all the allocations made to the DHI.
(Para 128)
 
            The Committee also objects to the practice of keeping sundry Loans for settling VRS/Statutory and salary dues as
Planned expenditure, irrespective of the objective of such loans which may eventually be waived as Non-Planned
expenditure.
(Para 129)
 
            The Committee observed that in RE 07-08, Rs 226.43 crores were allocated towards writing down the equity in
AYCL, Rs 2.31 crores for BYNL and Rs. 8.31 crores for NIL. The allocations in these respect were sought in very first
Supplementary Demands, however as per the information provided by the DHI, such writing off was actually implemented
in the last month of Financial Year 07-08. Considering that the Competent Authority had approved revival of AYCL and
NIL in February 2007 and that writing off was implemented in March 2008, the Committee reiterates its concern over delay
in implementing the revival plans by the DHI. The Committee also expresses its serious reservations over the recurrent
pattern of spending bulk of allocations in the very last month of Financial Year. Such pattern poses question over quality
and efficiency of allocations.
(Para 135)
 
            The Committee also notes that NIL and BYNL are unlisted companies. As such what purpose could be served by
writing down the equity when its actual worth remains unknown.  The Committee may also be informed as to how the extent
of writing down the equity of an unlisted Company is determined. The Committee may also be informed about the
instructions of the M/O Finance in case of writing down of equity.
 (Para 136)
 
            Even if the conversion was only a book adjustment and did not entail cash out go, the Committee wonders that
against a token allocation of Rs 1 lakh indicated in RE 07-08, a  Supplementary Demands was sought to convert loan of Rs
116.52 crores into equity. Considering that such conversion had financial implications in terms of Government’s investment,
the full amount instead of Token amount should have been indicated in the SBE in the RE for 07-08. The Committee is
unconvinced over such budgetary practice of indicating the token amount in RE and seeks reply from the Department and
M/O Finance.
(Para 139)
 
            The Committee questions if it is proper on the part of Government to implement the revival in a way to avoid tax.
Should this at all be a consideration in a revival package.  The Committee only wonders if similar options are available to
private companies in respect of their liabilities towards FIs/Banks.
(Para 142)
 
            The Committee expressed is serious dismay over the delay in settling the issue between the technology developer
