BHEL and the technology user NTPC, despite the fact that the technological and commercial feasibility of project has been 
assessed at various competent levels in the Government and the Government itself is ready to provide budgetary support to
the project. The Committee also took in view the competitive cost per MW produced with the technology developed by the
BHEL. Considering that the technology is suited to the quality of domestic coal and that there was a need to develop such
technology indigenously to address the future environmental issues, the Committee was agreeable to the DHI’s proposal that
in absence of NTPC, such project should be funded through budgetary support. The Committee however, expresses its
serious reservations over the intransigence shown by the NTPC for last five years. 
(Para 150)
 
            The Committee notes that only Rs. 54.60 crores were spent in the Second quarter of the FY, yet the Department
sought Rs. 84.31 crores in RE 07-08. However no further allocations were made out of the lumpsum even after the RE. The
Committee finds such hoarding of Funds unacceptable. The Committee further recommends that the M/O 158.        Finance
should monitor the utilisation of funds through out the year before conceding the Supplementary Demands.
(Para 157)
 
            The Committee finds a distinct inconsistency in seeking allocations in BE for such PSEs whose revival has not yet
been approved by the Government. This is despite the fact that no fund was used during FY 07-08. The Committee takes
serious view of non-utilisation of the funds despite a lower RE. Still a lumpsum amount of Rs 21 crores is again allocated for
BE 2008-09. The Committee expresses its reservation over practice of hoarding of funds by the DHI, without any definite
proposal for expenditure.
(Para 166)
 
            The Committee also observes the uneven  release  of funds out of the Lumpsum allocation   for loans to settle
VRS/statutory dues. The Committee also wonders the rationale for same PSEs being given money to settle VRS/ Statutory
dues in every quarter. The Committee also observed that by till the last week of the Financial Year 07-08, about Rs 209
crores could be spent against the Budgetary allocation of Rs 250 crores. Considering the Department’s assertion that no
money is surrendered, it is significant that about Rs. 41 crores have been spent within the last week of the FY. The amount
spent in last week is much higher than what is spent in entire first half of the Financial Year. The Committee therefore finds
spending patterns under this scheme rather questionable. 
(Para 173)
 
            The Committee observed that while two lumpsum allocations are made  - Rs 250 crores to provide loans to settle the
VRS/statutory dues and Rs 150 crores to provide loans for the revival of the PSEs, however both the allocations are being
used to serve the same purpose of settling the VRS/Statutory/salary dues. Given the commonality of objectives of both the
allocations, the Committee wonders if there were at a need to make two distinct lumpsum allocations. The Committee seeks a
detailed rationale for retaining the two distinct allocations for largely similar objective.
 (Para 182)
 
            The Committee observed that the terms and conditions prescribed by the Ministry of Finance have been repeatedly
relaxed in case of PSEs. The Committee should be informed of the applicability of the direction issued by the M/O Finance in
respect of availing the loans by the PSEs on their revival packages considering that most of the PSEs had availed waivers
during previous revival attempt in the 1990s. The Committee should also be informed if new budgetary outlays adjust the
defaulted amount as prescribed by the Finance Ministry.   The Committee recommends that terms and conditions on the
returns on the Governments loans must be incorporated in the MoU signed by the PSEs.
(Para 188)
 
            The Committee suggests if the total of the relocations from the lumpsum allocations to individual PSEs matches up
with the Rs 250 crores and Rs 150 crores, than what is the rationale of reducing the amount in RE, considering that the RE
are meant  for the entire financial year instead of the remaining Financial Year. Such reduction in RE is therefore
misleading without appropriate explanatory details.
(Para 191)
 
 
            Considering that BRPSE had already given its recommendations in respect of most of the PSEs referred to it, the
Committee finds the reply of the Department intransigent in view of the fact that the relocations to individual PSEs out of
such lumpsum are made only towards the end of the Financial Year and that the option of seeking additional funds as per
the approved revival plan in the Supplementary Demands is always open and preferable instead of hoarding the funds. 
(Para 195)
 
 
            The Committee observed that Rs 25 crores were retained in the RE 07-08, yet only Rs 12.69 crores could be spent in
third and forth quarters of Financial Year. The Committee found the repeat of recurrent trend of retaining the inflated

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/208threport.htm[04-07-2016 13:19:23]
estimates in RE without spending the money till the last months of FY and eventually underutilising the allocation.
(Para 203)
 
 
            In conclusion the Committee expresses its serious reservation over the performance of the Department in managing
its financial affairs. That significant part of the allocation remains unspent despite seeking higher RE, indicates an avoidable
tendency of hoarding the allocations and this has been the a predominant trend as far as the DHI is concerned.  That bulk of
the  expenditure is spent in last week of the FY indicates the quality of expenditure. Going by the replies given by the
Department in respect of allocations for the revival of PSEs, it appears that entire revival process is so tentative and ad-hoc
which makes even distribution of expenditure through the financial year,  impossible. That there has been a persistent and
serious imbalance in annual Planned and Non-Planned expenditures, with Non-Planned expenditure overshooting the annual
budget estimates every year in contrast to the Planned allocations that have remained unspent in most of the cases, is an
alarming pointer to the quality of revival   of the PSEs and the sustainability of such revival. Such apprehensions of the
Committee are corroborated by the revival packages of individual PSEs. Regardless the directions of the Ministry of Finance
regarding Government’s loans to the PSEs, the revival packages are charters of waivers and concessions without any
provisions to secure the Government’s investments. With such generous waivers and Budgetary support, it was only
expected that the PSEs shall start showing profit. However, the fact is that Order book positions of several of the revivable
PSEs have already started showing decline or stagnation.
(Para 204)
 
            The performance of the two major Planned schemes namely NATRIP and Modernisation of Capital Goods Sector,
has been rather unsatisfactory. The two schemes have suffered crippling delays due to administrative bottlenecks and
extraneous considerations. The Funds in case of NATRIP have remained unspent, whereas in case of Modernisation of
Capital Goods Sector, the Planning Commission has delayed the process.
(Para 205)
 
            In view of above the Committee recommends that in additions to the observations made at appropriate places in the
Report,  the DHI must justify the allocations made the Demands, the Department must also ensure the quality and efficiency
of such expenditure.
(Para 206)
 
            In view of the experience previous years, the Committee recommends to the Ministry of Finance to scrupulously
monitor the usage of allocations before committing any Supplementary Demands. In this regard the Committee notes that
the Department does not seek cash demands in the Supplementary Demands, instead Token and Technical allocations are
sought. The Committee sought to know from where these token and technical allocations were drawn. However, no reply was
provided by the Department.  The Committee apprehends if the savings from several under-utilised allocations are relocated
in the Supplementary Demands. It is desired that the DHI should apprise the source of such savings in its future
Supplementary Demands.
(Para 207)
 
            Further, in its previous Reports too the Committee had commented upon the ambiguous classification of expenditures
and their inadequate explanation in SBE. In view of the inputs given the  Ministry of Finance, Planning Commission and the
observation made in the Economic Survey, the Committee feels that it is time that the Government must remove the existing
ambiguities which can not be explained even  by the senior representatives of the Departments.
(Para 208)

13.       The Committee noted that the Economic Survey termed the distinction between Planned and Non-Planned expenditures is illogical and dysfunctional.   It has been
recognized that such distinction gives a fragmented view of the resource allocation.   The Survey rather   found the distinction as Capital and Revenue expenditures more
significant.  Yet, in the presentation of Demands for Grants the allocations are indicated in terms of Planned and Non-Planned expenditures.   The Committee sought
Department’s comments. 
 
14.       In its written submission, the Department gave a generic reply that in the presentation of Demands for Grants, the allocations are indicated in terms of Plan and Non-
Plan expenditures as per instructions/guidelines of the Planning Commission in respect of Plan expenditure and Ministry of Finance in respect of Non-Plan expenditure. 
 
15.       However, during the oral witness before the Committee on the 2
nd April 2008, Dr. Renu Parmar, representing the Planning Commission conceded -
 
16.       “Sir, actually, this has been considered over a number of years in various working groups. In fact even as far back as in the Ninth Plan …… and this dichotomy was
considered even at that time. But in fact, there is no resolution to this issue”
 
17.       The Ministry of Finance in written submission on the issue, stated :
 
“Classification of  Government expenditure as Revenue and Capital expenditure is a Constitutional requirement  whereas classification of  expenditure as plan and Non-
plan is   non-statutory; and
 
The distinction between plan and Non-plan expenditure is essentially “ Institution  Driven”.  Plan expenditure generally refers to the expenditure provided for by the
Planning Commission out of the Gross Budgetary Support (GBS).
 
18.       The Committee takes very serious note of inexplicable ambiguities in classification of Demands. The Committee takes cognizance of the reply presented by the
Ministry of Finance which concedes that while classification on the basis of Capital and Revenue expenditure was a constitutional requirement adding to it another
sub classification of Planned and Non-planned expenditure, just because it has been in vogue and institutionalised has led arbitrariness, which even the
representatives of the Department have found difficult to elaborate. In absence of a convincing reply from the Department, the Committee gets an impression that the
Department and its relevant wing too could not comprehend the current format of classification. Absence of any standardised definition of the hybridised categories
obviously has serious consequences and may have resulted in arbitrariness. The Committee in agreement with the observation made in the Economic Survey
regarding Planned and Non-Planned expenditure.  It is the considered opinion of the Committee that once the Budget is approved by the Cabinet for the presentation
to the Parliament, it is superfluous to indicate in the SBE the approval of Planning Commission or any other expert body to individual expenditures. The Committee
therefore feels that if a classification can not be explained even by the representatives of the Department and the Planning Commission, it must be must be done away
with. The Committee recommends that in view of the reply from the Ministry of Finance and the observations made in the Economic Survey, the Financial Advisor to
the Department must peruse with the Ministry of Finance to stop an institutionalised  practice in favour of constitutional requirement.

and duty structure issues, etc., (iii) the remedial action taken in the past to address the causes of sickness, (iv) explanations on how the proposed strategies for revival seem to be

years after the implementation of the proposed  scheme, (vi) funds required for the scheme and means of financing, (vii) competitive advantages of the company after
restructuring, (viii)  sustainability of the profits and responsibility of management and staff in ensuring it, etc. The proposals submitted by the concerned administrative
ministry/department to BRPSE are either prepared or appraised/vetted by independent consultants/operating agencies. The complete proposals received from the administrative
ministry/department are circulated in advance to all the members/permanent invitees and Controller General of Accounts as well as Planning Commission. The Secretary of the
concerned administrative ministry and the Chief Executive of the concerned CPSE make presentation before the Board explaining all aspects of the proposal including
justifications for the concessions sought from Government and sustainability of the revival of the CPSE. The concerned consultants/operating agencies who had prepared/
vetted the proposal are also requested to attend the Board meeting and explain to the Board various aspects of the proposal and answer the queries raised in the meeting.
Chairman and non-official members of the Board are experts in their field. The official members and permanent invitees are from other Government departments/ agencies. The
Board discusses the proposals in detail and makes its recommendations.
 
42.       The Committee observes that with such exhaustive details on the one hand  the Board had considered and recommended 51 cases in its 56 meetings till
February 2008 inter alia it took on an average just about one meeting to consider and recommend the revival or closure of a PSE, on  the other hand the Committee
also observed with reservation the delay in making reference of BRPSE’s recommendations to the competent authority. Considering that the BRPSE includes the
Secretaries of the Ministry of Finance, Department of Public Enterprises and that it relies significantly on the inputs of administrative Departments, the Committee
finds the practice of further referring its recommendations Inter-Ministerial Group or the Committee of Secretaries as superfluous and time consuming. The views of
the Government on the BRPSE’s recommendations are further ratified by the BIFR. Often the revival packages get stuck on the issues with the State Governments
and other agencies. The Committee objects to such a practice that leads to further critical delays. On the one hand BRPSE is not provided with adequate budget to
make its own independent assessment and is made to rely upon the administrative Ministry, on the other hand its recommendations are further referred to a
collateral body of Secretaries.  In view of the Committee such a practice only undermines the recommendations of the BRPSE.  The Committee recommends that the
BRPSE should also ascertain the views of other stakeholders particularly the State/local Governments  independently before making its final recommendations.

50.       It was informed that India is a founder member of the ICPE, which was set up in the year 1974 at the initiative of United Nations. With the passage of time, a number of

received advice from Indian Embassy, Vienna for strengthening ICPE.  On receipt of advice note of Indian Embassy, Vienna the Department examined the proposal with 
Ministry of External Affairs.  Ministry of External Affairs also agreed with the proposal of this Department for enhancing the annual contribution to ICPE. After that, the
concurrence of Department of Expenditure was also obtained.  Programmes conducted by ICPE provide Indian participants’ exposure to latest management techniques and an
exposure to international environment.   It was further conveyed to the Committee that Department of Personnel & Training also deputed central government officials for
undertaking short duration and long duration programmes being conducted by ICPE.  The participants gained exposure by interacting with faculty drawn from various countries
and by having the opportunity to observe the life, institutions and system of developed Europe. They also got opportunity to visit industrial houses and international
organizations in different parts of Europe.
 
51.       Keeping in view the depleting membership of the ICPE and also bearing in view the level of participation during the last three years, when only 28 executives
from 16 PSEs attended the courses at ICPE, the Committee considers that level of annual membership fee to ICPE can not be justified when the similar courses are
available in India at the competitive cost to the company ( CTC). The Committee also observes that most of the PSEs have sent only one executive to a course at
ICPE. It is obviously led to wonder if the training of a single executive could make any worthwhile change in any PSE, except for adding to the qualification of the
individual participant. The Committee finds such an approach of piecemeal training the executives, patently faulty. 
 
52.       Furthermore, the Committee rejects the view of Ministry of External Affairs that membership of a multilateral inter-government academic organization is
required to promote what is essentially bilateral relation between the two countries. The membership of ICPE can not be justified on the basis of an objective cost-
benefit analysis. Exposure of an individual executive to the European experience can hardly be an argument for such a costly burden on the budget. The Committee
therefore recommends that while individual PSE may negotiate price/fee with the ICPE, the membership must not be a burden on the budget.

            The Committee observes that the actual expenditure, both Planned and Non-Planned, have been less than the RE for the year. The Committee should be

            The Committee takes very serious note of inexplicable ambiguities in classification of Demands. The Committee takes cognizance of the reply presented by the
Ministry of Finance which concedes that while classification on the basis of Capital and Revenue expenditure was a constitutional requirement adding to it another
sub classification of Planned and Non-planned expenditure, just because it has been in vogue and institutionalised has led arbitrariness, which even the
representatives of the Department have found difficult to elaborate. In absence of a convincing reply from the Department, the Committee gets an impression that the
Department and its relevant wing too could not comprehend the current format of classification. Absence of any standardised definition of the hybridised categories
obviously has serious consequences and may have resulted in arbitrariness. The Committee in agreement with the observation made in the Economic Survey
regarding Planned and Non-Planned expenditure.  It is the considered opinion of the Committee that once the Budget is approved by the Cabinet for the presentation

TWENTY-FIRST REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
Having been authorised by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Industry, I, Ashok Mitra, hereby present the Twenty-first Report of the Committee. 
At the mid point of the fiscal year 1996-97 widespread misgivings were being expressed 
on the uncertain state of industrial growth in the country. The rates of growth of mining, 
power generation and other infrastructure industries were significantly lower compared to 
what these were in the corresponding months of the previous year; the rate of growth of 
manufacturing too was below expectations. Stock exchanges were marked by strong bearish 
sentiments, and there was few evidence of fresh investment activity. At its meeting on 
October 29, 1996 the Committee felt that it would be useful to have a wide-scale survey 
undertaken on its behalf to examine in depth the underlying factors inhibiting industrial 
growth. It was further decided that to facilitate the survey, five Sub-Committees be 
constituted which will assume responsibility for different areas of study. One Sub-Committee 
proposed to analyse the factors inhibiting industrial groups while two other Sub-Committees 
were assigned to concentrate on the problems which directly pertain to the activities of the 
Ministry of Industry, while two other Sub-Committees were assigned to cover the area of 
functioning of the Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines respectively. 
The reports finalised by the five Sub-Committees .are placed below. The purpose of this 
brief introduction is to draw attention to some of the more salient conclusions reached by 
the Sub-Committees at the end of their labour. Each Sub-Committee thought it useful to 
visit important metropolitan cities as well as several interior centres of the country in order 
to gain insight at first hand into the problems encountered in the different spheres of 
industrial activity, both organised and non-organised. 
Sub-Committee-III studied at some length the factors which explain the slowing down of 
industrial growth in the current year compared to the trends obtained in 1995-96. While 
arriving at its conclusions, the Sub-Committee has taken into account the generally 
depressed state of industrial growth in the years 1991-92, 1992-93 and 1993-94 as well. 
According to the Sub-Committee, the drying up of the process of investment in the different 
sectors of the economy needs to be reversed as early as possible. lnfrastructural growth in 
particular has been badly affected by the lack of capital formation. This is particularly in 
regard to the power sector. The Sub-Committee is concerned about monetary policy and the 
role in general of the Reserve Bank of India has been less than 'growth-friendly' in recent 
years. In the opinion of the Sub-Committee, the State should play a more active role in 
encouraging investment across-the-board and there must be appropriate resource allocation 
so that all major projects in the State sector should be completed within a given time frame. 
The establishment of a nodal agency which will monitor investments in the infrastructure 
industries and also coordinate between public and private sector activities is, in the view of 
the Sub-Committee, worth consideration. The Sub-Committee· has, in this connection, 
referred to the gradually disappearing role of the Planning Commission in the planning of 
,savings investment and growth in the country, which it regards as unfortunate. 
Sub-Committee-! concentrated on the problems faced by the small-scale industrial 
sector. It has a number of observations concerning the issue of raising the limits of 
investment in re-defining small and tiny sectors. The latest decisions of the government have 
partially

taken care of the suggestions offered by the Sub-Committee, but perhaps a few new 
questions have reached their head. The Sub-Committee is also of the view that the 
Government has the responsibility to ensure that liberalisation carried to excess does not 
create problems of survival for the small-scale units. The Sub-Committee has comments to 
offer on the limits of commercial turnover for determining concessions with respect to excise 
duties. In this matter too, the budget for 1997-98 contained provisions which will need to be 
examined in the light of the Sub-Committees recommendations. The Sub-Committee has 
strongly U{ged for a fresh census of small-scale industrial units including those engaged in 
fulfilment of specific export obligations. It has expressed concern about the bottlenecks in 
the supply of inputs faced by the small-sector, and it wants the Government to undertake a 
s~cial review of the subsidies and other fiscal concessions to encourage further development 
in small-scale activities. The Committee has some comments to offer on the problems faced 
by the coir industry and the difficulties posed by the high interest rate structure and the 
general reluctance of the banks to offer credit. The Sub-Committee has invited. attention 'to 
the necessity to facilitate supply of gas and power, equipment to the small-scale units. 
Government agencies, in view of the Sub-Committee,_ should take an active interest in 
improving the infrastructure such, as roads, drainage, etc., in areas where the small-scale 
industries are located. It has also suggestions to offer on such issues as a more satisfactory 
integration of activities between the Centre and the State Governments. It is a matter of 
regret, the Committee feels, that several State Governments do not still have a separate 
Directorate. or Department to deal with the problems of small industries. 
Sub-Committee-IV visited the major centres of activities and operations under aegis of 
the Ministry of Mines including Hindustan Copper Limited, Hindustan Zinc Lhruted, 
National Aluminium Corporation, Bharat Gold Mines, the Geological· Survey of India and 
the Indian Bureau of Mines. It has drawn attention to the problems faced by both Hindustan 
Zinc Limited and Hindustan Copper Limited because of the progressive lowering of tariff 
barriers which have affected the marketing of products of these two major units on which 
the ·Government has invested considerable amount in the past. This issue, the Sub­
CqJ;nmittee is of the opinion must be the subject of constant review between the Ministry of 
Mines and the Mini~try of Finance. There must be augmentation of funds, the Sub­
Committee feels, both for the Geological Survey of India and the Indian Bureau ·of Mines to 
enable them expand their activities. The Sub-Committee has commented that the rates of 
duty of royalty· on non-coal items must be uniformly converted from specific to ad valorem 
as a matter of policy. It is also the Sub-Committee's point of view that the Government 
should continue to assume direct responsibility for social welfare work pertaining to the 
workers engaged in the mining areas. 
Sub-Committee-11 visited a number of major industrial centres affected by problems of 
~losure and sickness of units both in the private and public sectors. It set for itself to two 
assignments: (1) review the working of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) 
Act, 1985 as well as of the performance of the Board of Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction towards the restructuring of units in difficulties; and (2) analyse the problems 
that stand in the way of using the resources of the National Renewal Fund not for payment 
of mere 'golden hand shake' to laid-off workers but for a meaningful reconstruction. of sick 
units. 
The Sub-Committee has several comments to offer on the slow pace of work by the 
BIFR. It has a number of suggestions for reforming the Sick Industrial Undertakings Act, to 
enable proceedings before the BIFR could be speeded up and surplus land available to the 
units be made easily available for purposes of the rehabilitation of the units. It has also 

3 
suggestions on how the process of consultations within the BIFR could be telescoped. The 
Sub-Committee is firmly of the view that the resources available with the NRF should be 
deployed to revive and expand the Area Employment Regeneration Schemes. The Sub­
Committee has made specific recommendations with regard to modalities for the revival of 
units belonging to the National Textile Corporation and the North-Eastern Paper Mills 
Corporation. 
It is to be hoped that the Ministries of Industry, the Ministry of SteE!l and the Ministry 
of Mines along with their relevant departments and directorates will carefully e:xamine the 
recommendations of the Sub-Committees. They should expeditiously offer their view on 
those of the recommendations of the Sub-Committees that are easily implementable and 
those they would like to examine· further. The Committee would urge the Ministry that the 
suggestions made by Sub-Committee regarding amendments to the. Sick Industrial 
Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, reviewing the performance of BIFR and the 
restructuring of the National Renewal Fund are ex~mined in detail and the Ministry's view 
on these recommendations communicated to the Ministry of Finance. 
In any event the Committee will have a further opportunity to gc> into the issues 
covered by the reports of the Sub-Committees at the time of examination of the Demands 
for Grants for 1997~98 and the Annual Reports of the· Ministries concerned.

The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry at its meeting 
held on the 29th October, 1996, constituted five Sub-Committees including one on Small 
Scale Industry. The Sub-Committee consisted ·:>f the following:-

2. The Sub-Committee has been assigned the job of undertaking a review of the role 
played by the small scale industries, including agro-based and other rural industries in the 
context of recent developments of the country and the problems they have encountered. The 
review covers aspects of problems including the need or otherwise of re-defining small-scale 
and tiny sector activities, the policy of reservations applied toward them, a critique of 
taxation and duty structures, appraisal of schemes of financial accommodation preffered by 
banks, financial institutions and State and Union Governments. The factors underlying 
endemic problem of sickness that often visited small-scale and rural industries also formed a 
part of the study. It is often alleged that while statutory and other measures are laid down 
for protecting small-scale industries from intrusion by outsiders, including multinational 
entities, in practice the measures are flouted with impunity, which render the entire legal 
structure of protection infructuous. The issues relevant in this connection also form a part of 
the study of the Sub-Committee. 
3. The Sub-Committee met on the 18th November, 1996 and decided that a detailed 
Questionnaire be prepared covering the area of study of the Sub-Committee. The Sub­
Committee also decided to visit Cochin, Bangalore and Chennai during January, 1997 for 
the purpose of interaction with the concerned people and an on-the-spot study. A copy of 
the Questionnaire alongwith the comments of the Ministry of Industry thereon covering the 
area of study of Sub-Committee is enclosed as ANNEXURE-I. 
4. The Sub-Committee undertook the study visit to Cochin, Bangalore and Chennai 
from the 2nd to 9th January, 1997 and had interaction with (i) the representatives of ape~ 
organisations of manufacturers, .exporters and workers engaged in main small scale industries 
in the States of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; (ii) the representatives of Nationalised 
Banks, Financial Institutions, Reserve Bank of India, etc. on the availability or otherwise of 
17 

18 
finances to the small scale industries and (iii) the representatives of the Government of 
Kerala, Kamataka and Tamil Nadu, respectively, in order elicit their views on the problems 
of small scale industry in their State. The list of representatives with whom the Committee 
had interaction during the course of the study visit is enclosed as ANNEXURE-II. The Sub­
Committee also visited some small scale units at Cochin, Bangalore, Mysore and Chennai 
with a view to see their functioning and for a better comprehension of their problems. The 
list of units visited by the Sub-Committee is enclosed as ANNEXURE-III. 
5. A brief summary of the points that arose during the course of the study visit are 
contained in the succeeding paragraphs. 
I. COCIDN (2ND TO 4TH JANUARY, 1997) 
A. Discussion with Representatives of Apex Organisations of manufacturers, exporters 
and workers engaged in main small scale industries in the State on 2.1.97 
(i) Small Scale Industries in Kerala were engaged in industries based on Coir, 
Coconut, Cashew, Spices, Sea Food, Rubber, etc. 
(ii) Representatives of all categories of Small Scale Industries complained about 
the higher rate of interest on term loans and the conditions precedent to their 
grant like, furnishing of collateral securities, etc. There was a demand that the 
gestation period for the term loan should be a minimum of 2 years of which 
12 inonths should be a interest holiday. The rate of interest on term loan 
should not be more that 6%. The Export Oriented Units in small scale sector 
should be provided with level playing field when compared with Multi-nationals 
that raise loans at an interest rate of 6%. 
(iii) The existing limit on investment in plant and machinery of Rs. 60 lakhs for the 
purpose of excise exemption should be raised to Rs. 1.00 to 2.00 crores. 
(iv) The limit turnover of Rs. 30 lakhs for excise exemption should be raised to 
Rs. 1.00 crore. 
(v) In order to avoid harassment at the hands of authorities collecting Sales-tax, 
Income-tax, etc. only excise duty may be collected from small scale industries. 
(vi) Keeping in view the high cost of advertisement, there should be a central 
subsidy for the purpose. 
(vii) Testing facilities should be made available in various parts of the country at 
concessional rates. 
(viii) Cost of packing for processed foods. in India is almost 65% of the cost of 
production. Concession should be provided in excise duty for packaging 
materials for new products for atleast 2 years from the commencement of 
commercial production. 
(ix) Presently, manufacture of value added products from fresh coconut is a priority 
industry only for Industry Ministry and not for the Reserve Bank of India. This 
should be re-classified as a priority industry for Reserve Bank of India as well 
to enable the Commercial Banks to provide finance on priority basis, to new 
integrated coconut processing units.

100% Export Oriented Units (EOUs) operating outside export promotion

Reluctance on the part of financial institutions to give adequate and timely 
finance is one of the reasons for lack of development of small scale industries 
in Kerala. The Credit Deposit Ratio which is presently 45% should be raised

Small Scale Industries should be provided credit at lower rates of interest. 
Normally, 20% of the annual turnover should be made available as working

There should be an insurance scheme for the small scale industries to cover the

C. Discussions with the Representatives of the State Government of Kerala on 4.1.97 
The representatives of the State Government informed the Committee that the economy 
of the State was basically agrarian, although there had been a decline in the share of 
agriculture in the State's income in the last few years. After the announcement of the New 
Industrial Policy of 1991, the State Gpvernment have followed a two pronged strategy for 
development of industry, viz. (i) provision of requisite infrastructural support for 
establishment of industries; and {ii) extension of promotional support in the form of 
monitory and fiscal incentives, training and marketing support, etc. 
2. The State was a pioneer in setting up the Kerala Industrial lnfrastructural 
Development Corporation (KINFRA) for developing and managing infrastructure for 
industrial units. The Export Promotion Industrial Park at Kochi, Apparel Park at 
Thiruvananthapuram and the Integrated Infrastructure Township at Palakkad were some of

3. The KSIDC, the premier promotional agency for industry in the State and the KPC 
the prime lending agency for the SSI, were the two major institutions in the State sector

4. The Small Scale Sector, with around 1,54,818 registered units as on November 30,

beverages followed by textile and wood products. Major segments of small scale industries in 
the State were electronics, beedies, agarbathi, readymade garments, bakery and roofing 
tiles.

RECOMMENDATIONS 
1. The Committee notes that the limits on investment in the plant and machinery of 
Rs. 60 lakhs (Rs. 75 lakhs in the case of export oriented units) for classification of an 
industry as a Small Scale Industry were fixed quite some time back. There have been a 
demand from almost every section of the Industry with whom the Committee interacted 
during the course of the study visit for suitable increase in the investment limit. ':fhe 
Committee, accordingly, recommends that the existing limits on investment may be revised 
upward to Rs. 1.00 crore (Rs. 1.25 crore in the case of export oriented units) for the 
purpose of classifying any industry as a Small Scale Industry. 
2. The Committee notes that the limits of annual turn over of Rs. 30 lakhs, Rs. 50 
lakhs and Rs. 75 lakhs for concessions in excise duty in varying degrees were determined 
quite some time back. The Committee recommends that these limits may be revised to 
Rs. 1.00 crores. Rs. 2.00 crores and Rs. 3.00 crores, respectively, taking into consideration 
the increase in the cost of production that has taken place over the period of time. 
3. The Sub-Committee notes that the problems being faced by the SSI are numerous. In 
order that the State Governments are able to pay adequate attention to these problems, the 
Sub-Committee recommends that there should be a separate Directorate or Ministry for the 
Small Scale Industry in the States. 
4. The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the fact that no census has taken 
place after the last census of Small Scale Industry which was held for the year 1987-88 and 
that the Central Ministry has no data to indicate the trends of manufacture of reserved and 
non-reserved items after the year 1987-88. The Committee feels that the Government would 
not be able to take proper decisions with regard to the promotion of the Small Scale 
Industry in the absence of basic statistics pertaining to these industries. It is also desirable 
that such statistics should be maintained at the State level even as had been pointed out by 
some of the bankers during the. course of the study visit. The Sub-Committee accordingly 
recommends that the Ministry of Industry sh9uld take immediate steps for undertaking the 
476/RS F-3-B 

29 
census of the Small Scale Industries and the State Governments may also be persuaded in this 
regard. 
5. The Committee notes with dissatisfaction that there is no clear cut machinery at 
present for monitoring whether the large/medium sector industries were complying with the 
requirement of export obligation of a minimum of the 75% of its production in case they 
create fresh capacity in an item in the reserved area. The Committee feels that non­
compliance of this condition would seriously affect the protective cover provided to the 
Small Scale Industry. The Committee further feels that obtention of a bond from the parties 
by the DGFT for the purpose of fulfilling the export obligation is not sufficient enough to 
ensure compliance. The Sub-Committee accordingly recommends that the compliance of the 
provisions of export obligation should be monitored more meticulously in the interest of the 
Small Scale Sector. 
6. The Sub-Committee is not convinced with the position as stated by the Ministry of 
Industry that there is no distinction between reserved and non-reserved items on the issue of 
exemption from excise duties. In the opinion of the Committee, relaxation in excise duty is a 
very valuable concession but the same has been denied to the industries engaged in the 
manufacture of reserved items. The Sub-Committee feels that the existing practice negates 
the very concept of reservation of items for the Small Scale Sector. The Sub-Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that the Government should review this aspect and see if 
concessions in excise duty can be allowed on the basis of the criteria whether an industry in 
manufacturing an item in the reserved list. 
7. The Sub-Committee notes that the laws framed by Government for the protection of 
SSis are not being properly implemented. The Sub-Committee accordingly, recommends that 
the SSis should be protected from undue competition on account of the entry of big companies 
in the sphere of activities reserved for Small Scale Sector. The Sub-Committee further 
recommends that areas reserved for SSI must be vigorously monitored against encroachment 
by MNCs and large companies and severe action must be taken against the infringing 
company. It not only harms the cause of SSI but it violates Indian laws as well. \ 
8. The Single Window Scheme deviced by Government for the convenience of SSis 
was reported not to befunctioning properly. The Sub-Committee, accordingly, recommends 
that the bottlenecks in the implementation of the Single Window System may be examined 
through interaction between the representatives of the Central and State Governments and 
suitable remedial measures be taken up. Government may consider placing the Single Window 
System effective under a separate Director appointed for SSI by the Directorate which shall , 
look into all aspects ranging from registration and setting up of the unit, providing technical, 
financial and marketing assistance and coordination between the Central ·and the State 
Departments. 
9. The Sub-Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ministry of Industry had taken 
up with the Ministry of Finance in their pre-budget proposal for allowing some fiscal 
concessions to the SSis for promotion of research and development. The Sub-Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Industry should pursue this matter with the Ministry of 
Finance once again for the purpose of promotion of Small Scale Industry. 
10. The Sub-Committee during the course of its study visit noted that the SSis lacked 
the resources for undertaking Research and Development activities for upgradation of the 
technology at their own level. There was also a demand for provision of making facilities 
from the Government side. The Sub-Committee accordingly recommends that the 
Government should take more initiative for making available latest technology to Small Scale

Sector so that their products are cost effective and receptive in the market. Government 
should also take Immediate steps for enhancing marketing facilities to the SSI units.

of the work force engaged in Coir Industry are women. The Committee recommends that the 
technology being adopted in the Coir Industry needs to be modernised for the conv~nience of 
the workt!rs engaged in the industry majority of which are women.

visited by the Sub-Committee complained that they were not getting adequate financial 
support from the Commercial Banks and the Financial Institutions. Some of them also

Ahmedabad 
Textile LliliOur Association (TLA): 
6. The 1LA lamented that Ahmedabad, once the Manchester of India, has now turned into 
a graveyard of closed textile mills. Thousands of workers of the closed mills have still not 
been paid their terminal benefits forcing them to lead a miserable life.. They demanded 
immediate payment of legal dues to such workers to enable them to rehabilitate themselves.

64 
The Association also felt that the stipend for the trainees, training period and other financial 
limits put under the NRF needed suitable revision. 
State Government Omclals : 
7. It was impressed upon that the benefit of NRF should cover displaced ·workers prior to 
1991 also as it presently covers post-1991 workers. There should be a provision to train the 
children of the workers as most of the workers are quite old and relatively less productive. 
Revision of stipend and training period under the NRF was also emphasised. It was felt that 
the procedure under the BIFR was cumbersome and time-consuming and needed suitable 
amendment. Besides, the following points relating to NRF and BIFR were emphasised: 
(i) Strengthening the expertise in BIFR; 
(ii) Abolition of AAIFR due to its redundancy; 
(iii) Decentralisation of BIFR; 
(iv) Converting BIFR into Liquidation Court to avoid going to High Court; 
(v) Making cut-off dates in SICA mandatory; 
(vi) Expediting decision making by BIFR; 
(vii) Expanding the scope of NRF to cover the State level undertakings and the private 
sector units; and 
(viii) Creation of State Renewal Fund in all States by contributions from employees, 
workers, Central and State Gov~mments and financial institutions for providing 
resources for restructuring for the State level public and private enterprises and 
payment of wages and other legal dues to the employees of the closed units. 
8. The representatives of the Gandhi Labour Institute (GLI) informed that after 24th July, 
1991, 48000 workers were displaced. Among these, nearly 33,000 workers are only from 
Ahmedabad. The present scheme of NRF is applicable to this group only. 49,000 workers 
displaced between 1977 and 1990 are unfortunately not eligible for training and 
redeployment under the NRF for which there seems to be no rationale. Recently, 14,000 
workers have been rendered unemployed because of closure of GSTC Mills. Consequently, 
1.11 lakh workers have been rendered jobless in the last decade and a half. Majority of the 
workers displaced from the private sector mills have not been paid their legal dues. The GLI 
has retrained more than 5000 workers in various vocational trades during the last 18 month 
and most of them are engaged in self-employment. 
9. The representatives of GLI also highlighted the following points for a policy decision by 
the Government of India for effective retraining and redeployment scheme: 
(a) The workers who are 50-plus in age often request for nominating their dependents 
for training which should be permitted under the scheme. 
(b) There are 10% of the workers who are suffering from various types of diseases and 
1% of them are dead. There is a necessity to take a dependent from this category 
for training with the . available benefits to ensure their effective deployment to 
support the family. 
I , 
(c) Fmancial assistance to set-up self-employment by the retrained workers in view of 
poor response from the ·banks. 

65 
(d) The ideal training period should be twenty days per month for four months and for 
four hours a day. 
(e) A provision for tool kit immediately after retraining is expected to motivate workers 
to continue the work for which they have taken training. 
(f) 49,000 workers displaced between 1977 and 1990 should be covered the NRF 
scheme. This is the demand from the workers displaced before 1991. 
(g) While private closed mills have not paid legitimate dues of workers rendered 
unemployed, GSTC has paid about Rs. 250 crores to the 14000 employees now 
rendered jobless. Government of India should share this burden on the State 
Exchequer.

Mumbai 
NaUonal Bicycle CorporaUon of India Ltd. (N,CIL): 
11. The NBCIL established by Birla Group in 1939 was taken over by Government of 
India in 1974 and was nationalised in 1980, thus making it as a wholly-owned Government

12. As the Company was chronically sick, it was referred to BIFR in February, 1992.

66

scheme is evolved. The next date of hearing is fixed for 7th February, 1997. 
14. The Sub-Committee was also informed that some employees of the Company have 
also filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi against the BIFR's order of 1993,

the majority of them are likely to opt for it. ', 
NatlODIII Bicycle Karmacbarl Sangb : 
16. The National Bicycle Karmachari Sangh in its submission emphasised the following 
pointS:-
(i) The duty of every welfare state is the welfare of its people through providing jobs 
and generation of employment. Even our Constitution lays ample emphasis on this. 
Therefore, Government should make such laws which may help sick units to become 
viable and thereby generate employment. 
(ii) BIFR should be equipped with more legal powers and have the status of a full 
fledged statutory body so that its order could be binding for Promoters and other 
parties. 
(iii) BIFR should have its own team of technical/ financial experts to examine and make 
revival schemes for sick companies rather· than depending upon outside agencies. 
(iv) BIFR should consider all the reasons of sickness, such as outdated plants and 
machinery, corruption in the Management, mismanagement, etc. 
(v) BIFR should be authorised to sanction I recommend loans from NRF for revival of 
sick units. 
(vi) Government of India should protect the interests of workers by means of reviving all 
sick industrial units and guaranteeing their employment as unemployment \l}ay cause 
social unrest in the country. 
(vii) The scheme of retraining of retrenched employees should be stopped which is being 
funded from NRF because there is no point in training a qualified and trained 
worker. Instead, efforts should be to revive the sick company with the help of this 
fund. 
(viii) BIFR should be empowered to direct promoters of the Company to arrange funds 
for revival from its other units which are economically viable. 
\ (ix) BIFR's Chairman should be a Judge of the Supreme Court or any High Court. 
(x) The use of petroleum-propelled vehicles should be discouraged to reduce import of 
petroleum and the use of bicycle should be encouraged. Therefore, NBCIL and 
CCIL, Calcutta should be revived to restrict monopoly of other bicycle 
manufacturers. 
17. The Director, Centre for Workers' Management, Delhi in his submission before the 

67 
Sub-Comittee stated that the NRF has in effect been reduced to an unemployment 
generation fund. The major share of NRF funds have been used to pay for Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme in the public sector without a clear focus on the precise needs of these 
enterprises. This has not oruy resulted in the rendering of workers unemployed but also 
dearth of skilled workers in many enterprises. Very little attention has been paid to the 
schemes for re-training, redeployment and counselling and placement services under the 
National Renewal Grant Fund (NRGF) and the coverage under them is extremely small. 
The primary focus of these schemes is to develop entrepreneurship. Studies, however, 
indicate that across the world less than 1% of workers trained for entrepreneurship were 
actually able to set-up small enterprises while even fewer succeded. 
18. The Sub-Committee was also informed that the NRF has failed to make a 
meaningful contribution to sick industries. This is particularly the case where the sick 
Company was found to be viable by the BIFR and the workers were willing to take-over the 
sick Company through workers' cooperative. The workers take-over however, does not 
fructify since the workers are not able to satisfy the banks and financial institutions of their 
ability to raise finances. Necessary funds for the take-over and the rehabilitation of sick 
Companies through worker's cooperative have not been forthcoming from the NRF. 
19. With regard to the functioning of BIFR, the Sub-Committee was informed that one 
fundamental problem is the role of banks and financial institutions in the revival of sick 
enterprises, their failure to comply with the BIFR directions and the inability of BIFR to 
discipline these institutions. In a majority of cases, where workers' t~ke-overs failed to 
fructify the enterprises, was because of the fact that banks and financial institutions and the 
State Government concerned failed to provide the requisite and permissiple reliefs and 
concessions. Even where workers or their unions have managed to convince the banks and

RECOMMENDATIONS 
58. BIFR and AAIFR under Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA) 1985 and National 
Renewal Fund have been established to deal with the growing industrial sickness in the large 
and medium industries in the public and private organised sectors and for restructuring of 
the industries in India. At present the industrial sickness in India is of massive proportion 
which is eating into the vitals of Indian economy and has made India a high cost and low 
productivity economy making it non-competitive in the world market. 
59. BIFR is supposed to prevent the industrial sickness by restructuring a unit, cure the 
industrial sickness by rehabilitating and/or restructuring the unit and facilitate exit of the 
terminally sick units. The objective of establishing NRF is to provide a social safety net for 
476/RS F-6-A 

76 
the affected workers both in organised public and private sectors and the unorganised sectors. 
due to macro economic adjustment and the Structural Adjustment Programme (Government 
of India, 1991). The objectives of NRF are: 
(i) To provide assistance to cover the cost of retraining and redeployment of 
employees arising as a result of modernisation, technology upgradation, and 
industrial restructuring. 
(ii) To provide funds, where necessary, for compensation of employees affected by 
restructuring or closure of industrial units both in the public and private sectors. 
(iii) To provide funds for Employment Generation Schemes both in the organised and 
unorganised sectors in order to provide a social safety net for labour, (GOI, 1992-
93). Hence the whole endeavour of NRF is to reduce the adverse impact of the 
New Economic Policy, NRF is supposed to ensure transition from regulated 
economy to market economy with minimum adverse impacts on the people. 
60. However, most of the representations made before the Sub-Committee felt that the 
two instruments of BIFR and NRF have not been able to fulfil the objectives for which they 
were established. Therefore, there is urgent need for strengthening these two instruments by 
restructuring them so that they can deal with growing industrial sickness in an effective 
manner. 
61. At the outset, the Sub-Committee felt that BIFR has not been able to serve the 
purpose for which it was created. Meanwhile, after the New Economic Policy of 
Government of India, SICA was amended in 1991 to bring Public Sector Undertakings 
under its purview. The Act was further amended in 1994. The constitution of NRF and 
amendment of SICA to bring Public Sector Undertakings under its purview created a hope 
that the loss making and sick PSUs will now be restructured and will make profit, and these 
goals will be achieved smoothly while providing safety net to the affected workers. 
62. The expenditure of five years indicates that nothing much happened on both these 
fronts. On the contrary, the Sub-Committee during its discussion with various forums got an 
impression that because of reference to BIFR and delayed decision, Banks discontinued the 
Working Capital which these PSUs were getting earlier and crisis became friore severe. Even 
funds from NRF which by September, 1996 covered 94, 332 employees under VRS could not 
bring them out of sickness or losses. At some places complaint was received that enough 
grant from NRF was not given even though employees were willing to accept VRS. The Sub· 
Committee feels that it is worth examination that instead of spreading the coverage of NRF to 
all PSUs, whether it would have been worthwhile to concentrate on few, so that at least these 
few units would have come out of sickness. Gujarat State Textile Corporation has done this 
with the help of Government of Gujarat and had saved the State from continuous annual 
losses of GSTC. 
63. The Sub-Committee carried an impression that in the case of Tyre Corporation of 
India things would not have been that dimcult if proper attention and immediate action were 
taken.

and costly particularly for workers and trade unions. Therefore, there is need to speed up 
process in the BIFR and make it cost effective. The suggestion for this is to decentralize the 
BIFR by creating regional benches in the States where the incidence of industrial sickness is 
very high. (Suggested by RMMS Mumbai, Mr. K.N. Raval, Senior Advocate, Ahmedabad 
and Dr. S.S. Mehta, GLI, Ahmedabad). A decentralised State level BIFR will be able to 
cover , even small scale units which are at present not considered by the BIFR. Government 
should not hesitate to provide more than one bench at Delhi, if so required to expedite the 
cases and process ·thereon. 
76. The number of benches are inadequate to deal with the volume of work. As result of 
this the companies which ar.e defined as potentially sick, namely those whose networth is 
eroded by more than SO percent and not wholly, are by and large not faling the forms and 
there is inadequate monitoring process to ensure preventive work. Unless the number of 
benches are increased, this monitoring can not be done. With the decentralised State level 
BIFRs, this ina~equacy wm also be taken care of. 
77. Benches are mostly manned by retired Government servants. Goswami Committee 
bas pointed out that the members of BIFR are generalists. Most of the members of BIFR 
are retired or seconded officers from the civil services. It is necessary to associate 
professional management consultants or even functioning or retired Public Sector 
Undertakings officials, who h~ve field experience of running an industry to man the benches. 
(Mr. K.N. Raval Advocate, Dr. S.S. Mehta, Gandhi Labour Institute). In fact, Section 4(3) 
of SICA, 1985 states that BIFR members should have special knowledge an professional 
experience of not less than fifteen years in science, technology, economics, banking industry, 
law, labour matters, industrial finance, industrial management, industrial reconstruction, 
administration, investment, accountancy of marketing. 
78. The Sub-Committee also feels that as we have acceptef;l: policy of liberalisation 
with human face there should be also suitable members from' 'labour movement on these 
benches. Not only this, but at present, concerned Labour Union in neither made party nor 
called upon to appear. The Sub-Committee feels that concerned Labour Union should also be 
given opportunity to appear before BIFR. 
79. The Sub-Committee also feels that wherever in any case workers of the unit offer to 
turnaround the unit by forming Workers CooperatiiVe, BIFJ{ should give priority to such 
workers cooperative and give necessary support once such scheme is approved. 
80.· BIFR bas, by and large, appointed senior retired Government officers as its 
nominee directors on the Board of sick companies. This requires to be looked into for 
ensuring that the concerned persons take a more protective role and do not restrict their 
participation in the process of revival merely to attend the Board meetings. They should be 
called upon to continuously visit the plant and give monthly report of their visits so that the 
BIFR is kept informed of the developments in the company on a day-do-day basis. A constant 
monitoring scheme should be provided to have the best possible results. 
81. The Act provides for an operating agency to be appointed by the BIFR from the 
several financial institutions like IDBI, IFCt etc. Some of these institutions are reluctant to 
act as such because of time and other constraints. Sometimes the institutions are not able to 
take a fresh view and continue to give the assessment of the viability of prospects on the 
basis of their past perception and in a given case, even past prejudices. It is, th·erefore, 

79 
suggested that the BIFR should be equipped with an independent agency manned by 
competent persons to assess the viability of various schemes which may 'be suggested. The 
practice of appointing the concerned financial institutions as the operating agency can never 
give a fresh picture or approach which is sometimes absolutely critical for reviving the 
company. This will require amendment of Section 3(1) (i). 
82. BIFR should have power to sanction the scheme without the consent of the concerned 
bank or rmancial institution if BIFR is satisfied that the scheme is workable even though 
institutions are not willing to consent. This will require amendment of Section 18. 
83. The power to give interim directions is restricted to Section 22(a) of the Act which 
permits BIFR to prevent disposition of assets. This is inadequate. BIFR must be given far 
more interim powers pending the inquiry not only to prevent disposition of assets, but also, in 
a given case appoint a provisional receiver in case where the company's operations are shut 
down or a provisional manager or agent to take over the management and run the 
management of the existing unit in any opinion is formed that the unit is being operative in a 
dishonest or fraudulent manner. 
84. The method of functioning by which the BIFR hearings take place like a court 
hearing is not fully appropriate. Such hearing should take place at the final stage but in the 
interaganum there should be greater interaction between the operating agency of the BIFR, as 
suggested earlier, and the company so that the various implications can be gone into in detail. 
85. One of the greatest attractions of taking over a sick unit is setting of losses U'S. 72(a) 
of the Income Tax Act. Earlier, BIFR had power to sanction the schel.e with orders U'S. 
72(a). Now even if the BIFR sanctions the scheme approval under section 72(a) is still 
required. This is time consuming and leads to duplication of efforts and there is no reason 
why the BIFR should not have the power to grant relief U'S.72(a). 
86. One of the reasons of dewy of about two to three years is that in over 50 percent of 
the cases owners have challenged before the AAIFR the closure as recommended by BIFR. 
During the pendency of the appeal to AAIFR, all legal proceedings are suspended U'S. 22 of 
SICA. Therefore, it is recommended that since AAIFR is redundant and leads to unnecessary 
delay and therefore AAIFR should be abolished. Instead, the expertise in the BIFR should be 
increased so that judgement by BIFR is based on better information. 
SICA to Override ULCA for a Viable Area Employment Regeneration Project 
87. SICA 1985 overrides Section 25 M, Section 25 N and Section 25 0 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 for the purpose of restructuring of a unit uls. 18(4) of SICA 1985. In a 
similar way SICA 1985 should override Urban Land Ceiling Act for the purpose of a Viable 
Area Employment Regeneration Scheme for the prompt re-entry for new viable economic 
activities. The best example is that of proposed Ahmedabad Local Economy Rejuvination 
Trust (ALERT) to be created out of the sale of redeveloped land of 15 mills under 
liquidation which would have created over 50,000 jobs. 
SICA to Override . FERA 
88. Under Section 32 of SICA it overrides all Acts except Foreign Exchange Regulation 
ACT (FERA), 1973 and Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act (ULCRA), 1976. It is 
suggested that SICA should override FERA so that non-resident Indians are encouraged to 
take over the sick companies. 
89. BIFR is empowered to recommend liquidation. According to the present procedure 

80 
these cases have to be referred to the High Court. In the cases which are before BIFR under 
SICA 1985, the Companies Act may be amended to authorize the BIFR to pass the orders for 
winding up as if it were in the liquidation court. (Section 20-1 of SICA). This step will save 
about ~12 months. 
90. There is a legal ambiguity in Section 20 of SICA that requires clarification and 
amendment. Section 20(4) states that (i) notwithstanding contained in Section 20(2) and 20(3), 
BIFR can sell the assets of a company that is recommended to be wound up and (ii) the sale 
proceeds must be forwarded to the concerned High Court for distribution according to Section 
529 A of the Companies Act. The first part implies that Section (I) is winding up. However, if 
this is so, then once the opinion of winding up is forwarded to the High Court, the case goes 
outside SICA and enters the realm of the Companies Act. That being so the courts can insist 
that sales u/s. 20(4) of (SICA) be structured according to the time delaying detail, strictly 
sequential procedures laid down by the Companies Act, the Companies (Court) rules and the 
civil procedure court. Therefore, this ambiguity in Section 20 should be removed so that BIFR 
can sell the assets of a company after deciding to wind it up u1; 20 (1). 
Policy Package for Restructuring Industry and Sector 
91. BIFR has been so far dealing on case to case basis, even though it is very apparent 
that the sickness is in the industry/sector like cotton and jute textile industry as a whole for 
preventing further sickness in the sector, sectorial recommendations are necessary. Therefore, 
BIFR must also apply its mind for restructuring of the sector or a policy package for the 
industry/sector which would be a preventive measure which is one of the objective of the BIFR 
and SICA. 
92. This issue is highlighted before the Sub-Committee on the basis of cases with regard 
to NEPA, NTC and Kamani Tubes. It was brought to the notice of the Sub-Committee that 
NEPA was a thriving industrial unit with positive networth. It has been supplying newsprints 
to the major newspaper establishments spread all over the country who were making huge 
profits. NEPA Mill is closed since August, 1996 on account of serious financial constraints due 
to adverse market conditions for indigenous newsprints arising out of liberalised import of 
newsprint under OGL. Because of the non-payment of energy bill, Madhya Pradesh 
Electricity Board disconnected power supply. 
93. The management suggested that if some policy measures are taken immediately, the 
loss making unit can be converted into a profit making unit in only two years. These are the 
preventive steps which should be taken by BIFR. 
94. The case of NTC is another unique one. If all the units of NTC are aggregated they 
become unviable. However, several individual units under NTC are viable, but since they can 
not be examined individually by the BIFR and therefore they are also turning sick. It is also a 
matter of policy which should be taken up by BIFR. 
95. The third case is of the Kamani Tubes and other workers cooperatives recommended 
by BIFR. Even after the BIFR has recommended that these units must be taken over by the 
workers cooperatives the banks and financial institutions continue to treat them as sick units. 
Therefore, inspite of the sacrifices by the workers, the tum around has not taken place 
because the banks and financial institutions have not played their assigned role to which they 
have agreed in the BIFR. Therefore, BIFR should make it mandatory for the banks and the 
financial institutions that once they have recommended a case for rehabilitation they should 
come forward and help in the turnaround of these units. This is an important issue for policy 
making. 

81 
96. At present, 185 references of the Government companies have been made to BIFR, 
of which 140 were registered. Registration with BIFR means that its functioning becomes 
loose and losses increased and turnaround becomes more and more difficult as time goes off. 
The efforts are slackened by the authorities. The flow of funds particularly working capital 
flow is difficult to get. The purpose of referring public sector units to BIFR, was that they 
should recommend its restructuring to make them viable. This has not happened. Therefore, 
BIFR as a matter of policy should take up and recommend restructuring of the public sector 
units without delay. 
Performance of NRF 
97. The National Renewal fund of Rs. 200 crores was established by Government of 
India in 1991-92 to provide a social safety net for the affected workers, both in public, 
private and unorganised sectors due to macro-economic adjustment and the structural 
adjustment programme. Between 1992-93 and 1996-97, Rs. 3100 crores have been allocated 
to National Renewal Fund. Of this, Rs. 1769.66 crores have been transferred to Public 
Account. Rs. 1505.17 crores have been released for voluntary retirement scheme of 94,332 
workers in the Central Government Public undertakings upto 30th September, 1996. 
98. All the representation made before the Sub-Committee have found the working of 
the National Renewal Fund very unsatisfactory and a large deviation from the original 
objectives. NRF has failed to provide the social safety net for the workers, both in the 
organised and unorganised sectors. NRF has in no way reduced the adverse impact of the 
macro economic adjustment and the structural adjustment programme on the workers. 
99. The biggest failure of the NRF is to provide for the Area Employment Regeneration 
Scheme which was supposed to be the key to success of the objective of NRF. The original 
budget allocation of NRF Rs. 150 crores for Ahmedabad project of area regeneration was 
not transferred because of the bureaucratic rigidity. The Empowered Committee of the NRF 
and even other concerned officials found this scheme viable and yet the funds were not 
released and therefore the benefits of the NRF have not come forth. The failure to 
implement area regeneration project under NRF in a sad commentary on the functioning of 
NRF. The implementation of the area regeneration project and its success would have 
ensured the faith and confidence of the workers in the NRF and the Government. Even now 
if NRF has to make significant impact in the labour market then it is only through proper 
implementation area regeneration schemes in Ahmedabad, Kanpur, Indore, Calcutta, etc. 
Therefore, the Sub-Committee feels and recommends very strongly that NRF must be utilised 
to provide social safety net to workers and it must adhere to its original objectives as spelt out 
in 1991-92. Leaving apart the generation of new jobs, the rehabilitation of workers should be 
done in such a manner that they do not remain without work. 
100. Non-implementation of the area regeneration projects have another implicit 
danger. In places like Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Calcutta, Kanpur and Indore where large 
amount of valuable land resource are lying unutilised if they are not recycled in a planned 
manner, it would result into haphazard growth of the area leading to environmental 
problems. There is also· possibility that this valuable land might be grabbed by the builder 
lobby at throw away prices without any significant benefit to the society. This is the lesson 
which we have in some places in Ahmedabad and in Mumbai. By not taking up area 
regeneration scheme a great opportunity has been lost of developing a suitable policy 
package to recycle the valuable land resource. 
101. Voluntary Retirement Scheme has been able to get rid of 94,332 workers upto 30th 

82 
September, 1996 but it is not necessary that it might have led to becoming those units viable 
and therefore obviously VRS to 94,332 workers does not fulfil any objective or any benefit 
to the society. 
102. In a major sense VRS is a very unproductive scheme which has neither helped the 
country nor the concerned units or even the workers who have taken VRS or the workers 
who have remained behind. 
103. Even the retraining programme undertaken under NRF has remained of a very 
small size looking to the requirement of the affected workers. Even where the programme 
has taken its roots (Ahmedabad, Indore, etc.), the institutions running such programme find 
that the structure is too rigid. 
104. At Ahmedabad, Gandhi Labour Institute which runs the training programme, told 
the Sub-Committee to: 
(a) relax the age limit which is of 35 years 
(b) lower the educational qualification 
(c) lengthen the duration of course from 50 days to 180 days 
(d) increase the stipend 
105. The Sub-Sub-Committee feels that the Ministry should give little more flexibility 
looking to the local environment and largely accept the suggestions. 
106. In initial period of NRF it was also mentioned that the problem of legal dues of the 
affected workers will get priority. But nothing has so far happened in this matter. Workers 
of 46 Textile Mills of Ahmedabad have not received their legal dues of Rs. 222 crores. And 
when these Units are taken into liquidation and assets are disposed of, it is not likely that 
workers will get even sizable portion of their dues. This problem also needs some solution. 
107. Thus most of the trade unions and workers have found the functioning of NRF to 
be very unsatisfactory and non-productive. The following suggestions have come forward 
with regard to the concept of social safety net: 
(i) At present, it seems that NRF has come to a standstill. It seems there is no 
provision for it in 1996-97 and onwards. This implies that the adverse impact of 
macro economic adjustment and structural adjustment programmes on workers has 
come to an end. This is not true. The adverse impact would continue in the new 
economic regime. Therefore, the social safety net would be required. Therefore, 
NRF should be augmented by creating State Renewal Funds. Punjab and 
Rajasthan have already created State Renewal Fund but unfortunately only for 
State level public enterprises. Gujarat has also proposed State Renewal Fund which 
is likely to be funded by the Asian Development Bank. The major objectives of the 
NRF and SRF will be to provide human face to liberalisation. The State Renewal 
Fund but unfortunately only for State level public enterprises. Gujarat has also 
proposed State Renewal Fund can be created through a regular contribution from 
healthy units by the de facto partner of the unit, i.e. the entrepreneur, the 
employees, the financial institutions, Central and State Governments. It can also 
be supported by NRF. Such a fund on a regular basis can provide social safety net 
on a continuous basis. 
(ii) The Centre for Worker's Management, Mumbai has drawn the attention of the 
Sub-Committee that the present scheme for retraining, redeployment and 
counselling is extremely small. It has suggested that the schemes for retraining need 
to be fine-tuned with the specific skills and capabilities of workers concerned as· 

83 
well as in relation with where realistic and feasible opportunities of redeployment 
exist. On the question of development of small business for generating employment, 
this scheme also needs to be extended to the creation of new enterprises through 
workers cooperatives. 
(iii) The Working Committee of INTUC expresses its reservations over the present 
functioning of NRF. It is of the view that NRF should be converted into a statutory 
fund through a new law assuring adequate representation to the working class so 
that funds may flow directly to the NRF instead of the Consolidated Fund of India. 
108. Taking the views expressed before the sub-Committee, the Sub-Committee felt that 
the functioning of NRF has totally neglected the area of providing funds for Employment 
Generation schemes, both in the organised and unorganised sector in order to provide a social 
safety net for labour. VRS existed even before NRF was created. The basic approach should 
be to provide immediate alternative employment to an affected worker who became 
unemployed for no fault of his. At one stage NRF made an effort to evolve some scheme of 
unemployment insurance. One does not know why that effort was abandoned. 
109. The Sub-Committee urges upon the Government to consider the views expressed 
and suggestions made before the Sub-Committee seriously and give NRF the proper status and 
see that aims enumerated at the time of formation of NRF are achieved during the Ninth 
Plan. 
110. Overall representations before the Sub-Committee has been that functioning of the 
BIFR and NRF is not very satisfactory. However, they are very important for the 
imple~ntation of the new economic policy with a human face which, of course, calls for 
restructuring them on the lines suggested above. 
SANAT MEHTA 
Convenor, 
Sub-Committee II on NRF and BIFR.

SUB-COMMITTEE-III ON TRENDS IN INDUSTRIAL OUTPUT 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry at its meeting held 
on the 29th October, 1996 constituted five Sub-Committees to examine five different 
subjects pertaining to the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. Sub-Committee-Ill has 
been assigned the task of examining the prevailing trends in industrial output. 
2. In the process of examination, the Sub:Committee heard the views of the Secretary of 
the Ministries of Industry and Power. It also studied the notes and papers received from 
the Planning Commission, the CII, the ASSOCHAM and the FICCI. The Sub-Committee, 
however, could not hear the views of the representatives of the Ministries of 
Communications and Transport as well as the Planning Commission due to paucity of time. 
3. The Sub-Committee began its study with the oral evidence of the Secretary, 
Department of Industrial Policy Promotion, Ministry of Industry and had an interactive 
discussion on the wide ranging interconnected issues reflecting upon the industrial growth 
rate in the current financial year. 
4. The Secretary, at the very outset, admitted that industrial production during the 
period April to August of the current financial year declined to 8.6% as compared to 
12.6% in the corresponding period of the last year. Several sub-sectors of the industry 
namely, electricity, fertilizer, petroleum, textile, steel; etc. were showing signs of 
slowdown. Since, all these sub-sectors belong to the core sector of the economy, any 
negative trend in their growth rate was bound to have a telling impact of the overall 
growth rate. Electricity and mining have, largely, been responsible for bringing down the 
total growth of industrial sector. In case of electricity, it recorded a meagre 2. 5 per cent of 
growth rate in the first quarter of the financial year 1996-97 whereas it was 12.5 per cent 
in the corresponding period of the financial year 1995-96. The performance of Mining 
sector was even worse than the electricity as it could manage to have a nominal growth 
rate of only 1.8 per cent in the same period this year as against the growth rate of 15.4 
per cent last year. Manufacturing sector continued to be in a fluid state. The decline in 
performance of infrastructure industries and major industries can be seen from the
