5. The Sub-Committee was further informed that Ministry of Industry tried to identify 
the reasons for this downturn and after an analysis it came to the conclusion that there were 
three major reasons responsible for the present state of growth rate as given below: 
(i) High cost of capital and non-availability of Funds: The cost of capital available 
to the industry is very high. The industry is getting money at an interest rate as 
high 
• 

95 
as 20%. This led to the non-availability of funds thus making the situation in 
money market very tight. 
(ii) Lack of Liquidity in the market: Another factor responsible for downward trend 
has been the liquidity crunch. The squeeze in money supply growth effected by 
RBI resulted in a liquidity crisis. There was acute shortage of money in the 
market because of short supply from RBI. 
(iii) Poor Infrastructure: After liberalisation, the economy registered an increase in 
growth rate. This put extraordinary strain on infrastructure and brought out its 
weaknesses and state of unpreparedness to the fore. Every constituent of the 
infrastructure proved incapable and was found wanting. The performance of 
sectors like electricity generation, petroleum, steel, fertilizers, etc. can be 
quoted as best examples for highlighting the poor state of infrastructure. 
6. Apart from these factors, the analysis of the Ministry identified a couple of other 
reasons such as lack of coordination among Government ministries and departments, 
absence of a coherent picture vis-a-vis liberalisation policy, marginal fall in the savings, delay 
in decision-making as a result of which less foreign direct investment (FDI) proposals were 
received, slump in stock market, increase in PSUs liabilities, etc. 
7. Government were, however, taking all remedial measures to revive the industrial 
output. Accordingly, RBI issued instructions to public sector banks to cut their prime 
lending rates (PLRs). Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was also reduced by 2% to ease the 
money market. All ministries and departments were taking steps to improve the situation. 
This apart, the Secretary expressed confidence that the growth rate should be in double digit 
though it was too early to say whether it will reach 12 per cent. Since, a number of players 
were involved in the whole process, the growth rate might fall short of the target. 
8. Elaborating further on what needs to be done, the Sub-Committee was informed on 
the issue of foreign investment that an economy, liberalising after years of closed door 
policy, needed free flow of money. But the tight money policy adopted by RBI resulted in 
shortage of capital in the market. This crisis was further compounded by less availability of 
foreign capital. At a time when its neighbouring country, China was attracting more foreign 
investment, India could manage only two billion dollars as foregin investment in 1995-96 as 
against thirty-five billion dollars investment in China. Therefore, India required billions of 
dollars as foreign investment to prop up its economic reforms. He opined that improvement 
in existing facilities and efforts to get more investment for creating new capacity should form 
a part of the strategy to be evolved to get over the crisis. As far as, lack of coordination and 
delay in decision-making was concerned, the Secretary admitted that these two factors were 
also proving to be major hurdles in increase in growth rate. The suggestion for having a 
nodal agency preferably the Department of Industrial Development tor monitoring and 
maintaining the tempo of growth rate was well received by the Secretary. Such a nodal 
agency should also be entrusted with the task of coordinating among all ministries and 
departments in order to ensure speedy disposal of investment proposals and to reach the 
targeted mark of growth rate. 
9. Commenting upon the poor infrastructure, the Sub-Committee was informed that the 
infrastructure was wholly and solely dependent on the public sector or for that matter the 
Government. There has been no private participation or investment on infrastructure as it 
did not yield any profit or financial return. What actually is required to be done is to 
encourage and attract both private as well as foreign investment in this sector. 
10. Similarly, the Secretary emphasized the need to increase savings. As per the data 

96 
available with the Ministry, the savings stood at 24-25% whereas to achieve a growth target 
of 7-8%, there had to be savings to the tune of 28% of GDP. Savings need to register an 
increase of 2%. Government expenditure should be reduced in order to increase the savings. 
At present, larger revenue expenditure has resulted in increased borrowings by Government. 
This continues to be a major impediment in the progress of the economy. Fiscal and revenue 
deficits stood at 5.9 per cent and 3.1 per cent of GDP respectively in 1995-96. Though fiscal 
deficit declined from 8.3 per cent of GDP in 1990-91 to 5.9 per cent in 1995-96, the size of 
the deficit continues to be high. What is more worrying is the high revenue deficit which has 
fallen only by 0.4 percentage point in the last five years, from 3.5 per cent of GDP in 
1990-91 to 3.1 per cent in 1995-96. As a result of high revenue deficit, Government has to 
borrow from the market to meet current expenditures. 
11. The Secretary, in all, was for inprovement of the existing infrastructure, more inflow 
of foreign direct investment, cut in the interest to ease the liquidity crisis, proper 
coordination among various ministries and departments of the Government, reduction in 
Government expenditure and increase in savings, evolution of a coherent industrial policy 
especially vis-a-vis private and foreign investment and so on and so forth. 
12. The Sub-Committee next heard the Secretary, Ministry of Power. Power being a 
major constituent of the infrastructure, has been the most decisive factor in bringing down 
the growth rate of industrial output. First six to seven months of the current financial year 
witnessed drastic fall in the electricity generation. This fall, in turn, had resulted in a 
slowdown in industrial output. The Secretary, Ministry of Power, in his submission informed 
the Sub-Committee that the country had 86,000 MW of installed capacity, out of which, 
about 35,000 MW was hydro and the remaining was completely thermal. The average 
shortage at the national level was 10%. The growth rate in demand is almost about eight per 
cent per annum, whereas the energy generated is about seven per cent per annum. So, there 
is a gap of one per cent year after year. This one per cent gap in demand and supply is the 
reason for power shortage all over the country. The availability of power is dependent on 
rains and availability of coal. This year, the hydro generation has dropped by almost 8% 
because of scanty rains in the catchment areas of almost all the regions of the country. 
Similarly, erratic supply of coal to the thermal power stations led to steep decline in 
electricity generation. The requirement of coal stood at 195 million tonnes last year. It fell 
short by 10 millions tonnes in 1995-96. Non-availability of coal has uniformly been affected 
the performance of power stations. In the current year, the power stations require around 
215 million tonnes of coal but the Ministry of Coal have already made it clear that they 
would not be able to supply more than 195 million tonnes of coal. So, there is a gap of 20 
million tonnes. Same is the case with gas-based units. Due to non-availability of gas, 
production never goes beyond 50---60%. As a result, the gap between demand and supply is 
widening. The demand for power is increasing every year by 8%. But the target is not being 
achieved. The reason why the target is not being achieved is the lack of investment. Private 
participation as well as foreign investments have somehow not been able to materialise. In 
this way, the power shortage continues to persist. 
13. The Sub-Committee was further informed that the Ministry of Power had prepared a 
National Action Plan to improve the condition of the power sector. Modernisation and 
increase in the efficiency of existing power plants, priority to hydro projects, autonomy to 
the State Electricity Boards and improvement in their management, rationalisation of tariffs, 
participation of private sector in distribution and setting up of central as well as State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions are some of the highlights of this plan. A copy of the 
action plan is placed as Annexure-H. 
14. The Sub-Committee also had the opportunity to examine the background papers and 
notes received from the Planning Commission and various Chambers of Commerce and 
Industry. Close scrutiny of these papers proved helpful for the members to further grasp the 
gravity of the problem. All these papers, in a nut shell, pointed out that the downturn in 
industrial growth has been mainly due to (i) infrastructure bottlenecks, (ii) liquidity crunch, 

97 
(iii) high interest rates; (iv) slump in demand, (v) nsmg revenue expenditure and 
(vi) slowdown in the production activity of major sub-sectors of the industry. 
CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
1. The most important factor which had led to slow growth in the industrial production 
is the lack of infrastructure in the country. No parti'YUlar attention has been given during the 
last so many years to develop this sector and to meet the increasing demand of the 
industries. Our ports are congested which takes days and weeks for the ships to get a berth 
at the ports. Similarly, there is a shortage of wagons. The roads cannot cope with the 
increasing demand of the the transport sector and other basic infrastructures are also 
lacking. In fact, the Finance Minister while replying to budget debate last year in the Lok 
Sabha was candid enough to admit that Indian infrastructure was trailing at its seams. He 
had added that as regards electricity, the shortage was around 20%. As regards roads, the 
Finance Minister had this to say: 
" ..... we have only about 74,000 kilometres of-what is called National Highway. But in 
many places the facetious statement is that, it is only a National Highway. It is not a 
National Highway. It ought to be world class roads. 
A gentleman from the Ford Motor Company who have set up a plant now in 
Maharashtra and who are setting up another plant in Tamil Nadu, told me that it takes five 
to nine days for a truck to go from Mumbai ·to a place in Tamil Nadu. If we have an 
efficient and cost effective system and if it takes nine days for goods to move from Mumbai 
to Madras, how is it possible? It should take not more than two days if we have world class 
roads there. That is why we have identified the infrastructure challenge as the second 
challenge after the fiscal challenge."* 
It is a matter of grave concern for the country that in all these years of planned 
economy, the infrastructure had totally been neglected. It speaks volumes of the lack of 
foresightedness and casts a serious reflection on the functioning of the Planning Commission 
which overseas and coordinates the planned development in the country. 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, suggests that action to augment the infrastructure in the 
country should be developed on a war footing and cooperation of all concerned should be 
secured. The policy for private investments should not only be crystal clear but also 
transparent. 
2. Industry has been virtually cash-strapped over the last few months. Two most 
discernible reasons for this are the adoption of tight money policy by RBI and the less flow 
of foreign capital in terms of direct investment. As far as, money policy of RBI is 
concerned, the situation was eased out to some extent by the reduction of CRR by 2%. This 
step made available around Rs. 8,000 crore to the market. With regard to the foreign direct 
investment, the indications have not been found to be as much encouraging as they were 
when the economic reforms were first introduced in India. It has been observed that 
whatever foreign capital has been invested or is being invested, is limited only to consumer 
durables or luxury items, whereas the basic infrastructural areas have been left untouched. 
Understandably, the attraction of foreign investors seems to be to make megabucks with 
scant regard to the creation of infrastructural facilities. The intention of this Sub-Committee, 
is not at all, to concetrate on infrastructure alone, the investment should be evenly dispersed 
so that overall growth could be achieved. It should never be lopsided in any manner. 
Therefore, this Sub-Committee is of the view that steps should be taken to attract foreign 
investment not just for one sector of the economy but for all the fields of economic activities, 
Priority, defmitely, be accorded to hitherto untouched or haltbeartedly touched sectors of the 
economy. 
*Finance Minister while replying to Budge~ deba~ In tbe Lok Sabha on 6.9.1996. 

98 
3. Another problem that dogged the industry is the high rate of interest on the funds 
provided by banks and other financial institutions. Though efforts were made on the part of 
RBI to control the situation, the timing of its intervention was little too late. Almost all the 
public sector banks have lowered their prime lending rates (PLRs) following the guidelines 
issued by RBI. Similarly, the reduction in Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) provided succour to 
the market which was bearing the brunt of liquidity crunch. In this regard, the Sub­
Committee has come to the conclusion that non-availability of easy money to the industry has 
assumed the proportions of a perennial problem. Here the role of RBI becomes significant. 
It being an apex body should take initiative to see that lending norms are further Iiberalised 
so that dying spirits of the market could be revived. Moreover, it should maintain mo:-e 
watchful control over the way the money market moves. 
4. Perhaps, the most crucial factor that has adversely affected the growth rate of 
industrial production, is the actual shortage of power, the survival of modem hi-tech 
industries depend mainly on the availability of power. If the availability of electricity is 
disturbed, the industrial activity gets equally affected within the possibility of its coming to a 
grinding halt within the stroke of a second. Apparently, little over sixty per cent of 
electricity is generated by thermal plants which have to depend on the supply of coal. 
A little delay, in the supply of coal, leads to the closure of generation units. On the other 
hand, in spite of having abundance of water resources, the contribution of hydel electricity 
plants is a mere thirty five per cent. In other words, this is a classic example of improper 
and poor management of natural resources. Although the Ministry of Power has chalked out 
a national action plan in order to improve the power situation, what remains to be seen is as 
to how successful this programme would be. In the opinion of this Sub-Committee, the entire 
power sector needs complete overhauling and restructuring. The present spate of unabated 
power crisis is swaping the entire country. It should be checked and this problem needs to be 
addressed with the help of both short-term as well as long-term measures. Foreign investment 
in the power sector should be encouraged with the emphasis being on hyde) electricity. As a 
short-term measure the focus should be on the modernisation of the existing plants so that 
their efficiency could be enhanced. The transmission and distribution losses of electricity, the 
present rate of which is too high all over the country, also needs to be checked with a strong 
hand. The various State Electricity Boards also need to be revamped with a view to instil 
efficiency in their operation. 
5. Revenue expenditure of the Government has been steadily rising. This compels the 
Government to resort to borrowings. Borrowings in. tum result in diversion of funds away 
from the corporate sector and ultimately leading to the shortage of funds in the market. This 
shortage pushes the interest rates up and creates liquidity crunch. All this is caused by the 
mounting fiscal deficit owing to which the Government has to tum to the market to meet its 
current expenditure. Therefore the need of the hour is to curb the wastefull expenditure and 
to bring the level of fiScal deficit down to manageable limits. The Sub-Committee strongly 
feels that Government should take immediate steps to curb the revenue expenditure with a 
view to increase the savings. The Sub-Committee recommends that all the mega and major 
Government projects should be completed within the given time frame. 
6. Another issue closely linked with the Government expenditure is the domestic 
savings. At present, the domestic savings stand at 24-25% of the GDP. To achieve a growth 
target of 7-8% the percentage of savings should go up. It should in the opinion of the Sub­
Committee, at least regis!..::r an increase of 2%. Requisite incentives need to be offered to 
increase the domestic savings. In this way, the issues of government expenditure, fiscal deficit 
and savings are interconnected and should be dealt with a common frame of mind. 

99 
7. There has been much talk about the lack of coordination among various ministries 
and departments of the government. Lack of coordination hampers the upward movement of 
growth rate as the projects and proposals get stuck at different stages for one reason or the 
other. Although, the policy of single window clearance was given too much media hype, yet 
many a project are delayed because of bureaucratic redtapism and indifference. The need is 
to create an atmosphere of change where each and every agency of the government is well­
acquainted with its work and putting in its best effort to achieve the target. The Department 
of Industrial Development, may be the choice for this job. Such a nodal agency will not only 
do the coordination work but will also be instrumental in putting forward a coherent picture 
of the Indi;tn ..... economic reforms to the world business community. 
Further, the Sub-Committee notes with discontent the statement of the Secretary. IPP 
made before the Sub-Committee that there is no proper coordination in the process of decision 
making in the various departments and industries. This, in the opinion of the Sub-Committee 
leads to delay in the process of decision making. The Sub-Committee fails to understand the 
reasons for lack of coordination in the process of decision making among the various 
Ministries I Departments when there exists & Planning Commission as well as the Committee 
of Secretaries where the differences, if any, among the MinistriesDepartments can be sorted 
out conveniently. The Sub-Committee recommends that efforts should be made to increase 
coordination in the process of decision making so that the projects are completed within the 
prescribed time frame and cost over-runs are also avoided. 
8. The Sub-Committee is constrained to note that the Planning Commission have not 
yet been able to make known details of the 9th Plan which is to be implemented in a little 
over a months time. This, in the opinion of the Sub-Committee prevents the public from 
going in for an advance planning which is very essential for maintaining a steady growth rate. 
The Planning Commission had also not come out with a mid-term review. At present we are 
only 3 years ahead of entering into the year 2001 and the Sub-Committee is apprehensive that 
if the present state of planning continues, India would enter into the next millennium on a 
bullock cart. 
9. The Sub-Committee is of the view that in order to reduce the Government expenditure 
a time has now come that Government should come out with unambiguous policies with 
regard to central public sector undertakings. The country can no longer afford to carry on 
with dilly-dally policies with regard to this important sector of the economy. The Government 
must take hard decision wherever necessary. Time has now come when ideological issues 
should take a back seat and investment decisions should be made only on the basis of pure 
economic considerations. A decision in respect of such of those public sector undertakings 
which have over the year been incurring losses year after year and their equity has become 
zero, must be taken without any futher delay. In respect of such of the undertakings it is not 
necessary for the Government to give non-plan support merely to protect the employment. 
Alternative schemes ought to be thought of such industrial units in a time bound programme. 
The Sub-Committee notes with deep regret in respect of large number of such loss making 
units most of which are now before the BIFR, the Government has not come out with any 
clear cut policy. These units are a drag on the country's economy.

* Appeals against orders of SERCs will be to respective High Courts unless any State 
Government specificully prefers such appeals being made to the Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission. 
Ill. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
• Union Government will set up a eentral Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). 
• CERC will set the bulk tariffs for all Central generating and transmission utilities. 
• Licencing, planning and other related functions could also be delegated to CERC as 
and when the Central Government notifies it. 
• All issues concerning inter-State now and exchange of power shall also be decided by 
the CERC. 
• To enable setting up of CERC, Central Government will amend Indian Electricity 
Act, 1910 and Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. 
IV. Rationalisation of Retail Tariffs 
• Determination of retail tariffs, including wheeling charges etc., will be decided by 
SERCs which will ensure a minimum overall 3% rate of return to each utility with 
immediate effect. 
\ 
• Cross-subsidization between categories of consumers may be allowed by SERCs. No 
sector shall, however, pay less than 50% of the average cost of supply (cost of 
generation plus transmission and distribution). Tariffs for agricultural sector will not 
be less than fifty paise per Kwh to be brought to 50% of the average cost in not more 
than three years. 
• Recommendations of SERCs are mandatory. If any deviations from tariffs 
recommended by it are made by a State/UT Government, it will have to provide for 
the financial implications of such deviations explicitly in the State budget. 
• Fuel Adjustment Charges (FCA) would be automatically incorporated in the tariff. 
• There shall be a package- of incentives and disincentives to encourage and facilitate 
the implementation of tariff rationalisation by the States.

V. Private Sector Participation in Distribution 
* State Governments agree to a gradual programme of private sector participation in 
distribution of electricity. The process of private participation shall be initially in one or 
two viable geographical areas covering both urb<Jn and rural areas in a State and the 
State may extend this to other parts of the State gradually. 
VI. Role of Central Agencies 
* The Central Government would make a comprehensive review of the role of Central 
Electricity Authority (CEA). Techno-economic approval of competitively bid power 
projects will be simplified and CEA shall not be concerned with capital cost, tariff and 
other commercial aspects of the project. Powers regarding approval of projects shall 
stand delegated to the States in respect of thermal power stations upto 250 MW. 
However, in respect of thermal projects beyond-250 MW capacity and other schemes, 
CEA's appraisal will continue in respect of planning and other related matters, such as to 
promote best optimal development of the river and its tributaries for power generation 
including proper hydro-thermal coordination; the suitability of location and size of 
thermal power stations; fuel linkages; adequacy of power evacuation facilities covering 
inter-state and intra-state and the transmission schemes form and integral part of the 
National Power Grid for maximization of benefits for the country as a whole. Subject to 
such technical cle,afances which shall be accorded within two months State Governments 
will have powers tb accord approval for power projects. 
* The role of FIPB will be minimised by putting as many projects on· the automatic 
clearance route as feasible. 
* Government of lndia will issue transparent guidelines and delegate more powers for 
environmental clearance to State agencies. State agencies should equip themselves with 
requisite physical and technical expertise. 
* Government of India will delegate more powers to the States for issue of forest 
clearances. Statutory amendments will be made in the relevant Central statutes. 
* Ministry of Environment and Forests have proposed the following delegation to the 
States for environment clearance: 
(i) All co-generation plants and captive power plants up to 250 MW. 
(ii) Coal based plants upto 500 MW using fluidized bed technology subject to sensitive 
areas restrictions. 
(iii) Power staHons upto 250 MW on conventional technology. 
(iv) Gas/Naphtha based station upto 500 MW. 
vn. Autonomy to the State Electricity Boards 
* States will allow maximum possible autonomy to the State Electricity Boards. The State 
Electricity Boards will be restructured and corporatised and run on commercial basis. 
VIII. Improvements in the Management Practices of State Electricity Boards 
* State Electricity Boards will professionalize their technical inventory manpower and 
project management practices.

* Government of India will carry out necessary amendiiMMI in the relevant Acts/Rule to 
allow private participation in transmission. 
* State Governments will provide higher allocation for early oompletion of public sector 
projects. 
* Renovation and modernization of existing power plots allall be done in a time bound 
manner. PFC and other fmancial institutions will give hiahk priority for funding of R & 
M schemes. Clearance to R & M projects will fully be del-sated to the States and no 
clearance will be required from CEA. 
* PLF of those thermal power stations having less tho 40% PLF at present would be 
increased by 3% annually, by 2% in case of those plants vmh PLF between 40 and 60% 
and by 1% for those plants with PLF over 60%. ·The overall PLF in the State sector in 
the country must come up to a minimum of 65% and tile national average to 70% by 
2002 A.D. 
* Compulsory metering at substations and on all major feeders would be introduced. 
Compulsory metering of all ~ew electricity connections as also of connections to 
agriculture sector exceeding 10 HP will be undertaken and completed in two years. All 
electric supplies would be metered by 2002 A.D. · 
* Compulsory annual energy audit of large consumers i.e., 100 KV A and above would be 
undertaken. 
* Time of the day metering would be introduced for big power consumers for better load 
management. 
X. Co-generation/Captive power plants 
* State Governments will encourage Co-generation/Captive power plants. To facilitate 
evacuation of power from these plants to the grids, States shall formulate clear and 
transparent policies for purchase of power and wheeliD& charges which provide fair 
returns to the Co-generation/Captive power plant owners. Captive power plants could 
also sell power to a group of industries as well as other categories of consumers in the 
said industrial zone or area. Wheeling of power from captive power plants to consumers 
located at a distance or through displacement basis shall be encouraged and the States 
will issue clear and transparent long term policies in this regard. 
XI. Advance Action and ffigh Priority for Hydro Projeds ---. 
* A national policy on hydro power development will be evolved by the Central 
Government which, inter-alia, would include development of mega hydro projects, both 
in the public sector and the private sector, at locations with substantial hydro potential, 
along with concomitant transmission facilities for evacuation of power to other Regions/ 
States. States shall prepare a shelf of fully cleared hydro projects for implementation on 
high priority. Special efforts will be made to promote hydro-electric projects in Himachal 
Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir.

The Convenor introd.uced the Members and officers of the Sub-Committee and explained

Shri K.N. Ghosh, C.M.D. of H.C.L. introduced his team of officers and welcomed the 
Committee and informed that presently H.C.L. is the sole producer of primary copper in the 
country with designed capacity to produce 47,500 tonnes of refined primary copper from 
indigenous sources. The main operating units are Khetri Copper Complex at · Khetri, 
Rajasthan; Indian Copper Complex at Ghatsila, Bihar, Malanjkhand Copper Project, 
Madhya Pradesh and Taloja Copper Project, Maharashtra. 
He also informed the Sub-Committee that India is not fortunate in respect of Copper' 
deposits. Inspite of intensive geophysical and geological survey and prospecting and 
exploration activities, no major new deposits could be discovered. The grade ore in India is 
very poor i.e. around 1% as against 2.5 to 3.5% copper content in other parts of the world. 
The geometry of ore body in India is very much unfavourable for large scale mechanisation. 
The by-product content in Indian ore is very low i.e. 4-5% as against 20-40% in other 
116 

117 
parts of the world. The combined effect of all these has made cost of rnmmg and 
beneficiation in terms of copper metal very costly but the smelting and refining cost of 
HCL's plants are comparable to the international cost of production. Copper being a 
strategic metal required for use in Defence, Telecommunication, Space Research, Railways 
and power sector the Government had evolved earlier a number of protective measures like 
levy of varied higher customs duty; canalising the,import of copper and controlling the prices 
of copper through administered pricing system which was much higher than landed cost of 
imported copper. 
However with the liberalisation of economy, canalisation of copper and the system of 
administered prices were done away with from March, 1992 and the import duty on copper 
was reduced to 45% ad valorem on C.I.F. With reduction in customs duty coupled with 
unprecedented fall in LME price of copper. HCL has suffered a huge loss of 69.55 crore 
during 1993-94. But during 1994-95 the scenario changed with increasing customs duty from 
45% to 50% as well as increasing the LME prices and thus the company made a. profit of 
72.26 crore during 1994-95 and a record profit of Rs. 75.84 crores in 1995-96 as the company 
has achieved all time high production of 37,280 tonnes of wire rod at Taloja. 
But at present the customs duty on import of copper has been brought down from 35% 
ad valorem for cathode and wire bar and 40% for wire to a flat rate of 30% for all the 
items. Moreover, the petroleum products have hiked their prices. All these resulted in a loss 
of Rs. 73.22 crore during the first half of the year 1996-97. 
On the efforts of H.C.L. the Sub-Committee was informed that a number of 
uneconomic mines like Lapso Kyanite mine, Dariba mine and operations like Brass Rolling 
mill operation etc. has been closed. H.C.L. is also taking action to close down Mosaboni 
mine in phases where the cost of production is very uneconomical due to the depth 
(1230 m). 
On a specific question by a Member the Sub-Committee was informed that reasons for 
less production than the targets was power shortage and the shut out period of the smelter, 
which for 2 to 21/ 2 months in a year does not work. However the company is considering 
some alternative arrangements. In reply to another question it was informed that now no 
licence is required for import of copper and any body can import it. 
The Sub-Committee was further informed that due to losses the staff was reduced by 
4012 through Voluntary Retirement Scheme and that if no financial assistance is given the 
company will be heading towards closure. The Rakha mines can be further developed if 
funds are made available. 
There was no ecological problem in and around the Company's units. The Company 
was fully aware about the social and welfare activities of its employees. 
Once the expansion of highly profitable Project of Khetri is commissioned the Company 
will be in much better position to face the fluctuations in LME. For the intervening period 
of 2-3 years the company has requested the Government for some temporary relief and 
support on immediate basis to combat the situation arising out of crash LME price so that 
the company could take care of wages of the employees and its growth is not halted. The 
capital investment for green field copper smelt~r and refinery complex of 100,000 TPA 
capacity is around Rs. 1370 crore whereas the same for expansion of capacity of KCC 
smelter and refinery to 100,000 TPA is expected to be only Rs. 528.65 crore. 
The Sub-Committee visited the Ghatsila Copper Complex and was taken inside the 
copper mine. The Sub-Committee received a number of representations from the workers. 
Wherein they demanded that those working for a number of years as contract labour should 
be regularised and their social and welfare needs be attended to. They also demanded that 
their service conditions be improved. It was pleaded that the lease for Sidheshwar-Chapri 

118 
may be renewed in favour of H.C.L./I.C.C. in order to facilitate expansion and at the same 
time the proposed closure of Mosabani and Badia Mines of HCI./ICCIMSB group of mines 
be stopped to save about a lakh of employees and their families. The closure of these mines 
will have a wide ranging effect. 
Indian Copper Complex, Ghatsila has Mosabani Copper mine with 6923 hectare valid 
for 20 years from 16.6.1984. Presently only 187 hectare has been leased but permitted to 
mine from only 37 hectares. The State Govt. of Bihar should grant the permission for lease. 
There is a vast scope of expansion of this mine. It produced 0.02% Uranium worth 
Rs. 12 crores. The refinery for silver/gold requires strict vigil. 
Rakha mine has the area of 785.09 hectare, valid for 20 years w.e.f. 29.8.71. But the 
State Govt. intimated that renewal can be considered only for 23 hectares. Kendadih has an 
area of 1179.60 hectare valid for 20 years w.e.f. 3.6.73. The State Govt. intimated that 
renewal can be considered only for 35.50 hectare but later on the State Govt. agreed for 
669.97 hectare. If the State Govt. does not renew the lease there is a chance of lakhs of 
employees being rendered jobless. The authorities propose to increase the ore from 
900 T.P.D. to 2500 T.P.D. so that people may get employment. The capacity of smelter 
plant is proposed to be increased from 16500 T.P.A. to 31000 T.P.A. 
Shri B.P. Gupta a representative of Bihar State Govt. informed the Sub-Committee that 
H.C.L. extracts 75% of copper from Mosabani mine. They have not put up any extensive 
proposal to ensure the State Govt. that they need whole of the area. The State Govt. would 
never intend that the employees may be rendered jobless or the plant may be closed. The 
question of renewal of the lease is still under the consideration of State Mining Deptt. He 
told the Sub-Committee that in reality the required areas can be renewed but they 
themselves are surrendering some of the mining leases. 
The Sub-Committee recommends that-
(i) Sufficient . financial assistance may be provided to HCL expeditiously as per 
package Ill. 
(ii) Customs duty on imported copper should be increased again to protect the 
indigenous copper mining companies. 
(iii) If the organisation under the Government control fails to run the company 
profitably, foreign companies should not be allowed to take over the production of 
copper etc. and indigenous companies should be given a chance as far as possible 
to upkeep the interests of the organisation. The indigenous copper mining 
companies should be encouraged and joint ventures according to FIPB policies 
should be allowed where equity participation is mainly in the fields of 
infrastructure and equipment. 
(iv) The Mosabani and Badia mines may not be allowed to close down. 
(v) Western mines should be explored on a large scale. 
(vi) The Welfare and service conditions of the employees may be improved and all 
employees may be regularised. The provisions for the welfare activities of 
employees and their families should be sufficiently increased. 
(vii) The hygienic conditions as well as other medical facilities at H.C.L's hospital at 
Mosabani should be thoroughly probed and improved expeditiously. 
(viii) The teachers serving in Central Schools/K.Vs in the Copper Complex etc. may be 
paid by Government and not by H.C.L. 
(ix) The State Government of Bihar may be requested to renew the leases of 
Siddheshvari and Chapri mines expeditiously and the mining process at these may 
be expedited. 
(x) The areas where _gold and silver is refined should have sufficient reliable security 
to prevent pilferage of these metals.

smelting may be got enquired/verified secretly.

the contract labourers.

Meeting with Management 
The Chairman and Managing Director welcomed the Sub-Committee and informed 
that:- · 
(i) · Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited, a wholly owned Government of India 
Enterprise, was established in 1976 ~o develop mine and plant facilities to produce 
7.5 million tonnes of concentrate a year. The min..!and plant facilities were 
commisSioned in 1980 and the first shipment of concentrate was made in October, 
1981. A pelletisation ·plant with a capacity of 3 million tonnes per year was 
commissioned in 1987 for production of high quality blast furnace and direct 
reduction grade pellets for export. 
(ii) The deposits occur as banded magnetite quartzite with an average thickness of iron 
formation extending upto 100 metres. The top layer of iron formation is weathered 
where magnetite is partiully oxid~sed to haematite. The underlying primary BMQ is 
similar to taconite ore. The present scope of mining includes only the weathered ore 
which has an average iron content "of 38 per cent. This is beneficiated to produce 
concentrate of + 67 per cent iron. Kudremukb deposits are known to be one of the 
largest deposits in the world. In one deposit alone, where the mining is currently 
carried out, reserves of 700 milllon tonnes of weathered ore and 450 million tonnes 
of primary BMQ have been proved. Besides, there are other deposits in the vicinity, 
namely, Nellibeedu, Gangrikal, Dababudan, etc., with probable reserve of 3000 
million tonnes. 
(iii) Kudremukh the largest iron ore mine in India, is designed to produce 22.6 million 
tonnes of crude ore per year with a daily production capacity of ROM 100,000 
tonnes. The mine is plunncd for a three-shift operation. Blast holes of 12.25" dia are 
drilled in 14 m benches. The blasting is carried out using slurry explosives. Blasted 
material is loaded by 10.7 cu.m. electrical shovel into large dumpers of 108 metric 
tonne capacity. 
(iv) The mined ore is transported from benches to two Gyratory Crushers capable of 
crushing the ore to minus 7" size. ·n1e crushed ore is screened into coarse and fine 
fractions before feeding to Autogenous Mills. The ore ground to minus 20 mesh size 
is subjected to primary magnetic separation and the concentrate, after regrinding, is 
subjected to secondary magnetic separation to recover the magnetic concentrate. 
Tertiary magnetic separation system has also been incorporated to improve the 
quality of magnetic concentrate. The primary magnetic tailings are subjected to spiral 
separation to recover non-magnetic concentrate which is also gr:ound in ball mills. 
Floatation technique for improvement of concentrate quality has been incorporated. 
Process modifications are being curried out regularly with an objective of improving 
the product specification. The entire operation using the most sophisticated 
equipment from crushing to shiploading is fully automated and computer-controlled. 
Computerised mine planning techniques are used to maintain strict quality control. 

139 
(v) The process of pelletisation involves mining of iron ore concentrate with limestone 
· fines and bentonite as additives. Dry grinding mill for grinding limestone and . 
bentonite to pelletisation process is provided. A small proportion of coke/coal is also 
used as additive for improving the physical and metallurgical properties of pellets. 
The mixed material is fed to pelletising discs of 7.5 m dia for production of green 
pellets which are screened on roller screens to remove the undersize and oversize 
materials. 
(vi) Iron ore concentrate stored in two stockpiles having a total capacity of 400,000 
tonnes is reclaimed by reclaimers and loaded into ships through a shiploader with a 
rated capacity of 6000 tonnes an hour. A loading rate of 30,000 to 35,000 tonnes a 
day is guaranteed for Panamax type vessel. The pellets are reclaimed by a bucket 
wheel reclaimer of 4000 tonnes per hour capacity for shiploading. A captive iron ore 
berth has been provided to handle ships of 65,000 DWT with a loaded draft of 12.5 
meters. With the provision of an exclusive berth, waiting time for ships is eliminated. 
Detailed feasibility studies are being carried out to develop the Mangalore Port to 
handle ships of about 120,000 DWT size. 
(vii) The Company has undertaken quality improvement programme to meet the 
international market requirement and also to augment its concentrator plant 
production capacity to 8.0 m_illion tonnes per year and that of the pellet plant, 
capacity to 3.5 million ton.ries per year. The main process route for quality 
improvement is the incorporation of the Floatation system. The Company proposes 
to have its own Captive Power Generation Plant of about 50 MW capacity at 
Mangalore to reduce its dependence on the State Electricity Grid for power supply 
and also to maintain the committed supply of concentrate and pellets to the 
customers. 
(viii) Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited has taken adequate measures to maintain 
the ecological balance. A 65 metre high dam and two mini dams have been built at 
Kudremukh to store plant tailings and mine wash off to avoid pollution of perennial 
rivers. The flora and fauna of the area have been preserved. Over 7.5 million .trees 
have been planted as part of the large scale afforestation programme. Afforestation 
has also been undertaken a top the hills after mining. 
(ix) Kudremukh produces high grade iron ore concentrate ideal for use as sinter feed and 
for pelletisation. The concentrate has been used in Japan, Czechoslovakia, 
Yugoslavia, France, Australia, Romania and China as blend for sintering and in Iran 
and Bahrain as a blend in pellet feed. The remarkable feature of Kudremukh Ore is · 
its low alumina, sulphur, phosphorous, Vanadium and other deletrious elements. 
Magnetite content of ore has an added advantage in terms of lesser fuel requirement 
in sintering and pelletisation. 
Kudremukh pellets have been used in blast furnances of steel mills in Hungary, 
Yugoslavia, Turkey, Australia, Taiwan, U.S.A., China, West Germany, Japan, Poland and 
Czechoslovakia. The pellets have also been used in Malaysia, Iraq, Indonesia, France and 
Qatar for DRI production. Kudremukh pellets are used in the two large direct reduction 
plants set up in the west coast of India.

Marketing and Consumption of Steel 
37. Having gone through the information supplied by the Ministry of Steel, and 
discussions with the Managements and Workers' representatives of the Organisations/ 
Companies referred to in para 2 above and evidence of representatives of CII and FICCI, 
the Sub-Committee expresses its concern on the down ward trend in the entire steel sector, 
despite the appreciable growth in the production of steel in the country. The slump in steel 
sector has not only adversely affected the steel plants but also the industries connected with 
production of iron and steel. It is an indicative of lack of coordination between 'the 
production of steel in the country on the one hand and marketing thereof on the other. Jt 
also indicates that growth in production of the steel in the country has not resulted in 
corresponding growth of consumption of steel. Consequent to the industrial liberalisation 
policy of Government the public sector steel producing units witnessed a different era which 
they were not used to. Now there is a shift from production oriented units to market 
oriented units. Import duties came down drastically resulting in import of steel and leading 
to heavy competition in domestic market. The steel industry in the country is now facing 
problem on account of huge inventories build up in SAIL stockyards and steel plants worth 
Rs. 1800 crores. 
38. The Sub-Committee has been assured by the Ministry of Steel, Central Marketing 
Organisation, SAIL and steel plants visited by the Sub-Committee that this situation is for a 
very short period and that steel industry would pick up and future projection reveal that 
there would be global shortage of steel and the fact that about 30 new projects are coming 
up in the country is also an indication of future consumption trends. The Sub-Committee is, 
however, not convinced by the plea of the Government.

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having   been  authorized   by the Committee, hereby present
this  Two hundred  and Tenth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) pertaining to  the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.         The Committee held detailed discussions with the representatives of the Ministry of  MS&ME  alongwith the representatives of select Associations of MS
& ME sector.
 
3.         This Report of the Committee is based on the examination of the relevant documents furnished and evidence tendered by the representatives of the
Ministry. The Committee is thankful to the representatives of the Ministry and various organizations who appeared before the Committee. The Committee also
wishes to thank them for furnishing the replies to the questionnaire and the points raised during the course or oral evidence.
 
4.         The Committee in its meeting held on the 28
th April,  2008 considered and adopted the  report.
 
 
 
NEW DELHI                                                                                                                           V. HANUMANTHA RAO
April 29, 2008                                                                                                                                                 Chairman
                                                                                                                         Department –related Parliamentary
                                                                                                                         Standing Committee on Industry
 
 
 
 
REPORT
 
 
1.         The MSME sector constitutes a vibrant segment of our economy contributing significantly to the manufacturing output, employment and national exports.
Based on the 3
rd All-India Census (reference year 2001-02), it is estimated that there are about 128.44 lakh MSEs spread across the country as on 31 March
2007, providing estimated employment to over 312 lakh persons. Further, the MSE sector contributes 39% of the manufacturing output and 33% of the nation’s
exports. However, with the ten fold increase in the permissible investment limit, it is estimated that the redefined MSME sector may now account for as high as
45 per cent of the manufacturing output of India and nearly 40 per cent of the national exports. The most significant contribution of the micro and small
enterprises sector lies in creation of larger employment opportunities at lower capital cost.
 
2.         In keeping with the announcement made in the last Budget Speech, the Ministry of MSME has formulated first phase of a Central Sector Scheme on
‘Rejuvenation, Modernisation and Technology Upgradation of the Coir Industry’ at a total cost of Rs.243 crore, involving a budgetary support of Rs.99 crore
during the XI Plan. The Scheme envisages providing financial assistance for replacing the age old outdated ratts and looms and also to provide work shed in the
spinning and Tiny Household sectors, which are the most vulnerable sectors in the coir industry. The Scheme anticipates covering 4000 spinning units consisting
of 4 ratts each with 8 beneficiaries and 3200 Tiny/Household units consisting of 3 looms each with 6 beneficiaries. It is anticipated to generate 36,800 new
employment opportunities during XI Plan.
 
3.         Although, the primary responsibility for promotion and development of MSMEs lies with the State Governments, the Government of India, in recognition
of potential of these enterprises both in terms of creation of wealth and employment as well as the need for country-wide framework of policies and measures for
their promotion and development, has always taken active interest in supplementing the efforts of State Governments in a variety of ways.  The role of the
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises is mainly to assist the States in their efforts to promote growth and development of MSMEs, for enhancing
their competitiveness in an increasingly market-led economy and for generating additional employment opportunities.   Besides, the Ministry also attempts to
address common concerns of these enterprises and undertakes policy advocacy on behalf of the sector on issues critically affecting their sustenance and growth. 
 
4.         In order to achieve the stated objective the Ministry and its organisations have been implementing various schemes / programmes that seek to facilitate /
provide adequate flow of credit from financial institutions/banks; support for technology upgradation and modernisation; integrated infrastructural
facilities;modern testing facilities and quality certification; access to modern management practices, entrepreneurship development and  skill upgradation through
appropriate training facilities; support for product development, design intervention and packaging; welfare of artisans and workers; assistance for better access
to domestic and export markets; and cluster-wide measures to promote capacity-building and empowerment of the units and their collectives, in addition to all or
some of the above-mentioned supports.
 
5.         In addition, the Ministry has been implementing two nation-wide employment generation programmes, namely, Rural Employment Generation
Programme (REGP) and Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY). Both these programmes are credit-linked capital subsidy schemes, which are implemented
through commercial banks. While the REGP is implemented by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), the PMRY is implemented by the State
Governments through the District Industries Centres (DICs).
 
6.         The formulation and implementation of policies and programmes/projects/schemes is undertaken by the Ministry with the assistance of its attached office,
public sector enterprise, statutory bodies and autonomous organisations, namely, Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Organisation (MSMEDO),
the National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. (NSIC), Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board and three national level entrepreneurship
development institutes, viz. National Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NIMSME), Hyderabad; National Institute for Entrepreneurship and
Small Business Development (NIESBUD), NOIDA   and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship (IIE), Guwahati. Government has set up the National Commission
for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS) to suggest policies and programmes for addressing the wide range of issues affecting the productive potential
of the large segment of unorganised micro and small productive units.
 
7.         Pursuant to enactment of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 and framing of Rules the reunder, the Government has also
established a National Board for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NBMSME) which is chaired by Minister(MSME), and interalia includes,
Member(VSE), Planning Commission as Deputy Chairperson and six ministers of state Governments, three MPs, Administrator of a Union Territory, five
Secretaries to Government of India, Chairman of the Board of Directors, NABARD, SIDBI, and Indian Banks Association, one officer of the RBI and two

representatives of Central Trade Union Organisations, three persons of eminence and 20 persons to represent the associations of MSMEs. Development
Commissioner (MSME) is the Member Secretary of the Board. The Board examines the factors effecting promotion and development of MSMEs and reviews
policies and programmes relating to these enterprises with a view to make recommendations on these matters to the Government.
 
8.         Subsequent to enactment of "Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006" by the  Parliament, the President under Notification dated

Ministries of  Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries has resulted in better coordination and synergy in implementation of various programmes /
schemes being implemented by various organisations of the Ministry.  It is felt that the present organizational set up is  very effective and efficient in achieving
the targets set out for the Ministry and efficient delivery of services under various programmes/schemes during 2007-08

17.       The Ministry of MS & ME  informed the  Committee On the Credit Support Programme which consists of the following three Schemes:
(a) Credit Guarantee Scheme: To ensure better flow of credit to micro and small enterprises by minimizing the risk perception of financial institutions and
banks in lending without collateral security, the Scheme was launched in August 2000. Under the scheme, guarantee cover is provided to collateral free credit
facility extended by member lending institutions (MLIs) to the new as well as existing small enterprises on loans up to Rs.50 lakh. The guarantee cover available
is up to 75% of the loans extended. The extent of guarantee cover is 80 per cent for (i) micro enterprises for loans up to Rs.5 lakh; (ii) MSEs operated and/or
owned by women; and (iii) all loans in the North-East Region. The lending institutions availing guarantee from the Trust have to pay one time guarantee fee of
1.5% and service charges of 0.75% per annum of the credit facility sanctioned. For all loans in the North-East Region, the one-time guarantee fee is only 0.75%.
For loans up to Rs.5 lakh, the one time guarantee fee is 1% and service charges is 0.5% per annum of the credit facility sanctioned. The scheme is operated by
the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), set up by the Government of India and Small Industries Development Bank of
India (SIDBI).
(b) Scheme of Micro Finance Programme
: The scheme was launched in March 2004 and has been tied up with the existing programme of Small Industries
Development Bank of India (SIDBI), which is under operation since January 1999, by way of contributing towards security deposits required from the Micro
Finance Institutions (MFIs)/ Non-Government Organisations (NGOs) to get loan from SIDBI. The Government of India provides funds for Micro Finance
Programme to SIDBI under the ‘Portfolio Risk Fund’ (PRF), which is used for security deposit requirement of the loan amount from the MFIs/NGOs. At present,
SIDBI takes fixed deposit equal to 10% of the loan amount. Of this, the share of MFIs/NGOs is 2.5% of the loan amount (i.e. 25% of security deposit) and
balance 7.5% (i.e. 75% of security deposit) is adjusted from the funds provided by the Government of India. The scheme is implemented by the Small Industries
Development Bank of India (SIDBI).
(c) Scheme on Trade Related Entrepreneurship Assistance and Development (TREAD) for Women
: The scheme has been designed to empower women
economically through the development of their entrepreneurial skills by eliminating constraints faced by them. It includes assistance in the form of loans, grants,
trade related training, trade information, counseling and extension activities relating to product and market development. Under the scheme, women
entrepreneurs from any part of the country may take up any non-farm activities in a group through reputed Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs).
 
18.       The Committee notes that the TREAD envisages the development of Micro/Tiny   Women Enterprises both  in rural   and urban areas. To make
this scheme  operational in real sense it feels that the number of  participating Banks  should be increased. It also feels that the associations who have
availed grants from M/o MS& ME should be made eligible for proper implementation after their evaluation. Even in Credit Guarantee Fund  Scheme
specific time limit by Banks for appraisal of project once the application is accepted by the banks , as the Scheme allows additional comfort to bank
through the CGTSI. The Guarantee cover under the Scheme should be enhanced  to Rs. 50 lakhs and priority should be given to women entrepreneurs
who are not able to provide security.
 
19.       The Committee also feels that the associations in MSME sector should be benchmarked by the Government of India and only the benchmarked
associations should be made eligible to represent the industrial sector at various forums

57.       On  support services to micro & small enterprises the Committee was apprised  that NSIC undertakes Performance and Credit Rating Scheme,

            Marketing Assistance Scheme: The main objectives of Marketing Assistance Scheme are to enhance the marketing competitiveness of the micro & small
enterprises, to provide them a platform for interaction with the individual / institutional buyers, to update them with prevalent market scenario and to provide
them a forum for redressing their problems. NSIC acts as a facilitator to promote marketing efforts and enhance the competency of the micro & small enterprises
for capturing the new market opportunities by way of organizing/ participating in various domestic & international exhibitions/trade fairs, buyers-seller meets,
intensive campaigns/seminars and consortia formation.
           
            Performance & Credit Rating Scheme: The Scheme is aimed to create awareness amongst micro & small enterprises about the strengths and weakness
of their existing operations and to provide them an opportunity to enhance their organizational strengths and credit worthiness. The rating under the scheme
serves as a trusted third party opinion on the capabilities and creditworthiness of the micro & small enterprises. An independent rating by an accredited rating
agency has a good acceptance from the Banks/Financial Institutions, Customers/Buyers and Vendors. Under this Scheme, rating fee to be paid by the micro &
small enterprises is subsidized for the first year only at the rate of maximum of 75% of the fee or Rs. 40000/-, whichever is less.
 
            Incubator for Small Enterprise Establishment: Enterprise Development, one of the thrust areas of the Corporation, can be achieved by way of providing
hand holding support to the aspiring entrepreneurs in selection and operation of selected enterprises. Incubation is one of the appropriate tools to achieve this
goal, as it provides necessary facilities for the prospective entrepreneurs and start up companies to learn product manufacturing processes coupled with
technology development, business development etc under one roof. At these incubators, working projects depicting appropriate technology for small
entrepreneurs are installed in working conditions. The main objectives of the schemes inter-alia include creating self employment opportunities, accelerating the
development of new small enterprises, providing integrated support by way of training on working projects.
            Small Enterprise Establishment Programme: This scheme is to facilitate establishment of new small enterprises by way of providing integrated services
in the areas of skill upgradation training, preparation of project reports, identification of plant and machinery, imparting technical training and credit facilitation
in order to boost the development of small enterprises and create employment opportunities.

86.       There was no major shift in plan/policy for 2007-08.  Although the physical targets for the year 2007-08 have been achieved, the funds utilization under
MSE-CDP has been low.  This is mainly due to the fact that the major portion of funds under this scheme are utilised for ‘hard interventions’ i.e. creation of
fixed assets in the form of setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFCs) etc.  In case of hard interventions, besides GoI assistance, contribution of Special
Purpose Vehicle (SPV) and State Government is also required. GoI assistance for hard interventions are released only after necessary infrastructure has been
created, state government/SPV has confirmed their contribution in the project and purchase orders have been placed.   Hence, there is always a time lag between
approval and disbursement of funds. Since in most of the CFCs, the necessary infrastructure is at various stages of completion, there was lesser demand for the
funds than originally envisaged at the beginning.  While 21 Common Facility Centres (CFCs) are in the pipeline for disbursement of funds with approval of GoI
assistance of Rs.4592.33 lakh, an amount of Rs.3302.98 lakh is yet to be released for these CFCs, because necessary information/action at the level of state
government/SPV is awaited.
 
87.       Under MSE Cluster Development Programmes and MSME Growth Pole Scheme (with an outlay of Rs.4580 lakh for 2008-09), the BE for MSE-CDP
component is Rs. 3700.00 lakh (including for NE Region). The corresponding physical target consist of interventions in  55 new clusters and diagnostic studies
for about 100 clusters . Presently there is no proposal for enhancing ceiling for project cost.
 
88.       The projects under MSE-CDP are being implemented by Ministry of MSME through its field offices/autonomous organizations, state government and
their autonomous bodies, National and International Institutions etc. or any institution/agency approved by the Ministry.   Two types of interventions are under
taken in the cluster under MSE-CDP, soft interventions and hard interventions.   Soft interventions are basically capacity building activities in the cluster where
no fixed assets are acquired or formed.  Soft interventions are implemented by a Cluster Development Executive (CDE) normally for a period of three years. 
Hard interventions involve creation of tangible assets like setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFCs), Mini Tool Rooms, Design Centres, Testing/Training
Centres, R&D Centres etc.  For hard interventions, it is necessary to form a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), which could be a registered society, or a cooperative
society, or company, or a trust or any other legal entity.  Contribution of the Ministry of MSME will not exceed 80% of the total project cost (90% in case of
clusters owned and/or  managed by women entrepreneurs) subject to a ceiling of Rs. 10.00 crore per project including Rs. 10.00 lakh for soft activities.   The
proposals for seeking financial assistance from Ministry of MSME are considered and approved by the Steering Committee of MSE-CDP under the
Chairmanship of Secretary (MSME) for project costing Rs.1.00 crore and above and of the Development Commissioner (MSME) for project costing less than
Rs. 1.00 crore. 
 
89.       In case of project implemented by the State Governments, their autonomous bodies and SPVs with the State Government as one of the stakeholders,
monitoring of the projects to ensure satisfactory and time bound implementation of the activities is the responsibility of the State Government concerned.   For
other projects, Ministry of MSME is directly monitoring the progress through is State level offices, i.e., MSME-DIs.
 
90.       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take proactive action to ensure that State Governments and other stake holders take
action in time bound     manner.       
 
Khadi and Village Industries
 
91.       The Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC), established under the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956, is a statutory
organization engaged in promotion and development of khadi and village industries for providing employment opportunities in the rural areas.  The KVIC has
been identified as one of the major organizations in the de-centralised sector for generating sustainable rural non-farm employment opportunities at low per
capita investment.  It undertakes activities like skill improvement, transfer of technology, research & development, marketing, etc., in the process of generating
employment/self-employment opportunities in the rural areas.
           
92.       The KVIC through its programmes and policies seeks to achieve – the social objective of providing employment in rural areas; the economic objective of
producing saleable articles; and the wider objective of creating self-relianace amongst the people and building up a strong rural community spirit.

126.     Earlier, financial assistance to the Khadi institutions were provided by the KVIC from its budgetary support provided by the Government. of India. 
However, with the expansion of khadi activities, it was felt necessary to avail bank loan and the Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme was

are issued in favour of them to mobilize loans from banks. The institutions are to pay only 4% of the interest and the difference between the 4% and the actual
rate of interest charged by the banks is paid as interest subsidy by the KVIC under its budgetary source. The difference in the ISEC issued by the KVIC and its
availment is mainly due to the difference in the assessment of Working Capital requirement by the khadi institutions.  The issue has been studied by a Committee
appointed by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in 1994 and it was suggested that if the difference in the assessment made by KVIC and Banks is less than 10%, banks
are to accept the fund assessment made by KVIC and finance the institutions accordingly. KVIC has taken up the issues related to ISEC in all seriousness and
entrusted a study on the scheme, to an expert outside agency.  It is expected that the study report will be available shortly and the future course of action will be

Workshed Scheme for Khadi Artisans
 
129.     It has been noticed that generally  the artisans, especially the spinners normally fall under the category of low-income group or below poverty line (BPL)
group.  The ‘Workshed Scheme for Khadi Artisans’ has been formulated for the artisans working in khadi sector on the lines of a similar scheme being
implemented by the Ministry of Textiles (Office of the Development Commissioner for Handlooms) for the handloom weavers. .  It aims at  providing a
workshed/place having about 20 square meters space per unit  to these artisans  which would considerably improve their work environment which in turn will not
only enhance their productivity and earnings but also prove  a major step in improving the quality of life.
 
130.     Around 38,000 khadi artisans are estimated to be provided facility of workshed during XI Plan. During 2008-09, it is proposed to provide facility of
worksheds to around 10000 kahdi artisans . The beneficiaries will be selected from all the Sates/UTs of the country, keeping in view the number of institutions
functioning in a State/UT
           
131.     The main objectives of this scheme to provide financial assistance for constructing workshed for khadi artisans to provide better ambiance by providing a
better workplace to enable them to carry out their spinning and weaving work efficiently, provide more space for housing their implements and storing
accessories, yarn, cloth, etc. ,provide a better, airy working place, thereby providing better hygienic conditions at the workplace, improve both quality and
productivity through improved facilities including electrical connection and lighting to the workshed and,provide adequate room for housing improved looms
and the design equipment like dobby, jacquard, etc.
           
132.     Since the scheme has not so far been finalized, the amount of Rs. 5 crore earmarked in BE 2007-08 has been reduced to Rs. 2.00 crore (including NER) in

earmarked for 2008-09

Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP
)
 
146.     Both PMRY and REGP are credit linked subsidy programmes with no financial contribution from State Governments to support entrepreneurs to set up
micro enterprises.  PMRY with its comparatively inferior design/subsidy parameters and lower recovery rate is proposed to be merged with REGP.  With slightly
higher level of subsidy to the projects at lower range of cost (upto Rs.5 lakh), focused identification in targeting of beneficiaries, improved monitoring,
implementation and verification processes, the merged scheme is expected to lead to increased participation of beneficiaries from rural areas in particular, setting
up Micro Enterprises leading to creation of entrepreneurs as well as indirect wage employment.   The proposal for merger and forming Prime Minister’s
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) has been recommended by Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC). PMRY and REGP are to be merged in 2008-
09.  PMEGP which  seeks to remove the anomalies between PMRY and REGP, targets marginalized sections of beneficiaries by earmarking the quantum of
Government subsidy, allocates higher proportion of  units to the marginalized sections for promoting inclusive growth, introduces electronic tracking of
applications, expand the EDP training (duration and content), associates Gram Panchayats and reputed NGOs for improved targeting and selection of
beneficiaries, updates project profiles in consultation with Banks, seeks aggressive publicity of Credit Guarantee Trust Fund Scheme and 100% verification of
projects that would be set up.    Rs. 823 crore have been provided in BEs 2008-09, out of which 740 crore would be towards subsidy and Rs. 83 crore would be
utilized for various backward forward linkages and meeting the residual claims of PMRY and REGP.

Scheme
  of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI)
 
151.     A scheme titled the “Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI)” has been launched by the Ministry in October, 2005 with a
view to developing around 100 traditional industry clusters (of khadi, village industry and coir) for comprehensive development over 5 years.  It is a central
scheme, and is being implemented by the Ministry without any share of financial contribution by the State/UTs. KVIC and Coir Board are the nodal agencies for
the scheme, which is the first  comprehensive initiative for focused regeneration of the khadi and village industries sector, based on the cluster development
methodology.  The 13 member Scheme Steering Committee (SSC) has approved 124 clusters (34 Khadi, 64 VI and 26 Coir) with additional clusters serving as a
reserve/cushion against any possible ‘dropouts’.  7 clusters have been launched in KVI Sector under this Scheme.  Annual  Action Plans and diagnostic study
reports have been approved for 71 clusters by Scheme Steering Committee (SSC).  Funding for hard component will commence in all these clusters in 2008-09
beginning with last quarter of 2007-08.  All approved clusters will be operationalised during 2008-09. 
 
152.     Implementing Agencies (IAs) under SFURTI are Non-Government Organizations (NGOs), institutions of the Central and State Governments and semi-
Government institutions with suitable expertise which undertake cluster development.  Generally, one IA has been assigned only one cluster.  The selection of
IAs, based on their regional reputation and experience of working at the grassroot level, has been done by the Nodal Agencies (NAs), with approval of SSC.
 
153.     The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (erstwhile Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries) is the co-ordinating Ministry providing overall
policy, coordination and management support to the Scheme.
 
154.     Under this scheme, 18 reputed national level institutions with expertise in cluster development methodology have been appointed as Technical Agencies
(TAs)  to provide technical support to the  Nodal Agencies (NAs) and the  Implementing Agencies (IAs).  The responsibilities of the TAs also include assisting
the NAs in identification of clusters, conducting training of the Cluster Development Executives (CDEs) and other officials of the IAs and NAs, validation of
cluster action plans, monitoring and evaluation, etc.
           
155.     The Cluster Development Executives (CDEs) have been appointed exclusively for each cluster and are located in the cluster on full time basis and
responsible for implementation of the Scheme in the assigned cluster.
 
156.     SFURTI envisages need-based assistance for replacement of production equipment, setting up of common facility centres (CFC), product development,
quality improvement, improved marketing, training and capacity building, etc. for selected development of clusters in KVI and coir sectors. Financial assistance
is provided for the interventions, also known as ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ components:
 
 
 
Hard Component-  75% - Govt. Grant and 25% - beneficiary’s grant
 
1.         Replacement of charkhas and looms in khadi sector.
2.         Setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFCs).
3.         Development of new products, new designs for various khadi and village industry (VI) products, new/improved packaging, etc.
 
Soft Component- 100% Govt. grant
 
1.         Market promotion activities.
2.         Capacity building activities, such as exposure visits to other clusters and institutions, need-based training, support for establishment of cluster level
networks (industry associations) and other need based support.
3.         Other activities identified by the Implementing Agency (IA) as necessary for the development of the cluster as part of the diagnostic study and included
in the Annual Action Plan for the cluster.

completed. Annual Action Plans and Cluster Development Coordination Groups (CDCG) have been formed in 95 clusters.

Coir Sector/Coir Board
 
164.     India is the largest coir producer in the world accounting for more than 80 per cent of the total world production of coir fibre. The coir sector in India is
very diverse and involves households, co-operatives, NGOs, manufacturers and exporters.        
 
165.     The coir industry employs more than 6.4 lakh persons of whom a majority are from rural areas belonging to the economically weaker sections of society. 
Nearly 80% of the coir workers in the fibre extraction and spinning sectors are women.           
 
166.     The development of coir industry has all along been in areas where there is a concentration of coconut trees and availability of coconut husk. 
Historically, the coir industry started and flourished in Kerala which has a long coast line, lakes, lagoons  and backwaters providing natural conditions required
for retting.  However, with the expansion of coconut cultivation, coir industry has picked up in the States of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa,
West Bengal, Assam, Tripura, Pondicherry and the Union Territories of Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands through the efforts of Coir Board.
 
167.     It was informed to the Committee that the Coir Board is a statutory body established under the Coir Industry Act, 1953 for promoting the overall
development of the coir industry and uplifting of the living conditions of the workers engaged in this traditional industry.  The Coir Board consists of a full-time
Chairman and 39 Members representing all stakeholders in the coir industry.          
 
168.     The functions of the Coir Board for the development of coir industry include undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and
development activities; collection of statistics relating to exports and internal consumption of coir and coir products; development of new products and designs;
publicity for promotion of exports and internal sales; marketing of coir and coir products in India and abroad; preventing unfair competition among producers
and exporters; assisting in the establishment of units for the manufacture of products; promoting co-operative organizations among producers of husk, coir fibre,
coir yarn and manufacturers of coir products; ensuring remunerative returns to producers and manufacturers, etc.
           
169.     In order to continue existing and implement new schemes an outlay of Rs.55 crore has been kept for 2008-09 as per the details given below:-
 
            Plan General-Coir Board is looking after the promotion, growth and development of the coir industry.  The Coir Board is implementing a number of
schemes for the coir sector which include training extension, quality improvement, Mahila Coir Yojana (MCY) and welfare measures.  MCY envisages
distribution of motorized ratts to the trained women artisans.  Under the scheme of development of production infrastructure, financial assistance is provided for
setting up new coir units and for modernization of existing units.  Coir Board also undertakes number of activities for domestic and export market promotion.  
An outlay of Rs.23 crore has been kept for the year for these activities.   It is expected that with these initiatives, production of coir fibre will be increased from
4,70,000 MT (target for the year 2007-08) to 5,00,000 MT during the year 2008-09.  Employment opportunities will be provided to 6.90 lakh persons
(cumulative) at the end of the year in comparison to 6.60 lakh target fixed for the previous year.  The export of coir and coir products will be enhanced from
Rs.680 crore to Rs.750 crore at a growth rate of 10.2% over the previous year.
            Plan S&T -     The fund under this head are utilized for the Researach & Development activities of the Coir Board which are carried out through its
Research Institutes. In the Science and Technology projects undertaken by Coir Board, emphasis is given on process improvement in the extraction of fibre,
pollution free retting process, reduction in the period of retting, modernization of production infrastructure, product development, product diversification etc. 
These projects will demonstrate possibility of reducing drudgery in work, improving the quality of Coir products and introducing new products/processes.  Rs.7
crore has been kept under this head for the year 2008-09.
