against sanctioned cases as utilization of funds that was prevalent under the earlier REGP 
scheme to a more challenging system of release of funds to implementing agencies only

under PMEGP. Stricter financial discipline and proper appreciation of this requirement by 
implementing agencies and financing / nodal bank branches in particular were required, which 
took time. Pil ot project for establishing ‘one bank one nodal branch ’ concept to reduce the 
time taken in release of funds to the beneficiaries has also been discussed with selected banks 
for improving the performance.

appointment of Cluster Development Executive (CDE) from amongst the eminent Khadi 
workers having a good understanding of Khadi sector ,  so that CDE could play an active 
and catalyst role in this regard .  This role will further strengthened if  the technical 
agency appointed under the scheme provides suitable technical support at the same 
time.  In view of the important role played by SFURTI scheme for cluster development 
the Committee desires that it should continue for 2010 -11 and should be ex tended to 
continue further.  
 
102.  The Committee views with concern that non utilization o f money earmarked for 
a specific purpose is the poor reflection on the face of the premier institution like KVIC.  
The Committee recommends that t he money allocated s hould be utilized properly and 
put to better use.   
 
103. The Committee observes that inspite of KVIC ’s repeated request, funds flow to 
KVI Institutions from commercial Banks under ISEC is not up to the desired level.  The 
committee while discussing the is sue with some commercial banks found to its dismay  
that the scheme has not been properly publicized and even top brass of banks and 
financial institutions providing loans to entrepreneurs are not aware of this.  The 
Committee is therefore concerned to not e that KVIC is not pursuing all its schemes 
/policies seriously and strictly to reach out to the entrepreneurs properly.    
104. The Committee recommends that KVIC should take steps to generate internal 
resources on its own so that its dependency on budget ary resources of the Government is 
reduced by evolving suitable mechanism like aggressive marketing of KVI products, 
brand building and so on to become self reliant which is still lacking and is not 
frequently seen either in print media or electronic media  despite the claims made by 
KVIC. 
 
105. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry and KVIC to make all out efforts in 
the form of special drive in the states/districts where it is not so successful.  
 
106. Looking on the performance of the KVIC in North Eas t Region the Committee is 
of the  opinion  that KVIC should set  up more central silver plants in North East Region 
and provide them support in the form of grant in lieu of working capital so that the 
production activities in North East Region are enhanced a nd thus creating more 
employment and development of economic conditions.  


 30 
107. The Committee recommends that KVIC should  strive hard to bridge the gap 
between sanctioned cases and actual disbursal of loans.  The number of beneficiaries 
should be increased  and if deemed fit the allocation may be increased at RE stage.

should be promoted in a way so that it may replace the rebate on khadi slowly and 
gradually.  Since the  common m en’s sentiments attached to khadi for a  long time, it

commensurate with the prices and thus it is no longer  within  the reach of the poor man.

   Coir Board  
 
123. The Coir Board is a statutory body established under the Coir Industry Act, 1953 for 
promoting overall development of the coir industry and improving the living conditions of the 
workers engaged in the traditional industry. The coir industry employs more than 6.50 lakh 
persons of whom majority is from rural areas belonging to the economically weaker sections 
of society.  Nearly 80%  of the coir workers in the fibre extract ion and spinning sectors are 
women. The activities of the Board for development of coir industries, inter -alia, include 
undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and development activities; 
developing new products & designs; and marketing  of coir and coir products in India and 
abroad.  It also promotes co -operatives  organizations among producers of husks, coir fiber, 
coir yarn and manufacturers of coir products; ensuring remunerative returns to producers and 
manufactures, etc.  The Board has promoted two research for undertaking research activities 
on different aspects of coir industry, which is one of the major agro based rural industries in 
the country.  
 
 


 33

Industries 
(ii) Scheme for Training, Extension Quality Improvement Mahila Coir Yojana 
and Welfare Measures 
(iii) Science and Technology 
(iv) Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries  (SFURTI)

128. The Committee was informed that in the coir industry spinning is the main area 
where women are working.  The industry need upgradation of spinning machines by 
making lot of chan ges, removing the drudgery and have higher income for the workers.

carry bags, Venetian blinds, upholstery etc. 
 
130. For production of finer coir yarn partial success has been achieved by blending coir 
with sisal, mainly to produce good yarn.  However, there is a need to develop machinery for 
proper blending with different types of fibre so as to get the best quality yarn.  As a result of 
this light weight coir nets will be developed for providing shades on the sea beaches and for 
roof gardening,  so as to protect the persons and the plants against the UV light.

only up to Rs. 1 crore but according to Ministry of MSME it should be upto Rs. 10 
crores.  The Committee therefore  recommends that this issue should be examined and 
the capital investment subsidy should be increased to Rs. 10 crores and the capital 
investment subsidy and the interest subsidy should be allowed in the Coir sector for its 
overall growth.

common Effluent Treatment Plant for that entire area and for that seeking permission 
to transport the coir waste in closed Trucks from the factories to the plant but the

Committee desires that the Ministry of MSME take up the issue with the State 
Government of Kerala to solve the problems of Coir units in the State.

big plant is set up by the Government the power problem of the coir industry can b e 
solved and Government can also generate revenue.  The committee desires that Ministry 
of MSME take up the issue with the State government of Kerala in this regard and 
pursue the matter for positive conclusion.

150. National Small Industries Corporation, established in 1955, has been working with its 
mission of promoting, aiding an d fostering the growth of micro, small and medium 
enterprises.  It has been working to promote the interest of micro, small and medi um 
enterprises and to enhance their competitiveness by providing integrated support services 
under Marketing, Technology, Credit and Support services.  
 


 37 
151. The C orporation has been introducing several new schemes from time to time for 
meeting the change aspirations of the micro, small & medium enterprises.  The main objective 
of these schemes is to promote the interest of the micro, small & medium enterprises (MSME) 
and to put them in competitive and advantageous positions.  The schemes of NSIC have been 
found to be very useful in stimulating the growth of micro, small and medium enterprises in 
the country.  
  
152. The Committee appreciates that t o make regular and timely availability of the raw 
materials to MSME’s for their smooth operations, NSIC has made arrangements with the bulk 
manufactures for providing raw materials to the MSMEs at competitive rates.  In case the 
MSME un it needs any credit support, NSIC provides financial assistance for raw material 
procurement by making the payment to suppliers. Any unit seeking this facility may approach 
to any office of the Corporation and submit its application in the prescribed forma t. The 
branch office after evaluating the proposal of unit sanctions the limit to the unit. The unit is 
required to provide a Bank Guarantee of the sanctioned value to NSIC to start availing the 
Raw Material Assistance on credit. 
                 
153.     The manufacturers of aluminum conductors has availed the highest credit facility and 
wax product manufacturing sector has taken the lowest credit facility under our Raw Material 
Assistance Scheme during the current financial year.  
 
154. NSIC has been impl ementing two schemes on behalf of the Government. These two 
schemes are Performance & Credit Rating Scheme & Marketing Assistance Scheme.  
 
Performance & Credit Rating Scheme: NSIC has been implementing “Performance & 
Credit Rating Scheme” for micro and small enterprises (MSEs) on behalf of the Government. 
The scheme is being operated through 06 accredited rating agencies i.e. CRISIL, SMERA, 
ONICRA, CARE, FITCH and ICRA. The Scheme is aimed to create awareness amongst 
micro & small enterprises about the strengths and weakness of their existing operations and to 
provide them an opportunity to enhance their organizational strengths and credit worthiness. 
The rating under the scheme serves as a trusted third party opinion on the capabilities and 
creditworthiness of the micro & small enterprises. An independent rating by an accredited 
rating agency has a good acceptance from the Banks/Financial Institutions, Customers/Buyers 
and Vendors. Under this Scheme, rating fee to be paid by the micro & small enterprises is  
subsidized for the first year only and that is subject to maximum of 75% of the fee or Rs. 
40000/-, whichever is less.  During the year 2008-09, Rs. 7.15 crore was released to NSIC for 
meeting the expenditure under Performance & Credit Rating Scheme. As t he scheme has 
been getting good response from micro & small enterprises, during the year 2008 -09 rating 
was assigned to 5011 units which has resulted into deficit of Rs. 11.71 crore as on 31.3.2009. 
In the year 2009 -10, approx 7500 units would be rated und er the scheme. Hence, the 
budgetary provision in RE 2009 -10 has been increased from Rs. 20.90 crore to Rs. 40.00 
crore, which includes Rs.3.27    Crore for the sub-plans( NER, SCSP, TSP). As this scheme is 
demand driven and proposals from the MSEs of sub -plan categories have not been received 
for rating under the scheme, Rs. 3.18 crore has been surrendered.  
 
Marketing Assistance Scheme:   The main objectives of Marketing Assistance Scheme are to 
enhance the marketing competitiveness of the micro & small ent erprises, to provide them a 
platform for interaction with the individual / institutional buyers, to update them with 
prevalent market scenario and to provide them a forum for redressing their problems. NSIC 
acts as a facilitator to promote marketing effort s and enhance the competency of the micro & 


 38 
small enterprises for capturing the new market opportunities by way of organizing / 
participating in various domestic & international exhibitions/trade fairs, buyers -seller meets, 
intensive campaigns/seminars and other marketing promotion activities.  
 
  155.  NSIC helps micro and small enterprises to participate in International/national 
exhibitions/trade fairs at the subsidized rates to exhibit and market their products. 
Participation in the marketing events pro vides micro & small enterprises an exposure to the 
national/international markets. Bulk and departmental buyers are invited to participate in 
buyer-seller meets to bring them closer to the small enterprises for enhancing their marketing 
competitiveness. Th ese programmes are aimed at vendor developments from small 
enterprises for the bulk manufactures. Intensive campaigns and other marketing events are 
organized all over the country to disseminate/ propagate about the various schemes for the 
benefit of the m icro & small enterprises and  to enrich their knowledge  w.r.t. the latest 
developments, quality standards etc. 
 
156.    RE 2009-10 is having provision of Rs. 10 .00 crore which would be utilized fully for 
meeting the expenditure on marketing promotion activities under the scheme.

 40

 The Committee, therefore recommends that the recommendations of the Task

INTRODUCTION 
 
  
 I, the Chairman of the Departme nt-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Industry, having   been authorized by the Committee, hereby 
present this Two Hundred and Eighteenth Report on the Revival and Restructuring 
Of Hindustan Paper Corporation L imited pertaining to Department of Heavy 
Industry. 
 
2. The Committee held detailed discussion with Hindustan Paper Corporation  
Limited at Guwahati on 25th October, 2010.  The representative of the Department 
of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Indus tries and Public Enterprises) was also 
present there. 
 
3. I thank the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises 
(Department of Heavy Industry) and Hindustan Paper Corporation  Limited for 
furnishing the valuable inputs during the meetings.  
 
4.  The Committee in its meeting held on 15th February, 2011 considered and 
adopted the report. 
 
   
Tiruchi Siva 
Chairman

New Delhi 
15 FEBRUARY, 2011 
 
 
(ii) 
 

 
 
REPORT 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
The framework of mixed economy adopted in our country after 
we attained independence  encompassed in its sc ope the vital role of 
both the public and private sector s for regenerating our economy 
which suffered retardation due to cent uries of colonial rule. At that 
point of time the magnitude of the task involving the massive scale of 
investment and employment of expe rtise and technolo gy was beyond 
the capability of the private sector. Therefore the State through public 
sector enterprises remained in the forefront for laying the foundation 
of our economy, genera ting employment oppo rtunities for people, 
addressing the challenge of ba lanced regional development and 
ushering the process of industrialisa tion. It was the responsibility of 
unparalleled significance for building infrastructure for the revival and 
growth of our economy so that other players could play their 
legitimate role in the field of bu siness and the larger interests of 
society and nation are served. No wonder that our first Prime Minister 
Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru hailed th e PSEs as the commanding heights 
of economy. The growth and devel opment of our country and the 
accelerated movement to register new heights of progress owes a lot to 
the basic and substant ial work done by the PSEs in the formative 
period of our nation building.  T he prominent leaders  of the private 
sector have duly acclaimed the perf ormance of the PSEs in taking the 
country forward and creat ing supporting conditions for unleashing the 
economic and entrepreneurial poten tial of our people. While taking 
due note of the role played by t he PSEs in serving the nation, it is 
important to be mindful of the fact  that we have not  been able to 
harness their full potential. In spit e of the monopoly enjoyed by them, 
some of these enterprises b ecame sick and unviable due to 
inefficiency, bureaucratic control and many other factors. 
 
2. With the onset of reforms u ndertaken to deregulate our economy 
to a considerable extent the era marked by a protective environment  
 
 
 

2 
 
for the functioning of the public sector has come to an end. The 
process of economic globalisation an d the progressive integration of 
Indian economy with the worl d economy have created a new 
competitive and challenging environm ent for all segments of industry 
which includes the public sector enterprises. The advantages these 
enterprises had before the economic reforms are no more there. A new 
and expanding enviro nment marked by comp etition, innovation, 
adoption of new technologies and  varied and improved customer 
preferences is determining the cour se of trade and commerce. The 
trend of our new geo-economic age is  customer entitlement for wide 
variety of choices, continuously improved quality of product and 
efficient and fast delivery of services.  
 
3. These revolutionary changes have altered the way in which 
business is conducted. The Public Sector Enterprises have no option 
but to remain tuned to these chan ges and adopt innovative ways to 
improve their productivity and com petitive edge. They have to raise 
the bar of their performance and at the same time discharge their 
obligations to society which constitute their core mandate. Even as it is 
a formidable challenge and arduous task, it is doable. While displaying 
managerial competence these enterpri ses have to live up to the social 
commitment. It demands high degree  of entrepreneurial ability and 
innovative practices. Many of ou r PSEs have set an example of 
combining these two core aspects.  
 
4. The Prime Minister of our country Dr. Manmohan Singh has 
categorically stated that the Government of India is committed to a 
strong and effective public sector pu rsuing both social objectives and 
commercial principles. It is hearte ning to note that the Standing

 Hindustan Paper Corporation Ltd. (HPCL), Nagaon & Cachar

Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited (HPC) 
An Over View of Paper Industry 
 
9. In our scheme of industrial development the paper industry 
occupies a prominent place. Since our freedom from British rule it has 
forged ahead and registered im pressive progress by congenial 
atmosphere created by the Governme nt in extending support which 
includes fiscal incentives. In spite of shutting down of  98 units with a 
capacity of 1.1 million mt due to their non-compliance with 
environmental standards, we have in our country  around 666 units by 
the completion of the tenth five year plan with the installed capacity to 
produce 8.50 million mt of paper and paper board. The 5.80 million mt 
we produce is indicativ e of the capacity utilisa tion of these units. The 
Paper industry is rated as one of the 35 high priority industries in India 
and is presently growin g at a rate of 6.3% per annum. The magnitude 
of its importance is indicated by its annual turnover which stands at 
approximately Rs.17000 crore. It gives about Rs.2500 crore to the 
national exchequer. It creates dire ct employment opportunities for 0.3 
million people and indirect employ ment opportunities for around 1 
million people. All these facts br ing out its significance for our 
economy.  
 
10.  India is self sufficient in pr oducing a wide variety of papers and 
paper boards to meet our requirements and our dependence on imports 
is limited to some special varietie s such as coated  paper and cheque 
paper. We stand unfavourably with many developed countries and  

5 
 
even some of the Asian countries which include China and other East 
Asian countries in terms of per capita  use of paper. While ours is 7.2 
kg, China is way ahead of us with 45 kg and the figures for the East 
Asian countries is more than doub le that of India. However there 
seems to be good future prospects fo r the industry.  This is due to 
strong possibility for increasing de mand for paper in our country on 
account of growth in economic activities, rise  in literacy rate and 
expansion of opportunities to our growing population to have greater 
access to education and learning.  
 
11. To prepare itself to meet the growing demand fo r paper in our 
country the industry has to adop t new technology in place of the 
existing ones which ar e not helpful to face the new challenges. The 
failure of the industry in doing this will arrest its growth and 
expansion. High production cost com bined with pollution the industry 
causes has always been its major problem. Besides, the quality of the 
paper manufactured by our paper mills does not match with the 
international standards. These issu es are of paramount importance 
which merit serious attention.   
 
12. One of the major constraints faced by the industry is the 
restricted availability of raw materi al.  While wood and agro products 
required by many paper mills are met from indigenous sources the raw 
material in the form of waste paper and wood pulp used in other mills 
are imported. The quantity of importe d raw material and its cost has 
been increasing over the years. Availability of inadequate raw material 
particularly the wood and agro based raw material is the most 
important reason behind lack of growth of industry.  
 
13. Thus, the issue of technological  obsolescence and accessibility to 
raw material has to be addressed boldly by the industry to keep it 
competitive. Besides, efficient and prudent use of water and energy 
and measures to properly treat effl uent discharged by it will go a long 
way in making the industry environment friendly.

manufacturing of paper in the units  of the HPC located in the north-
eastern region. The Committee was informed that due to the  
 

 
13

may make a difference between succ ess and failure.  I have no doubt 
that the normal government procedure applied to a public enterprise of 
this kind will lead to the failure of that public enterprise”. 
 
47. In recalling these words of Pr ime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru we 
need to pay serious attention to the issues involving the effective 
functioning of the HPC.  Quick decis ions have to be taken to address 
the concerns and constraints fa ced by the Hindustan Paper 
Corporation.  These concerns and constraints are genuine and sound.  
Quick decisions have to  be taken by the Ministry of Railways, the 
Department of Heavy Industries, the Government of Assam and all the 
stakeholders for making the HPC an  efficient, effective and socially 
responsible enterprise.

INTRODUCTION 
 
  
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Industry, having been aut horized by the Committee, hereby 
present this Two Hundred and Nine teenth Report on the Revival and 
Restructuring of C ement Corporation of India Limited pertaining to the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public  Enterprises (Department of Heavy 
Industry)  
 
2. The Committee held de tailed discussion with C ement Corporation of 
India Limited at Guwahati on 25 th October, 2010.  The representative of the 
Department of Heavy Industry (Minis try of Heavy Industry and Public 
Enterprises) was also present there. 
 
3. I thank the Ministry of Heavy I ndustries and Public Enterprises 
(Department of Heavy Industry) and C ement Corporation of India 
Limited for furnishing the valuable inputs during the meetings.  
 
4.  The Committee in its meeting held on 15 th February, 2011 
considered and adopted the report. 
  
Tiruchi Siva 
Chairman                          
Department related Parliamentary 
                                         Standing Committee   on   Industry 
 
New Delhi 
15 February, 2011 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 

REPORT 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
One of the defining features of modern civilisation is the 
foundation of durable and concrete structures by extensively employing 
cement. As the construction activit y occupies central place in the 
expanding economic domain, the manufacture and use of cement assumes 
greater and critical importance. In fact it is well said that fifty per cent of 
all investment takes place in the cons truction sector which is nothing but 
steel and cement. Our accelerated constructio n activities and the 
expanding work in the infrastructur e projects are critically dependent on 
the quality and quantity of  cement used.  The i ndispensability of cement 
to further the modernisation process has been well documented.  Cement 
is, therefore, a critical ingredient for augmenting growth and development 
of our economy and advancem ent of the country as a whole. That is why 
our national leadership accorded due importance to the manufacture of 
adequate cement right since our independence. Within  the scheme of 
mixed economy conceived to rebuild  and modernise India the public 
sector was assigned crucial responsib ility to provide leadership in the 
sphere of cement production. A few y ears before the Cement Corporation 
of India was set up the se cond five year plan docum ent justly stated that 
“The output of cement ...is an im portant indicator of the volume of 
investment in the econo my...” and observed, “C ement ranks next in 
importance to iron and steel as a de velopmental commodity and hence a 
high place has to be given to it in the scheme of priorities.” The 
incorporation of the Cement Corpor ation of India (CCI) as a wholly 
Government of India Enterprise in 196 5, when the third five year plan 
was being implemented was a step to achieve that grand objective.  Later 
during 1970 and 1990 eleven cement plants were set up by the CCI in 
socially and economically backward regions of our country to produce  
 

2 
enough cement for meeting the growing demand in the market for this 
“developmental commodity”.  
 
2. It is important to note that as  part of a well formulated national 
plan for industrialisation of our co untry particularly of the backward 
regions’ a conscious decisi on was taken to locate i ndustrial units in areas 
which had no industry worth the name. Dispersal of industry was 
accorded importance for balanced regi onal development. In fact the third 
five year plan document observed, “P reference... has al ways been given 
to the location of the public sector pr ojects in relatively backward areas 
whenever this could be done without  significant prejudice to technical 
and economic considerations; and this  will be the guiding principle for 
the future also. Similarly in the li censing of private sector projects the 
claims of underdeveloped regions have generally been kept in view to the 
extent possible”.   
 
3. The eleven cement plants established in the remote and 
economically backward areas were to be  the nucleus of development of 
those regions. It was expected that  those units would spur economic 
activities and help remove their back wardness. Therefore, the decision to 
set up these units were taken not so lely on the basis of economic 
considerations but also on the basis of the larger objective of promoting 
development and growth of areas untouched by industrial development.  
 
4. The units of the Cement Corpor ation of India were established in 8 
States/Union Territories of India. Th e details of the locations of each 
plant are given below.  
 
 
  

3 
1.Bokajan                                    Assam 
2.Rajban                                Himachal Pradesh 
3.Tandur                                Andhra Pradesh 
4.Mandhar                              Chhattisgarh 
5.Kurkunta                              Karnataka 
6.Nayagaon                            Madhya Pradesh 
7.Akaltara                               Chhattisgarh 
8.Charkhi Dadri                       Haryana 
9.Adilabad                             Andhra Pradesh 
10.Delhi                                        Delhi 
11.Yerraguntla                       Andhra Pradesh 
 
5. It is extremely significant to note that out of th e abovementioned                     
11 plants only three plants at serial numbers 1 to 3 ar e operational. The 
Yerraguntla plant at serial number 11 was sold out to M/s India Cements 
Ltd. on 21 January 1998 for R s. 200.70 crore to meet  the demand of 
creditors as per the directions of Ho n’ble BIFR. Therefore, as of now,   
seven units are non-operating plants. The total installed capacity of all the 
plants was 42.48 lakh MT which is less than 2% of total installed capacity 
of India.  However, the installed cement capacity of three operating plants 
is 14.46 LMT and in contrast the in stalled capacity of 7 non-operating 
plants stands at 24.52LMT. The authorised share capital of the CCI is Rs. 
900 crore, whereas its net wo rth as on 31 March 2010 is (-) Rs.213.61 
crore and its net profit during 2009-10 is Rs. 52.75 crore. In spite of 
incurring heavy losses for several ye ars it could genera te profit during 
2006 and 2010 which is a positive sign. Its manpower as per the 
presentation made before the Committe e in Guwahati stands at 1037 as 
on 30 September 2010 with 117 Exec utives, 174 supervisiors and 746 
workers.  The figures for productivity per  employee  are going  up  from  

4 
600 MT during 2005-06 to  898 during 2009-10.  A ll the above facts have 
to be seen in the context of the vi sion and mission of the Corporation.  
While its vision is “To emerge as one  of the leading cement companies 
committed to contribute to the eco nomy and to enhance value for the 
stakeholders” its mission is “To a ugment the wealth creation for the 
company, deliver superior product and sustain market value.” 
 
6. The vision and mission sound audaci ous in the face of the installed 
capacity of only three operating plants and many other complex 
challenges confronting the Corporati on. However, its performance has to 
be seen against India’s position as th e second largest cement producing 
country in the world after China.  The per capita consumption of cement 
in our country is 156 kg which is quite low as compared to Thailand, 
Vietnam, USA and Dubai. While in case of Thailand and Vietnam, per 
capita consumption of cement is 400 kg, in case of  the USA and Dubai it 
is 800 kg and 4000 kg, respectively.  The Eleventh Five year Plan 
document noted that “Cement consum ption has generally grown at 2%-
3% higher than growth of GDP. Ke eping the past trends in view and 
taking into consideration the rene wed emphasis on infrastructure, the 
cement industry can be e xpected to grow at a bout 11% corresponding to 
the GDP growth of 9%”. With the accelerated growth  of construction 
work the requirement for cement will also get multiplied.  Therefore, the 
prospect for cement indu stry is very bright. In  the context of growing 
demand for cement, the Cement Corporat ion of India has to take the best 
foot forward for taking advantage of the situation and for becoming a key 
player for supplying quality cement to the expanding market. 
 
7. The Committee painfully notes that the Cement Corporation of 
India suffered huge losses right since the inception of the operation of  
 

5 
its plants.  The Corporation cited ho st of reasons for incurring such 
losses.  One of the key reasons, ac cording to the Corporation, was the 
very location of the cement fact ories in areas which did not have 
ample infrastructural facilities.  Th ose areas where these plants were 
set up did not have minimum ameniti es and conveniences in the form 
of township, communit y centres and health centres, etc. The 
investment made by the Corporation for the availability of such basic 
facilities added extra cost to its primary responsibility for producing 
cement. Over and above the cost required for the manufacture of 
cement, these facilities escalated its expenditure and, therefore, 
contributed to the over-capitalisat ion of the project. The Committee 
was informed by the officials of the Corporation that such extra 
burden in building up bare minimum facilities constituted a major 
factor behind the higher cost of production of cement. The 
background note supplied to th e Committee noted “Almost every 
plant of CCI has been over-capitali sed due to time and cost overrun 
resulting in very high interest an d depreciation costs. This has 
resulted in very high fixed costs of these plants as compared to the 
industry standards”.   
8. It is rather sad to note that some of the plants had to bear 
enormous expenditure for the purpo se of getting access to quarry 
which is located in a very difficult  and rough terrain .  For instance, 
the topography of the quarry for the Bokajan and Rajban Plants was 
such that it required extra cost  for mining the raw material and 
transporting it by employing ropeways. It seems that these plants had 
to face a hurdles race for producing  cement and at the same time 
develop the region by their manufactur ing activities.  It is distressing 
that owing to such factors the company could never register profit up 
to the year 2004-05 barring insignificant profits on few occasions.   
 

6 
9. The Corporation continued to incur loss which subsequently 
assumed proportion of a crisis.  Earlier in 2006 the Committee expressed 
its serious concern on the recurring lo sses of the CCI when it presented 
192nd Report after examining The Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited 
(Acquisition and Transfer of Undert aking) Amendment Bill, 2006. Over 
the years the mounting losses sharply eroded its net worth.  By the middle 
of 1990s the Committee wa s informed that the CCI suffered accumulated 
losses to the tune of Rs. 527.16 crore.   That staggering amount was more 
than it’s paid up capital of Rs.  406.74 crore and reserves worth Rs. 0.99 
crore.  The collapse of the net wort h sounded alarm bell to safeguard the 
very survival and commercial viability  of the Corporation.  It graduated 
from a loss making Corporation to a sick industrial undertaking. It, 
therefore, resulted in its reference to the BIFR under section 15(1) of 
CISA and was declared sick in August 1996.   
 
10. The crisis was further aggravated  when the accumulated loss of the 
Corporation by 31 Marc h 2005 mounted up to Rs. 2152.86 crore which 
sharply stood in contrast to its paid up capital of Rs. 429.28 crore.  Its net 
worth went to the sub-zero level and became nega tive.  It was worth               
Rs. 1723.58 crore.  All those catastr ophic developments took place even 
before the rehabilitation scheme was approved by the BIFR.  
 
11. In face of such gathering crisis of negative net worth, the 
Corporation had absolutely no mean s of modernising its units or 
upgrading technology and production and operation process.  At a time, 
when the cement industry in Indi a was looking up due to accelerated 
economic, industrial and construction activities, the Cement Corporation 
of India was in dire straits. Its difficult conditions were further 
compounded  by  its  inability to  have  its  captive  power  plants  and  its  
 

7 
reliance on the power s upplied by the electricity  boards of different 
States.  Erratic supply of power a nd even frequent breakdown of power 
made available to the plants  becam e one of the important factors behind 
its reduced output which over a period of  time led to the closure of some 
of its plants. 
 
12. In 1990, the Government of India came out with a slew of 
measures in favour of the cement i ndustry in the form of transport 
subsidy and capital subsidy and waiver of excise duty  and sales tax.  The 
new plants commissioned in remote and backward regions or the old ones 
already functioning there and expa nding their capacity for producing 
more cement were eligible for those benefits. While the  private players 
could avail of those incentives the Cement Corporation of India, however, 
lagged behind as it hardly could take any step for capacity addition.   
 
13. The Committee was also  told that the Corporation could not at all 
match up to the cut throat compe tition in the relatively open market 
which witnessed more supply of cement  much in excess of the demand.  
It was further accentuated by the r ecession which affected very badly the 
cement industry till 2004-05.  
  
14. The escalating loss of the Corpora tion remained at the root of its 
multiple problems.  It went from one cris is to another.  Even its working 
capital declined to an alarming leve l and eventually got depleted. There 
was no option for the Corpor ation to overcome it other than resorting to 
short term borrowings at  very high interest rate. The Committee was 
informed that the taking over of the sick Charkhi Dadri Unit of the 
erstwhile Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. and the failure of the management in  
 
 

8 
making available functional Directors to carry out key responsibilities 
such as Marketing, Finance and Oper ations also constituted major factors 
behind the sickness of the Corpora tion. Absence of clear guidelines to 
deal with non-operating un its which have been cl osed down for almost a 
decade and thereby imposing a heavy burden on the functioning units and 
draining their working capital further compounded the financial crisis. As 
a result employees had to go without salaries and arrear s in this respect 
went up to a very high level. The loss of morale of the employees hit hard 
the operations of the Corporation and contributed to its decline.   
 
15. The Committee notes with concern that the Cement 
Corporation of India which was est ablished to be a leading player in 
manufacturing cement and pr omoting balanced regional 
development had to go through such tr agic state of affairs.  It also 
notes with concern that no attempt was made for renovation, 
replacement and modernisation of its plants .  In the background note 
supplied to the Committee, it has been  stated under the heading ‘Future 
Strategy for Sustainable Revival’ that  “The company learning from past 
mistakes plans to continue to invest  a part of its pr ofit for renovation, 
replacement, modernisation of its plan ts so as to keep them updated and 
avoid occurrence of obsolescence  of technology in future”. The 
Committee feels that the Corporation committed a costly mistake.  It 
is heartening to note that the Corporation has adopted a future 
strategy for sustainable revival one of the key components of which is 
to use part of its profit fo r modernisation and renovation.  In fact, the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan dealing w ith the cement i ndustry has observed 
that “The industry has been modernising and some units can now boast of 
having the state of the art technol ogy plants with energy consumption 
comparable  with  the  best in  the  world”.  The  Committee is happy to  
 

9 
note that the officials of the Corporation are hopeful to not only 
register profit but also compete wi th the key players in the market.  
In fact, in its presentation befo re the Committee, the Corporation 
outlined the measures taken to turn around the company. The 
Committee sincerely feels that the stress given on expansion and 
modernisation of the operating plants would result in its revival and 
progress.   
16. The Committee also takes note of  the fact that the Corporation 
is introducing new product range su ch as 53-S Grade, special cement 
for manufacturing Railw ay sleepers and also introducing cement 
brand names Maha shakti (43 Gr ade), Param shakti (53 Grade), 
Poorna shakti (33 Grade) and Jal shakti (33 Grade PPC) for better 
brand image.   
17. The Committee was informed of the follow ing additional 
measures taken by the Corpor ation to make it buoyant and 
profitable.    
(1) Adopting aggressive marketing by entering into 
marketing alliance with reputed industrial houses. 
(2) Advertising campaign, TV hoardings, glow signs, wall 
paintings, etc., by allocating a budget of Rs.0.50 per bag. 
(3) Reducing employees’ strength  by introducing Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme with the assistance of Government of 
India. 
(4) Boosting of employee’s morale by clearing their dues and 
cultivating confidence amongst them. 
(5) Employees’ participation in decision making process. 
 

10 
(6) Cost reduction in all areas of activities, i.e., controlling of 
operational and non-operational costs. 
(7) Revenue generation by utilising idle infrastructure.   
18.  The rehabilitation scheme sanc tioned by the Hon’ble BIFR on 3 
May 2006 suggested closure of seven unviable plants located in Mandhar, 
Kurkunta, Akaltara, Charkhi Dadri , Delhi Grinding  Unit/Bhatinda 
Grinding unit, Nayagaon and Adilabad and sale of assets of those plants 
through Asset Sale Committee. Th e employees working in those units 
were kept under the category of Volunt ary Separation Scheme to get rid 
of unproductive fixed expenses. Th e liabilities of the company were 
further reduced due to the waiver of interests, penalties and surcharge on 
the Government dues.  The revival pa ckage also consisted of concessions 
from the Government, financial institutions, banks and creditors. 
 
19. The other three operating plan ts such as Rajban, Tandur and 
Bokajan are to be continued as these ar e viable.  The scheme stressed on 
expansion, technological upgradati on and modernisation of these three 
units to make them competitive and enhance the margin of profit. 
 
20. The Committee notes that the host of measures adopted to 
support the CCI has helpe d it to transform th is ailing Corporation 
and bring it to a level of profitable company at present. This is a 
noteworthy success.  It has to be  carried forward and the momentum 
of its revival has to be sustained.   
 
21. The Committee finds that the BIFR recommended for infusion 
of funds. While Rs. 153.62 crore have  been  given   as   non-plan  
loan  for  repayment  to  secured  and   unsecured  creditors  and  for  
 

-11- 
meeting the VRS/VSS expenses, the plan assistance involving Rs. 
30.67 crore for expansion of Ra jban and Bokajan plants and 
upgradation of Tandur plant have been provided for. It is also 
envisaged that the CCI would pay to the Government of India the 
existing plan loan of Rs. 150.90 cro re and fresh non-plan loan of Rs. 
153.62 crore out of sale proceeds of seven non-operating plants.   
 
22. The Committee while taking note of the measures of the 
Government of India for revival and r estructuring of the CCI, would like 
to know the outcome of the money spent. It recommends that the 
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI ) must closely monitor the way 
in which money is being spent fo r achieving the targeted goal and 
submit a detailed report in this regard to the Committee.   
 
23. On the basis of the information supplied to the Committee it is 
evident that the recommendation of  the BIFR to close down the 
aforementioned seven unviable units  (at para 18) was revisited.  
Based on the revised assessment it was found that it would be 
possible to revive the five non-op erating units (Adilabad, Kurkunta, 
Nayagaon, Akaltara and Mandhar Plants) and other three remaining 
non-operating units such as Char khi Dadri, Delhi Cement Grinding 
Unit and Bhatinda Cement Grinding Unit would be sold out after the 
re-evaluation of their assets. 
 
24. The Committee felt that it is a worthwhile effort as the 
aforementioned five non-operating units  have access to vast reservoir of 
limestone which is essential for manufacture of cement. The Techno 
Economic Feasibility Report for revi val of these units have been 
prepared and such repor ts indicate the possibility  of their revival to 
address the rising demand for cement in our country. The feasibility  
 

12 
report outlines the plan for next ten years which would enhance the 
capacity of the cement plants and increase its economic operations.    
 
25. It is worthwhile to refer to the Eleventh Five Year Plan document.  
Under the heading ‘Issues and Challe nges for the Cement Industry’ it 
observed that “Achievement of gr owth and targets for the cement 
industry is crucially dependent on vari ous inputs such as limestone, coal, 
power, and last but not the least, on transportation of limestone. Coal 
continues to be the main fuel for th e cement industry and will remain so 
in the near future”. Since the revival packag e for the above-mentioned 
five non-operating units, factor th e availability of limestone as a key 
issue, it is important that the CCI ta ke inspiration from the observation of 
the Eleventh Five Year Plan which also  lays emphasis on the inputs such 
as limestone for producing more cement.   
 
26. The CMD of the CCI informed the Committee vide letter 
No.Ref.CMD/CCI/12 (13)/2011, dated February 01, 2011 that the revival 
of non-operating plants was reviewed  in the Asset Sale Committee 
meeting held on 07 December 2010 wher ein it was decide d that the sale 
process for the disposal of non-operating  plants has been restarted. This 
would mean that the three plants which are functioning would be allowed 
to manufacture cement an d the other non-operating plants would be sold 
out.   
27. The Committee strongly recommen ds that due attention must 
be paid to the Techno Economic Feasibility Reports for the revival of 
non-operating plants either by starting production process there 
through joint ventures or by le asing them to the other cement 
manufacturing  bodies.   The Committee would like to get a detailed  
 
 

13 
report in this regard, both from the Cement Corporation of India 
and the Department of Heavy Industries.  
  
28. One of the reasons cited by the Ce ment Corporation of India for its 
uninterrupted loss is the absence of captive power and critical dependence 
on the electricity boards of the resp ective States which quite often could 
not supply adequate power for th e operation of the cement plants 
functioning under the CCI. The point advanced by the CCI in the meeting 
of the Committee is well taken.  The Eleventh Five Year Plan document 
also takes note of the point and obser ves “The producti on of cement is a 
continuous process requiring unint errupted power supply. Since the 
availability and quality of grid power  supply continue to be a problem, 
the use of captive power has been increasing.  Most of the cement units 
have installed captive power generation capacities to the extent of 60% to 
100% of their requirement. The cap tive power generation capacity of 
cement industry is estimated to be  1825 MW at present, of which 61% is 
based on diesel and the rest 39% on co al.  With growing uncertainties of 
grid power availability, it is estim ated that 2000 MW captive power 
would be required during Eleventh Plan”. 
 
29. The Committee strongly recomm ends both to the Planning 
Commission and the DHI to pay h eed to the above observations of 
the Eleventh Five Year Plan document and seriously undertake 
efforts for establishing captive power plants in the plants of the CCI.   
 
30. Human resource management is ke y to the revival and success of a 
company. It is noteworthy that the Cement Corporation of India has taken 
measures to improve the morale of its employees as part of its strategy for 
improving  its  performance. However,  the  Committee  notes  with  
 

14 
concern that due to si ckness of the company and the adoption of 
successive Voluntary Retirement Scheme the strength of executives of 
the CCI operated plants got reduced from 531 to 206 during 2000-04.  
The ban on recruitment and the absence of induction of new 
employees since 1998 has further added to the problem. The shortage 
of manpower has thus ba dly affected the operati onal function of the 
units.  It is sad to note that many employe es have left the CCI to join the 
private sector cement plants which have been doing well due to the 
upsurge of demand for cement.  There is another concern arising out of 
age profile and career stagnation of  executives which has resulted in 
serious lack of executive strength at  middle and senior management level 
which is key to the success of many ar eas such as operations, finance and 
human resource.  In te rms of manpower strength the CCI as of now has 
1037 employees consisti ng of 117 executives, 174 supervisors and 746 
workers.  The depletion of expert ha nd has been caused due to retirement 
age which is fixed at 58 years. During the presentation before the 
Committee it was strongly pu t forth by the CCI that the retirement age of 
the CCI employees should be raised to 60 years for retaining the ‘existing 
experienced, qualified and skilled ma npower at all the levels’. The CCI 
has already submitted a proposal for enhancement of retirement age to the 
administrative Ministry for seeki ng Cabinet approval. The Committee 
was informed by the Chairman and Managing Director Shri R.P. Tak vide 
his letter No.Ref.CMD/CCI/12(13)/ 2011 dated Februa ry 01, 2011 that 
“Due to upsurge in the cement i ndustry, experienced and technical 
manpower are likely to be or being attracted by the competitors as well as 
prospective entrepreneurs at very lucrative remuneration packages.  
Lateral entry from PSUs and private ceme nt industry is also not feasible 
since all the major PUSs and private companies are having retirement age 
of 60 years.   
 

15 
Even the existing employees who are retiring or have retired are being 
engaged by private sector cement companies on a handsome 
remuneration package. Even if the Corporation resorts to new recruitment 
for middle and senior level executives,  it is apprehended that it may not 
be able to attract expe rienced and qualified candi dates due to existing 
retirement age of 58 years as in most of the public sector and private 
sector companies, th e retirement age is 60 years and above. The 
employees working in such companies at  this level may not like to shift 
such organisations where retirement ag e is 58 years.  Therefore, the age 
limit should be immediately enhanced to 60 years to overcome the acute 
problem of manpower”.   
 
31. The Committee stro ngly approves the demand of the CCI 
seeking enhancement of retirem ent age from 58 to 60. The 
Committee also strongly supports  the stand of CCI for immediate 
posting of board level executive in  the key area of operations and 
marketing.  It is understood th at the public enterprises selection 
board is considering a proposal in this regard for creation of such 
posts. The Committee strongly recommends that the public 
enterprises selection board must clea r such proposals immediately.  
The Committee also would like to have a report from  the PESB in 
this connection.   
 
32. The Prime Minister of our country Dr. Manmohan Singh while 
giving away the MoU Excellence Awards and Scope Awards for the year 
2008-09 said that “It is no small measure due to th e robustness and

REPORT 
Authorised by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
I, Ashok Mitra, hereby present the Twenty-second Report of the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants for 1997-98 of the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
2. The background of this joint report on the Demands for Grants of the three 
Ministries calls for some explanation. FoUowing the adjournment of Parliament on the 
conclusion of the general discussion of the budget proposals far 1997-98 on March 21, 1997, 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Comminees were expected to avail of the 
period till April 21 to prepare and submit their reports on the Demands for Grants of the 
different Ministries alongwith the usual appraisal of the performance budgets for 1996-97 of 
each Ministry. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry 
accordingly met and examined witnesses on March 31, April1, April 2, April 3, April 7 and 
April 8, 1997. (See Appendix). The Standing Committee had scheduled meetings for April 
11, 15 and 17 to discuss the draft reportS on the Demands for Grants. However , these 
meetings had to be postponed because of political developments, including the non-passage 
of the vote of confidence in the Government in the Lok Sabha. In view of the directive of 
the President to the Prime Minister, Parliament is being reconvened on April 21 at 
11.00 a.m. Whether the business placed before Parliament on this date would be confined to 
the passing of a vote on account or whether more substantive issues arc proposed to be 
taken up is not yet known; the constitutional issues involved arc also not altogether clear. 
3. In this circumstance, the Standing Committee has chosen to present to Parliament a 
brief joint report on the activities and proposed Demands for Grants of the three Ministries, 
namely, the Ministry of Mines, the Ministry of Steel and the Ministry of Industry. 
4. The Standing Committee is perturbed at the persistent signs of a slackening in the 
rate of growth in industrial production in recent months. The depressed condition, it was 
initially thought, was a feature of only infrastructural industries such as power and mining. 
Developments in the second quarter of 1996-97 suggest that the malaise is much more 
widespread, and recession appears to be enveloping the capital and consumer goods sectors 
as well, including consumer durables. The growth in the small scale segments of industry is 
assumed to have been over this period somewhat higher than in the organised sector. But 
the reasons underlying the hypothesis are at best wobbly. The time perhaps has arrived 
when an expert committe~ is invited to undertake a thorough restructuring of the index of 
industrial production; such restructuring should proceed far beyond merely shifting the base 
year and reassigning weights to the commodities covered by the index, and concentrate on 
improving the scientific basis of data collection from the small-scale industrial sector. 
5. A major issue of concern which came to the fore during the Standing Committee's 
discussions with representatives of the Ministries is the apparent lack of adequate functional 
coordination between the different Ministries and even between the Departments of the 
same Ministry. In the wake of the on-going liberalisation and the progressive dismantling of 
industrial and exchange controls, the Ministries, it would seem, are proceeding on the 
assumption that inter-ministerial and inter-departmental coordination need not be as greatly 
emphasised as was the wont in the pre-reforms days. Two trends are distinctly visible of late: 
(a) a gradual reduction in Plan allocations for each of the Ministries this Standing 
Committee is concerned with, or at least a perceptible fall in the rate of growth of these 
allocations; and (b) a growing reluctance on the part of the Ministries to assume 
responsibility for projecting the pace and pattern of industrial growth in the foreseeable 
1 

2 
future; it is as if the en tire burden of responsibility in this area has already been shifted to 
the private sector and to foreign investors. What is equally dist urbing is the growing attitude 
that the promotion of infrastructural indus tries is a task that does not belong to any of the 
Ministries. 
6. The authofities may have, from their point of view, good reasons for withdrawing to 
such a positio n; contai ning the fiscal deficit must be one principal consideration. The private 
secto r may not necessarily concur with !he official view. For example, one or two major 
associations representing the chambers of commerce and industry in the organised sector 
had, on the eve of the presen tation of this year's budget proposals, pleaded for an across­
the-board increase in public investment so as to dispel the current spell of industrial 
recession. In the light of the many encouraging proposal s in the budget favouring indu.~try, 
art icula tion of the need for public investment o n a selective bas is in the infrastructural 
sphere as well as in basic industrial sectors has been temporarily halted; the lowering of 
interest rates may have also boosted the expectations with respect to private investment. 
What should, however , be discouraged is exaggerated expecta tion regarding the flow of 
direc t investment from over~eas. li essential investmen ts in key sectors are neglected in the 
immediate period on the ground that foreign investors would soon take up the slack, current 
perfornJ<mce might get still even depressed, thereby further inhibiting the intrusion of 
foreign capital. 
7. It is in view of such considerations that the Standing Committee does not have the 
least hesitation in recommending that Plan allocations indicated in the Budget for 1997-98 
for the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines, including allocations for the public 
undertakings under their umbrella, should be doubled . This would mean, other things 
remaining the same, realloc<Jtion, or fresh allocation, of around Rs. 1,500 crore ill favour of 
the three Ministries, which would still be less than one per cent of the Union Government's 
toral budgetary outlay proposed for the year. 
8. The Standing Committ~e is setting forth below reasons in justification of this 
particular recommendatio n. 
9. Despite the rap id de-regulation of industrial controls and nearly open-ended 
invitat ion to private enterprises to enter the industrial sectors of the economy-an invitation

secto r in important segments of industry has been till now most restrained: the only major 
beneficiaries of private capital expansion are the light consumer goods sector and a few 
service industries. The recent drop in the rate of industrial growth, might indeed have a 
·,uuJtipher' eiT<!ct, thereby fur!:hcr depressing investment activities across the length and 
breadth of the industrial sector. It is then:fore, in the Standing Committee's view, imperative 
for the State to activise itself beyond what has been its role in recent years. Not that the 
Comm ittee has made up its mind that private and foreign investment would continue to 
eventuate in constipated doses in the coming years. Its only tl10ught is to ensure that 
valuable time is not lost in the essential areas of investment while the government waits for 
an augmentation of private and external capital inflow.

measure of functional autonomy , including autonomy to enter into contractual arrangements 
with outside parties for expanding survey activities as well as for organising commercial 
exploitation of proven mines and fields with the help of external collaborators:

Recommendations/observations 
 
1. The Committee has made its serious concern on its l ong waiting list for 
establishment of power plants in the country. Commi ttee finds that it has a pending list

Para-26 
Action Taken Note 
 
 The setting up of power plant is a complex process  and is dependent on the 
performance of several players. The developer has t o provide several inputs starting from 
making available encumbrance free land, civil work including foundations, raw water, 
construction power etc. using which the equipment s upplied by BHEL is to be erected 
and commissioned. Several other Balance of Plant (B OP) vendors have to supply 
equipment like coal and ash handling systems, water systems, cooling towers etc. 
 
 The scope of work of BHEL for major portion of pre sent orders on hand for 
power projects in the country is limited to design,  engineering, manufacture, supply, 
erection & commissioning of Boiler, Turbine Generat or & Auxiliaries packages (BTG) 
only. The remaining portion including all Civil wor ks & several sub-systems of Balance 
of Plants (BoPs) like Coal handling plant (CHP), As h handling plant (AHP), De-
Mineralisation (DM) Plant and Pre-treatment (PT) Pl ant, Switchyard etc. are under 
project developer scope.  
 
 Most products of BHEL are custom designed and only  after receipt of an order is 
the design/manufacture undertaken. These can be bro adly classified for 2 types of 
customer segments viz. power and industry. For the industrial segment products, the 
period of delivery is relatively shorter and orders  are generally executed within a year 
after an order is received. On the other hand the m ain power plant generating 
equipment/products catering to the requirements of power utilities, are generally long 
cycle items. In this context, the execution period of power sector orders on hand varies 
between 36-48 months for 500/660/800 MW projects (2 8-33 months for 250MW 
projects), and for some hydro projects, the execution period could be even longer. Hence, 
at any given point of time, different customer orde rs with BHEL are at different stages of 
implementation. 
 
  

10 
 There have been some rescheduling in supplies from  BHEL mainly due to non 
availability of critical castings and forgings of a lloy steels, pipes and fittings and CRGO 
sourced from limited number of foreign vendors. Inf rastructure inadequacies with respect

 BHEL has also embarked on a plan for enhancing its  manufacturing capacity &

 Inspite of various factors beyond the control of B HEL, the company puts in extra

order to tide over the situation GoI took immediate  remedial measures and announced 
three stimulus packages [1 st  on 07.12.2008, 2 nd  on 02.01.2009 and 3 rd  on 24.2.2009] 
which included; reduction of excise duty from 12% t o 8% for smaller cars and from 24% 
to 20% for others, increasing liquidity and credit flow in the market, procurement of 
buses through JNNURM scheme, enhanced depreciation for commercial vehicles. The 
GoI in the budget 2010-11 has only partially rolled back the excise duty cuts by 2%.  
 
 The Department has already taken up the matter wit h Ministry of Finance in the 
past at various stages recommending measures for au tomobile sector. The matter has also 
been taken up during the pre-budget recommendations  of the year 2009-10 as well as 
2010-11. Some of the measures recommended by the Department includes: 
   
• Bringing down the excise duty on MUVs by 4-5% (from existing 20%)  
• Withdrawal of additional excise duty of Rs. 15000 imposed as a temporary measure 
on all cars (other than small cars). 
• Increasing the depreciation rates of vehicle from 15% to 25% 
• Setting up of an Auto Component Technology Development Fund with a corpus  of 
Rs. 1000 crore to provide financial support to comp anies by financing 50% of the 
project cost by way of a soft loan.  

15 
 
• Measures to encourage new technology vehicle, vehic les with alternate fuels and 
drives such as: 
(a)  Duty drawback equivalent to 50% of the customs duty  applicable on the 
 import of hybrid 4 wheelers and plug-in hybrid 4 w heelers and also 
making countervailing duty at 0% from present 4%. 
(b)  Excise duty exemption at par with electric vehicles  and their parts for 
 Hydrogen/Fuel Cell/Hybrid/ CNG/Hy-thane vehicles a nd other alternate 
fuel vehicles and parts. 
(c)  No levy of NCCD on hybrids vehicles including hybri d/plug in hybrid 4 
wheelers imported to India. 
(d)  Extending the benefit of custom duty exemption avai lable to parts of 
electric cars to parts of all electric vehicles inc luding parts for CVs, 2/3 
wheelers. Similar benefit may be extended to parts of CNG, LPG, 
Hydrogen, Hybrid, Hy-thane vehicles etc. 
(e)  Income tax relief on purchase of Electric/Hydrogen/ Fuel Cell and Hybrid 
Vehicles. 
(f)  Allowing weighted deduction of 200% under income ta x act for R&D 
expenditure for hybrid/hydrogen/electric vehicles i ncluding battery 
technology. 
(g)  Weighted deduction under section 35(2AB). 
 
Effect of budget 2010-11 on auto sector:  
 
(a)  Partial roll back of Excise duty: In the first stimulus package a general 
reduction of Cenvat by 4% was announced. As a resul t excise duty on small cars, 
auto components came down to 8%. Despite good perfo rmance of the auto sector 
in 2009-10, the, Government in the Budget 2010-11ha s decided not to fully roll 
back the excise duty cuts and has increased the exc ise duty by 2% and therefore 
only partially rolled back the stimulus measures announced earlier.   
(b)  The excise duty on electric cars has now been aligned with excise duty on parts of 
electric vehicles, the excised duty of which  has b een reduced from 8% to 4%, so 
as to allow the manufacturers to avail the cenvat credit on the parts.  
 
 The first quarter performance (April-June 2010) of  auto sector has continued to 
show a considerable growth of 33.27% in production,  29% in sale and 59% in export. 
This shows that the growth in the auto sector is su stainable despite partial roll back of 
stimulus measures.  
 
 As per the recommendations of the Department relat ed Parliamentary Standing 
Committee, the matter has been further taken up wit h Ministry of Finance  in respect of 
some of the issues which are still to be resolved such as;

have been authorized by the Committee, hereby do present this Two Hundred and Twenty-Third
Report on the Revival and Restructuring of North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development
Corporation Ltd. pertaining to Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.
2. The Committee held detailed discussion with North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms
Development Corporation Ltd. at Shillong on 26
th October, 2010. The representatives of the
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region, BRPSE and Department of Public Enterprises
were also heard on the issue.
3. I thank the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region, Ministry of Textiles,
