9th May, 2011 Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry

1
REPORT
Handicrafts and handlooms form rich textures of our civilisation and culture. Through the
length and breadth of our country these remain close to the lives of our people who are engaged
in producing them and are valued within and outside India. This is particularly so in the North
Eastern India which occupies a special place and receives focussed and sensitive attention. The
hills, forests, rivers and the larger natural setting of all the States of the region provide an artistic
and aesthetic backdrop for the handicrafts and handlooms to flourish and become part and parcel
of daily life of people. These are vital sources of employment for millions of people of the region
who quite often do not reap adequate benefits arising out of modern industrial enterprises and
economic establishments due to difficult terrain and topography. The plentiful availability of basic
materials such as cane, bamboo, Muga Silk and Eri Silk has nurtured a rich and enduring tradition
of making handicrafts and hand woven products which merit admiration from all parts of the
country. The wide variety of bamboo and cane products and decorative items which often adorn
premises, both residential and office, add charm and beauty to the surroundings. The handlooms
and handicrafts, as always, will evoke appreciation for their specific ethnicity and assume additional
relevance as eco friendly and biodegradable products in an age which is grappling with non-
perishable wastes seriously threatening environment.
2. Willing involvement of people of the North Eastern Region in making these products
testifies to their deep creative desire to produce beauty out of the material so abundantly supplied
by nature. These products cater to the daily needs of people and can be of immense use in
further improving their economic conditions and augmenting their entrepreneurial and commercial
activities.
3. The North Eastern Region was deliberately kept isolated from rest of India by the British
rulers. That led to its alienation and lack of tuning with modern development which other parts of
India had the relative advantage of experiencing. The observations of the Simon Commission
concerning the North Eastern region were indicative of the British mind. The Commission noted
“The stage of development reached by the inhabitants of these areas prevents the possibility of
applying to them methods of representation adopted elsewhere... Their contentment does not
depend so much on rapid political advance as on experienced and sympathetic handling and on
protection from economic subjugation from neighbours”. Such perceptions of the colonial masters
and the accompanied action led to the alienation of the North Eastern part of our country. As a
result it suffered in achieving modicum of progress and development.
4. Since independence several measures have been taken by the Government of India to
accelerate the growth and development of the States of the region. Of late the region has assumed
importance as the gateway for promoting trade and commerce beyond our boarders as part of our
vigorous look east policy.
5. It is heartening that a separate Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER)
has been set up by the Government of India since 2001 to give focussed attention to the region
and provide impetus to the Center’s efforts for augmenting the socio-economic development of its
people and make it as a nucleus of all round progress.
6. The Committee visited the North-Eastern India as per its decision to study the enterprises
of the Government of India working in remote regions of our country. It undertook a tour to
Shillong during 25 and 31 October, 2010 to have a first hand knowledge of the functioning of the
North-Eastern Handicrafts and Handloom Development Corporation Ltd. (NEHHDC) which is

2
established as a Government of India undertaking in 1977 under the Companies Act, 1956 with its
registered office at Shillong, Meghalaya.
7. Its primary objective is to further the cause of the Handicrafts and Handloom Sector of the
region. As part of this strategy to carry forward the rich heritage of making hand woven products,
it reaches out to people who are engaged in the production level and takes measures to markets
these products across the country and in many parts of the world through a chain of emporia,
exhibitions, exports, trade fares, expositions and crafts fares.
8. The Committee interacted with the officials of the NEHHDC in Shillong. From the
statements made by the officials and from the catalogue of documents supplied to the Committee,
it has been found that the NEHHDC has been incurring loss since its inception. It was referred
to the Board for Reconstructions of Public Sector Enterprise (BRPSE) in December, 2009 with a
package for turnaround of the Corporation. The BRPSE was also given a copy of the corporate
plan prepared by the Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) for its consideration.
9. The Committee was informed that the BRPSE advised the Ministry of North-Eastern Region
to convert the NEHHDC into a promotional body and finance its activity through budgetary support
for achieving its objectives. The BRPSE recommended for the liquidation of the company in its
present form and suggested its conversion from a commercial entity to a promotional body.
10. The Committee expresses its serious concern that the NEHHDC has not been
restructured even after the report given by the BRPSE for making it a promotional body.
All concerned must pay serious attention to the revival of this important organisation which
was set up to tap the enormous potential in the handloom and handicraft sector of the
region. It proposes a comprehensive revival package which should be implemented in a time
bound manner and not staggered over a long period of time. Till the Corporation is revived
and restructured full budgetary support should be extended by the Ministry for Development
of North-Eastern Region.
11. The Committee while interacting with the officials of the NEHHDC noted that they
were diffident in replying to the queries of the Members of the Committee and even were
not able to satisfactorily provide answers or clarifications on points raised by the Members
of the Committee. The Committee got the impression that the involvement of the officials
in running the affairs of the NEHHDC was not up to mark. It strongly felt that the half-
hearted manner in which they were dealing with the questions of the Committee and quite
often taking long pauses to say or make remarks on the points raised by the Members,
they were not at all efficiently running the work of the Corporation. The Committee,
therefore, tends to conclude that there is a high degree of mismanagement and lack of
interest in carrying forward the work of the Corporation.
12. The officials of the Ministry of Development of the North Eastern Region (DoNER)
deposed before the Committee on 17 April, 2011 and argued that the restructuring of the
Corporation by separating its promotional and commercial activities would not be helpful to the
cause of the Corporation and the artisans and weavers of the region. They pleaded that
promotional activities are closely interlinked with its commercial activities. Their main stand was
that while supporting the artisans, they have to ensure their access to the markets for their
products. Therefore, they stated that the commercial dimension would have to be inevitably
integrated with any measure to take forward the cause of promotional activities. The stand of
the DoNER was that it cannot be a fully commercial body due to the competition faced by it
from the Handloom and Handicraft Boards of the State Governments of the region and the private
players.

3
13. The officials of the DoNER differed with the officials of the Department of Public Sector
Enterprises on the issue of restructuring of the Corporation in the pattern of the India Trade
Promotion Organisation (ITPO) and National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC). The DoNER
officials maintained that the ITPO and NSIC are extending certain services and get compensated
by the concerned Ministry for implementing certain promotional schemes. Whereas, according to
them, the North Eastern Handlooms and Handicrafts Corporation is engaged in selling products and
goods of the artisans. They were of the opinion that the activities of the Corporation cannot be
equated with the activities of the ITPO and NSIC.
14. The Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises, while deposing before the Committee on
17 April 2011, raised a question as to why the Central Government should have NEHHDC when
all these sister States of the North Eastern Region have their Handlooms and Handicrafts
Development Corporation. He was of the opinion that both the NEHHDC and the Handloom and
Handicraft Development Corporation of each State are involved in doing the same job. He added
that the NEHHDC is duplicating the work of the State Handloom and Handicraft Development
Corporation. Adding further he emphatically put forth the point that multiplicity of organisations in
the same sector and doing the same job did not at all confirm to sound business principle.
15. Referring to the negative networth of the Corporation which stood at (-) Rs.27 crore as
on 31 March, 2010 he saw its bleak future and maintained that it had no hope at all to come up
as a profit making organisation. Raising the point that this is the age of competition he stated that
they faced competition from two sources: the State Governments and the private players.
Maintaining that it is a competition involving Government of India versus the State Governments,
he asked “Is it the right type of competition?”
16. Firmly arguing that the Corporation is plagued with the traditional problem affecting all
public sector companies, i.e., overstaffing, staggering overhead expenditure, etc., he gave a detailed
account of the sheer size of the Corporation which had 114 surplus staff members which included
ten executives. The Corporation, according to him, registered all attempts of giving VRS to its
employees in spite of the persuasion of the BRPSE to do so. He sensitized the Committee by saying
“Can this organisation which is overstaffed, overloaded, overburdened, completely at red, ever
sustain any market competition from private players? There is no chance of ever doing so.” He
was of the opinion that by bringing down overhead costs, the situation could be improved.
17. He recommended that the Corporation can be converted to a company under section 25 of
the Companies Act which provides that such companies can be engaged in some noble work as
decided by the Government of India. He argued that the example of ITPO and NSIC were given
not for making profit but for promoting design skills, marketing, opening new retail centres, etc.
The mother Ministry, i.e., the DoNER, can extend financial package to the Corporation to take
forward such goals.
18. When the officials of the DoNER and the Corporation expressed their opinion that given a
chance, the Corporation can register profit in two-three years, the Secretary, Department of Public
Enterprises, recommended for complete overhauling of the Corporation which would be include
upgradation of its efficiency, strengthen its delivery mechanisms, rectify its lacunae and a hard look
on the part of the Ministry of Development of the North Eastern Region to make it the best
possible outfit.
19. The good and sensible proposal of the Secretary was welcomed by the Committee. Besides,
the Committee felt that the huge interests on the loan accumulating over the years may be waived
off as an initial measure to help the Corporation to come out of its present pitiable condition. The
Committee also felt that the Corporation can establish its branches in all the States of the North

4
Eastern Region and thereby decentralise its activities from its headquarters located in Shillong. The
Committee strongly recommends that a monitoring mechanism may be placed to have a close look
on the funds supplied by the Central Government and judiciously check the way in which such
funds are utilized by the Corporation. The Committee took note of the statements of the officials
of the Corporation and the DoNER that suitable VRS Scheme should be introduced to rationalise
the staff strength in consonance with its capacity to emerge as a viable, vibrant and profit making
body. It is hoped that the budgetary support to be given by the DoNER would help the Corporation
to revive its financial health.
20. The paramount issue is the livelihood and well being of the poor artisans and weavers who
are mostly women. In fact, the North Eastern Handloom and Handicraft Corporation was
established in 1976 with its foundational objective of safeguarding the poor women engaged in the
handloom and handicraft sector. The central concern of the Committee, therefore, is the protection
of such weavers and artisans. It, therefore, strongly recommends that liquidation of the Corporation
may not be pursued and instead a chance may be given to it with adequate support from the
DoNER to restructure its size and make it competitive and business oriented. In doing so, it can
emerge as a successful public sector enterprise standing on its own strength and upholding the
cause of the artisans and weavers whose interests are of central concern in any scheme for revival
of the Corporation.
21. The Committee heard the Secretary, DoNER and the Secretary, Ministry of Textiles in its
meeting held on 27 April, 2011. The Secretary, DoNER in her presentation stated that as per the
prevailing scheme for organisation of exhibitions/craft bazars by the NEHHDC, the Ministry of
Textiles bears the 75 per cent cost and the rest of the 25 per cent is borne by the NEHHDC. The
Secretary pleaded for change of the funding pattern based on 75 per cent and 25 per cent to 90
and 10 per cent. She argued that in case of North Eastern States, which are special category
States, the funding pattern adopted for other Centrally-Sponsored Schemes is in 90:10 ratio. She
wanted the adoption of the such funding ratio for the NEHHDC.
22. The Committee understands that to move from 75:25 ratio to 90:10 ratio necessary changes
have to be affected at the Cabinet level and, therefore, the Ministry of Textiles has to initiate the
process in taking it forward and getting the approval of the Government of India.  The Committee
recommends that the 90:10 funding pattern may be seriously considered for the revival of
the NEHHDC.
23. The Secretary, DoNER also referred to the role played by the NEHHDC for conducting
many training/skill upgradation programmes and implementing projects like Design Bank and
Handicrafts Museums. She maintained that in respect of these programmes/projects, NEHHDC gets
only implementation cost without any services charges. Pleading that component of service charges
may also be included in the project cost of this programmes/projects, she stated that such
measures will help the NEHHDC to revive its financial health. The Committee strongly
recommends the Government to consider the aforementioned points raised by the Secretary,
DoNER and take appropriate steps for their early implementation.
24. Secretary, DoNER also put forth the point that the Ministry may also explore the possibility
of utilizing the services of the Corporation for implementing its various programmes by providing
it appropriate grant. The Committee feels that the observations of the Secretary, DoNER may be
seriously considered for making the NEHHDC a viable and profitable Corporation.
25. The Corporation through its replies to the questionnaires supplied to the Committee informed
that it is engaged in participating in regional exhibitions, craft fairs and special marketing events.
The Committee notes that its participation is confined to cities like Bangalore, Chennai, Kolkata,

5
New Delhi, Shillong and Guwahati. The Committee recommends that the Corporation must
explore markets in the eastern region of the country which has potential buyers for
handicrafts and handloom products. These regions would be nearer to the North-Eastern
part and, therefore, the cost of transportation of the goods and finished products would be
relatively less.
26. The Committee was informed that the activities of the Corporation to develop skills,
particularly the business skills of the artisans, and promoting awareness in the region is based on
organisation of limited number of seminars and workshops. The Committee feels that the
Corporation must intensify its activities to spread awareness among the youth of the region and
associate them in many of its programmes for generating interest among them on the rich heritage
of hand made and hand woven products. As stated earlier, the North Eastern Handicraft and
Handloom Corporation originated in the context of the pitiable condition of the poor craft persons
and weavers most of whom are women. Over a period of time, it is noticed that the middle class
is reviving interest on handloom and handicraft in a big way. The Committee is constrained to
note that the Corporation is quite inert in understanding this trend among the youth,
particularly those belonging to the middle class, and taking advantage of it for taping the
prospective clientele. It, therefore, recommends that both the Corporation and the Ministry
of Development of North-Eastern Region must prepare a strategy to explore new markets.
It is not enough to maintain, as the Corporation did before the Committee, that the private
players have better competitive ability to market handloom and handicrafts products at a
price which is difficult for the Corporation to match. This is the age of innovation and
creativity. The Government of India is observing the decade from 2010 to 2021 as the
decade of innovation. When the term ‘innovation’ is used, its applicability in every sector
including the handloom and handicraft sector assume critical relevance. The Committee
strongly recommends that the officials of the DoNER and the NEHHDC must come together
to take appropriate measures so that the Corporation is revived and serves the purpose for
which it was established in 1970s.
27. Net worth of a company is indicative of the health and outlook which drives it and impacts
its activities. It is rather unfortunate to note that the net worth of the company has always been
negative and now stands at (-) Rs 2700.50 lakhs. This issue has been discussed in an earlier para.
The Committee notes that during the preceding three years, i.e., 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10,
the turnover of the Corporation and its gross trading profit has increased. It is a heartening trend.
The Committee also notes that during the year 2008-09 and 2009-10, the Corporation could bring
down, if not completely reverse, its annual loss. The Committee recommends that this new found
strength must be bolstered to restore the economic viability of the Corporation.
28. The Committee was informed by the Corporation that inadequate working capital for
sourcing and procurement of handicrafts and handloom products from various craft clusters in the
region is one of the factors responsible for not achieving the target of sales and profitability. It
was also told to the Committee that logistic and topography of the North-Eastern part of India and
the high cost of transportation, especially of the sofa sets and other household products came on
the way of sourcing such products as per the demand. The Committee strongly recommends the
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region to look into these difficulties and take measures
for addressing the problems faced by the Corporation.
29. The Committee understands from the documents supplied to it that there are several factors
which might handicap the Corporation in expanding its activities and reviving its financial
efficiency. One of them is paucity of specific raw materials such as matured cane and wood for
meeting requirements of artisan of the region. The second factor outlined by the Corporation is that
the production, procurement and sourcing of the material suffers due to poor work culture and

6
attitude of the artisans of the region. The Committee feels that a campaign must be launched to
alter the attitude of the artisans and weavers on a sustained basis. It will take quite long time to
change their outlook. The campaign must be combined with economic incentives which will
certainly motivate them to show interest in the handloom and handicrafts business.
30. The Committee appreciates the strength of the Corporation as outlined in the background
note given to it. It also takes note of the weaknesses. However, the Committee feels that the
strength and opportunities available to the Corporation can overcome the weaknesses and threats.
31. In the modern period of twenty first century, it is important to integrate business principles
for running any organisation be it the public or private. The Committee understands that one of
the problem areas confronted by the Corporation relates to non-commercial nature of weavers and
artisans of the entire North-Eastern Region who pursue the age old habit of weaving and crafting
for meeting specific family requirements on cultural and religious grounds. This is a challenge
which needs to be addressed boldly and creatively. The widespread acceptability of the handloom
and handicraft products and the manner in which these are valued, both in India and abroad, raises
hope that a larger market can be explored and tapped for the benefit of the artisans and weavers.
The Committee feels that apart from budgetary support it requires enormous effort on the part of
the Corporation and those engaged in organising the artisans and weavers for making their
profession commercially attractive and viable.
32. The Committee is of firm opinion that all concerned must summon their energy to stem the
loss suffered by the NEHHDC and slowly but surely make it a profitable company. Even as
budgetary support will go a long way in strengthening the Corporation, attempts must also be made
to create internal resources which would be the source of its sustenance and forward movement.
It is, therefore, appropriate that a road map must be prepared to materialise this vision.
33. As stated earlier, the officials of the Corporation were evasive in dealing with the questions
and concerns raised by the Members of the Committee in its meeting in Shillong. It is quite clear
that the system of accountability has suffered serious erosion. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that every action of the management must be scrutinised and it must be held
accountable for all acts of omission and commission. By enforcing the principle of accountability,
the Corporation can take a major step forward for using the budgetary support or other funds that
may be infused to revitalise the Corporation.
34. The Committee also impresses upon the Department of Public Enterprises to take up the
matter with concerned Ministries/Departments and apprise the Committee of the progress made in
the action taken notes.

7

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having   been authorized by the Committee , hereby present this Two Hundred 
and Twenty Fourth Report on the Revival and Restruc turing of Hindustan Photo Films 
Manufacturing Company Ltd. pertaining to Ministry o f Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises (Department of Heavy Industry).  
 
2. The Committee held detailed discussion with the Management of Hindustan 
Photo Films Manufacturing Company Ltd., Employees a nd Officers Associations of the 
HPF at Ooty on 18 
th  May, 2011 and received inputs for this Report.   
 
3. I thank the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Pub lic Enterprises (Department of 
Heavy Industry) for furnishing the valuable inputs during the meetings.  
 
4. The Committee in its meeting held on 26 
th  May, 2011 considered and adopted the 
report.

(ii) 
 
 
 

 
 
REPORT   
 
The Incorporation of the Hindustan Photo Films Manu facturing Co. 
Ltd. in 1960 in Ooty as a public sector enterprise heralded a new beginning 
for our country for production of photo sensitive material in the Government 
sector.  Its mission statement “To cater to the nee ds of imaging products in 
the health and industrial sector in India with inte rnational quality products” 
brings out its grand vision. It manufactures range of materials which are 
widely used in sectors such as health care, educati on, entertainment and 
defence.  Apart from pursuing the core objective of  manufacturing photo 
sensitive material, the HPF, like all other public sector enterprises, had the 
larger goal of stimulating and promoting the development of the hilly district 
of Neelgiris of Tamil Nadu 75 per cent of populatio n of which constitutes 
the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward  class communities. 
Thus, engaging itself in the challenging entrepreneurial and commercial task 
of making the country self-dependent in photo sensi tive material, it 
embarked on an arduous path to transform the social  and economic 
conditions of people and the region.  
 
2. The Hindustan Photo Films Manufacturing Co. Ltd.  (HPF) has the 
enviable status of being the first such unit in Ind ia and South East Asia.  It 
undertook commercial production in 1967 and establi shed the brand image 
in the whole country for manufacturing Indu film.  Apart from making 
medical X-ray films for health care sector, it served the infrastructural sector 
by producing industrial X-ray films.  Besides, it c atered to the 
printing/publishing sector by manufacturing graphic arts film and served the 
cause of defence establishments by making aerial fi lms.  Its wide range of 

 
 
activities also included measures to process chemic als which are key and 
essential components for developing photo sensitive material in laboratories.  
 
3. The HPF formed part of the grand vision of build ing our nation by 
establishing public sector enterprises in key secto rs and which were integral 
to the scheme of mixed economy for shaping modern I ndia’s destiny.  It has 
acquired the status of an ISO 9001:2008 certified C ompany the annual 
installed capacity of which is 33.64 Million Sq.m.  It has the following four 
units:- 
(i)  Fully integrated Production Unit of Black and White  
photographic products and conversion of imported co ated wide 
stock (colour products) at Ooty. 
(ii)  Magnetic Tape Division at Ooty. 
(iii)  Polyester X-ray Plant (State of the Art technology) set up in 1997 
at Ooty. 
(iv)  Conversion Unit/processing Chemical Plant at Ambattur.     
 
4. Functioning under the administrative control of Department of Heavy 
Industry, it has a modern and state of the art manu facturing plant and is 
acknowledged as a sophisticated and capital intensi ve industry employing 
proprietary technology from M/s Dupont, USA.  It is  noteworthy that the 
manpower employed by the Company was trained by Dup ont for equipping 
them with technical skills and developing their mental faculties to run such a 
modern and technology driven establishment.  The HP F claims that its 
facilities for promoting research and development c an be counted as 
excellent.  It also asserts that experienced scient ists are engaged in carrying 
out R & D work which is critical to such companies engaged in 
manufacturing films in a highly competitive and commercial environment.   

 
 
5. The HPF established its reputation for producing  INDU film which 
promoted its brand image by 1970s.  It was reckoned  with great deal of 
patriotic spirit and acquired importance equal to i nternational brands such as 
Kodak, Fuji, Konica and Agfa. 
 
6. India has a huge and bourgeoning market for phot ographic films.  It is 
estimated that the value of such market is Rs.1663 crores and the key and 
commercially competitive players are many multinational corporations.  The 
HPF maintains that “Market potential for existing p roducts manufactured by 
HPF is around Rs.240 crores which includes Governme nt purchase alone of 
Rs.85 crores per annum”.   
 
7. The Company was justly proud that it had a count rywide vibrant 
market since the beginning of its commercial produc tion and was generating 
profit till 1991-92.  The profit level plummeted wi th on set of economic 
reforms and decisive opening of our economy to glob al competition.  The 
HPF which was riding high due to its profit with a turnover of Rs.238 crores 
had enjoyed sound financial health which started declining during 1992-93. 
 
8. Actuated by the sustained loss suffered by the G overnment of India 
referred it to the BIFR on 14 October 1995, which d eclared it sick on 23 
January 1996. Subsequently, on 30 January 2003, the  BIFR recommended 
for its winding up.  However, the Trade Unions of H PF moved to Madras 
High Court which granted an interim stay on 26 June  2005 on the orders of 
the BIFR.   
 

 
 
9. It is a matter of anxiety to note that the Compa ny which had 
authorized capital of Rs.210 crores and paid up cap ital of Rs.205.87 crores 
as on 31 March 2011, had a negative net worth of (- ) Rs.7985 crores and a 
accumulated loss of (-) Rs.8232 crores. 
 
10. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing C ommittee on 
Industry was greatly exercised by the pitiable cond ition of the HPF and its 
employees.  On several occasions, it had taken up t he matter and actively 
considered the crisis confronted by the Hindustan P hoto Films.  Many 
Reports of the Committee on Demands for Grants did focus attention on the 
gathering and mounting problems afflicting the Company.  
 
11. While considering the issues faced by the HPF o n 30 November 2005, 
it recommended for appointment of a consultant for the purpose of 
submitting a revival plan for the Company.  Accordi ngly, M/s Ernst & 
Young was appointed on 10 May 2006 for studying the  HPF and presenting 
a plan for its revival.  The Committee understands that the report of the 
consultant was considered and the proposal for the revival of HPF was 
placed before the Board for Reconstruction of Publi c Sector Enterprises.  
The said proposal gained strength due to the stand taken by the Tamil Nadu 
Government that the closure of HPF is not acceptabl e to the State 
Government.  It maintained that the HPF has to be s een not only in terms of 
its inherent value as a public sector enterprise bu t in terms of its close 
linkages to the economic and industrial regeneratio n of the Neelgiris district 
of the State.  It is crystal clear that the revival and sustenance of the HPF has 
the backing of the State Government.      
 

 
 
12. Thus the keen interest evinced by the Governmen t of Tamil Nadu for 
the revival of the Company seems to have given a fr esh lease of life to it.  
The Committee notes that the Board of Reconstructio n of Public Sector 
Enterprises in its meeting held on 17 July 2009 and  later on 22 December 
2009 requested the Department of Heavy Industries a nd Hindustan Photo 
Films to submit a comprehensive proposal for the revival of the Company.  
13. The Department of Heavy Industry prepared a rev ival proposal for the 
consideration of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.  It included 
the following:- 
 
(i)  To provide Rs.200 crore in the form of equity for O ne Time 
Settlement of Creditors. 
(ii)  To provide for shortfall in salary & wages of the e mployees of 
the company by way of gap filling over and above th e internal 
business resources generated by the company for a p eriod of up 
to three years, if required, and subject to total a mount not 
exceeding Rs.20.00 crore for all the years put together.  
(iii)  To provide Rs.9 crore in the form of grant for Repa irs, R&D 
and Sales promotion. 
(iv)  To provide Rs.43crore in the form of loan for diver sification 
into IV Fluid and Colour Photo Paper. 
(v)  Permission for implementing DPE’s 1997 revised pay scales in 
the company prospectively.  The revised salary and wages for 
subsequent years will be paid by the company from t he 
resources generated from its operation.   
(vi)  Write off Government of India Plan and Non-Plan loa n of 
Rs.344.51 crore as on 31.03.2010. 
(vii)  Write off of accumulated interest of Rs.655.78 cror e as on 
31.03.2010 on GoI Plan and non Plan loans and freez ing of 
interest beyond 31.03.2010.  
  
 
14. The Committee on Industry took a decision to go  deep into the matter 
during its visit to Ooty from 18 to 20 May 2011 and wholeheartedly examine 
the issue of revival and restructuring of the HPF.  During the interaction of 

 
 
the Members of the Committee with the employees uni on and the 
management of the HPF, many startling facts concern ing the loss incurred 
by it were brought to the notice of the Committee.   
 
15. During its presentation before the Committee on  18 
th  May, 2011 the 
management explained that the Company which registe red profit worth 
Rs.2.92 crores during 1991-92 had to incur loss of Rs.117 crores during 
1992-93.  The Committee was eager to know as to how  the HPF which was 
justly proud of its profit making status suddenly s uffered loss of Rs.117 
crores in one year.   In the beginning, the managem ent maintained that 
diversion of working capital to complete the constr uction of new polyester 
X-ray plant caused such heavy and unprecedented los s.  The committee was 
eager to know the reasons behind such sudden and massive loss. The Annual 
Report of the Hindustan Photo Films for the period 1992-93 contained the 
Directors’ Report which attributed the crisis faced  by HPF to the changes 
taking place in the industrial arena in the country  and the internal 
mismanagement.  The Directors’ Report in the aforem entioned Annual 
Report also gave some more reasons for which the co mpany suffered losses 
and observed, “The operating results for the year h ad to also bear the heavy 
interest burden of Rs. 39.8 crores, much of which i s the result of part 
borrowings taken to finance the massive inventories  and the losses which 
were camouflaged as “current assets”.  Another fact or has been the 
restrictions imposed by the banks on cash-credit an d non-fund based limits 
in view of the substantial overdrawal in these acco unts.  They resorted to 
impounding 50% of all receipts.  These stringent me asures led to a cutback 
in production and sales during the second half of 1 992-93.  The lower 

 
 
production & sales resulted in under absorption of overheads contributing to 
the losses”. 
 
16. In the face of shortcomings and draw backs adve rsely affecting the 
Company and paralyzing its performance, the Committee notes that the HPF 
with its skilled manpower has sustained operations and to a great extent 
withstood pressures caused by recurrent sickness.  The physical and 
financial parameters flowing from the current perfo rmance of the Company 
also indicate a good future trend.  For instance, the capacity utilization of the 
HPF has gone up considerably during 2006-07 and 201 0-11.  The value of 
production showed a rising trend from the figure of  Rs.17.68 crores during 
2006-07 to Rs.25.50 crores during 2009-10.  The val ue of sales has also 
gone up from Rs.14.59 crores during 2006-07 to Rs.2 6.25 crores during 
2009-10.  It deserves to be noted that the HPF has exceeded the MOU target 
for the years 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10.  Of cou rse what matters in 
respect of MoU targets is not the completion of suc h targets alone, but the 
rating the company has got.  In this respect it has  to be appreciated that the 
HPF while exceeding the MoU target should also stri ve for a better rating.  
Another noteworthy feature is that the Company has rationalized its 
manpower and reduced from 3824 during 1991-92 to 73 1 to 2010-11.  Any 
public sector undertaking which is in complete red needs to take a hard look 
to streamline every aspect of its activities.  The Hindustan Photo Films has 
already done it.  The reduction of manpower is indi cative of the mind set of 
the management of the HPF to look forward and take it to a level where it 
would be once again profitable and vibrant.  It is important to be mindful of 
the fact that a company overstaffed and with enormous overhead expenses is 
a liability on itself.  Taking into account the sta ff strength of the HPF, one 

 
 
takes heart from the measures it has taken, over th e years, to downsize the 
manpower.  
 
17. In the documents supplied to the Committee, the  HPF outlined the 
reasons for its sickness.  These are:- 
1.  Lack of timely funding, cost escalation, diversion of working capital 
to complete New Polyester X-ray Plant. 
2.  Absence of adequate working capital for a long peri od till the year 
2010. 
3.  Accumulation of heavy interest. 
4.  Lack of investment for modernization. 
5.  Photographic goods brought under OGL in Liberalisation. 
6.  Undue advantage of duty/taxe exemption to MNCs and importers with 
conversion units in Tax Free Zones. 
7.  Treating conversion of Finished Coated Jumbo Films as 
manufacturing activity. 
8.  Drastic reduction in Import duties for Finished Films. 
9.  Low morale due to 1987 pay scales.   
 
18. It appears that liberalized and open economy ca used many difficulties 
for the HPF to successfully compete with many playe rs and upgrade its 
technological capability.  However, the measures ta ken by HPF to improve 
its functioning merits attention.  It has reconfirm ed the consent of creditors 
for one time settlement.  Its successful bid and ac hievement in getting the 
Director General Supply and Disposal rate contract 2011-12 is yet another 
step towards its recovery.  The ploughing of workin g capital of Rs.30 crores 
by the HPF has helped it to scale up its operations  and raise the turn over 
significantly.  It is worthwhile to note that measu res have been taken for 
product diversification which include launching of Red Laser Scanner Film 
and development of Medical Imaging Films and Inkjet  Paper.  The renewed 
confidence of the HPF for restoring its financial a nd productive ability is 
indicated by its efforts to pursue export enquiries .  Its engagement with 

 
 
Technova for new business opportunity and its discu ssions for establishing 
Floriculture Project testify to its commitment to i mprove its performance.  
The willingness of the Government of Tamil Nadu for  giving concessions to 
the HPF under the incentive package for its revival is a shot in the arm of the 
Company to restore its financial health.  Prominent among these concessions 
offered by the Government of Tamil Nadu are: 
Concession sought Status 
Waiver of 75% of VAT for 5 
years 
Waiver of 75% Electricity Tax 
for 5 years 
100% refund/exemption sanctioned for 
10 years from 2008-09 
Reduction of VAT of Medical 
X-ray to 4% 
Sanctioned 
Bringing IV Fluids in the 4% 
tariff schedule 
4% rate confirmed 
Directions for procurement of 
HPF products  
Orders being placed on HPF 
Waiver of accrued lease rent  Waiver of Rs.9.58 cro res sanctioned 
 
19. It is understood by the Committee that some of the banks which have 
released loans to the HPF have given undertaking to  it to waive the 
accumulated interest amounting to Rs. 6472.15 crore s and partially write off 
portion of the principal amount worth Rs. 337.78 cr ores.  The lessening of 
interest burden will go a long way in restoring the  financial health of the 
Company.  The HPF maintains that it has incurred li abilities not because of 
operational reasons but due to the new Polyester X-ray Project.  It is hopeful 
of the fact that operational loss can be addressed.   In fact, it maintains that 
with the induction of Rs.30 crores working capital which forms part of the 
revival package, the process of revival has already  taken place and must 
reach its logical conclusion.   

 
 
20. The Committee strongly recommends that all conc erned which 
include the Department of Heavy Industry and the Ca binet Committee 
on Economic Affairs must come forward to revive thi s enterprise which 
is first of its kind in the entire South East Asia.   
 
21. The Committee was pained to note that the emplo yees of the HPF 
are getting pay scales according to the recommendations of the 1987 Pay 
Committee Report.  The Committee strongly recommend s for 
immediate implementation of the 1997 Scale of Wages  for them with 
immediate effect without linking it to Revival Prop osal.   It also 
recommends that salary support be continued to them  till 
implementation of the revival of the Company.   
 
22. The Prime Minister of our country, Dr. Manmohan  Singh, recently 
stated that one of the factors behind India’s abili ty to withstand financial 
crisis was the resilience of public sector enterpri ses.  There is resurgence of 
faiths of the Government on the strength of our PSE s.  The Eleventh Five 
Year Plan document very clearly stated that “Despit e the privatization 
accomplished up to the middle of the Tenth Five Yea r Plan, when the policy 
changed, the role of the Central Public Sector Ente rprises and their 
contribution to the GDP has not diminished.”  It al so observed that “The 
profits of profit making Central Public Sector ente rprises (CPSEs) have 
increased from Rs. 36432 crore to Rs. 76240 crore a nd the losses of loss 
making ones has come down from Rs. 10454 crore to R s. 5752 crore during 
the same period”.  The positive image of the CPSEs available from the 
macro picture makes one hopeful that Public Sector Enterprises can be as 
competitive as private sector.  In case of the HPF the operating loss has 

 
 
come down to 9.50 crores in 2010-11 from 16.37 cror es in 2006-07 after 
many measures including cost cutting measures were taken by the Company.  
Therefore, the Company deserves supports from the G overnment for its 
revival because of the good work done by it in redu cing its operating loss to 
single digit.  
 
23. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Government of India is 
committed to strengthen public sector enterprises a nd is considerably happy 
that such enterprises have performed quite well and  generated their own 
resources for improving their financial and non-fin ancial performances.  
Against this background, the Committee strongly rec ommends for the 
extension of Government support to the HPF for its revival.  The 
Committee, while interacting with the employees of the Company in its 
meeting in Ooty on 18 May 2011, understood their ea rnest desire for its 
revival.  The management is equally determined to t ake the HPF forward to 
a brighter tomorrow.  All of them just wanted one chance to do so.  And they 
are quite confident that they can revive the HPF an d subsequently sustain it 
by generating their own resources.  The world is painfully realizing the crisis 
caused by excessive deregulation and harking back t o a system of judicious 
regulation.  It is important for the Government whi ch includes the 
Department of Heavy Industry, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs 
and the Planning Commission to understand the loss suffered by HPF in a 
libralised economic environment which proved detrim ental to many our 
public sector enterprises.  It is in this context t hat the Committee strongly 
recommends for the revival of the HPF.     
    

 
 
24. The strength of an enterprise to a great extent  flows from the 
strength of the leadership whose vision matters a l ot to take it forward.  
The Committee understands that the HPF does not hav e a full time 
CMD.  There are many public sector enterprises in I ndia which have 
registered profit due to imaginative leadership of the CMDs.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends for the appointmen t of a full time 
CMD who would be in a position to convert adversities to opportunities.   
 
25. The Committee also strongly recommends for intr oduction of a 
system for holding the management and the officers of the Department 
of Heavy Industry accountable for their lapses in m aking the Company 
unviable.  This must be part and parcel of the revi val project.   There 
must be a monitoring mechanism to ascertain the man ner in which the 
revival package will be implemented.  Strict vigila nce in this regard is 
necessary. 
 
26. The Committee during its visit to several parts  of the country to 
study some of the sick public sector enterprises fo und that the role of 
the management was a key factor in making such ente rprises sick.  It 
has, therefore, noted that measures should be taken  to make the 
management more accountable and committed.  The per sonal 
involvement and dedication of the management will s et an example of 
professionalism for making the company dynamic, via ble and 
profitable.  In the instant case of the Hindustan P hoto Films it is 
important for the Government of India to retain thi s Company and 
revive it.  In case this only public sector enterpr ise in the Neelgiris 
district of Tamil Nadu is done away with, then the region will forever 

 
 
lose it and the Government cannot assure people to set another public 
sector enterprise.  The Committee, therefore, stron gly recommends that 
it is wiser to retain what is already available and  revive and restructure 
it and adopt measures for its modernization.  
 
27. The Committee feels that the bulk purchase of p hoto sensitive 
material by the Government hospitals from the HPF m ay help the 
Company to improve its financial position.  This ma y be seriously 
considered and pursued.   
 
28. This is the age of digital technology.  In all sectors be it health 
care, defence, infrastructure, etc., the demand for  digital technology is 
growing.  Even hospitals have adopted digital X-ray .  In view of such 
changing profile of technology, it is important for  the HPF to go for 
introduction of new methods and innovations to make  it more 
competitive and viable.  It has noted that lack of investments for 
modernization resulted in massive loss for the Comp any.  Let this not 
happen yet again.  In replying to the question of C ommittee Secretariat 
concerning the R&D efforts being undertaken, the HP F stated that it 
has taken up projects for introduction of non-silve r digital imaging 
technology.  It is gratifying for the Committee to note that such steps 
have already been taken by the Company in associati on with M/s 
Technova and these have yielded job order revenue f or it. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for the a doption of digital 
technology and modernization of all its functioning for making it a more 
profitable and socially useful Company.

INTRODUCTION 
  
  
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred and 
Twenty Fifth Report on the Revival and Restructurin g of Hindustan Machines Tools Ltd. 
pertaining to Ministry of Heavy Industries and Publ ic Enterprises (Department of Heavy 
Industry).  
 
2. The Committee held detailed discussion with the Management of Hindustan Machines 
Tools Ltd and received inputs for this Report.   
 
3. I thank the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Pub lic Enterprises (Department of Heavy 
Industry) for furnishing the valuable inputs during the meetings.  
 
4. The Committee in its meeting held on 29 
th  July, 2011 considered and adopted the report. 
 
  
 
  
Tiruchi Siva 
Chairman                                                                                   
                          Department -related Parliamentary  
                                                                                                  Standing Committee   on    Industry  
 
New Delhi 
29 
th  July, 2011 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 REPORT  
 
 
Establishment of Hindustan Machine Tools in 1950s constituted a giant step to regenerate 
our economy by ensuring accelerated supply of quali ty machines to different segments of 
industry.  A well acclaimed public sector unit the HMT set the trend for efficient management 
and proven capability for greater productivity.  Be ing part of the structure of mixed economy, it 
was seen as a role model of excellence, dynamism an d business efficiency.  Our first Prime 
Minister Jawaharlal Nehru during whose tenure the H MT was established cited the example of 
HMT to underline the success of public sector enter prises and drive home the point that the 
public enterprises had to be run with greater efficiency and profit.   
 
2. Our national leadership had comprehensive unders tanding that machine making assumed 
centrality in augmenting our economic and industria l strength.  As the private sector during the 
formative period of independence lacked expertise, economic resources and necessary 
infrastructure to engage itself in the mammoth task  of nation building, the founding fathers of 
our country conceived the scheme for providing lead ership role to the public sector in creating 
conditions for our growth and development.  The set ting up of HMT represented that grand 
vision to transform India along modern lines and cr eate machine building capability for 
economic renaissance and industrial progress of our country.   
 
3. The vitality of the public sector for the reviva l of our economy and taking it forward has 
been glowingly acknowledged.  The doyens of private  sector recognized that the strength and 
capability of Indian economy so carefully nurtured by the public sector enterprises enabled them 
to scale new heights of economic efficiency and pro gress.  It is in this broader historical 
perspective that the role of public sector enterpri ses in general and HMT in particular has to be 
understood.   
 
4. There was a time when HMT commanded the admirati on of the entire nation.  The 
watches produced by the HMT made deep impact on pop ular imagination and a countrywide 
craze for such watches made them popular and well-accepted.  The HMT products very well  
1 

 
 
represented the slogan ‘Be Indian buy Indian’.  The  late Prime Minister of India Smt. Indira 
Gandhi described Hindustan Machine Tools as one of the outstanding industrial enterprises of 
our country and referred to it as a model of dynami c management not only in the public sector 
but also in the public and private sectors combined .  Diversifying from the core activity of 
manufacturing of machine tools the HMT expanded its  scope by proving its worth in many 
sectors.  The wide variety of its products be it ma chine tools, tractors, watches and capital goods 
were extensively used in many areas of our economy including the defence sector.  It had the 
record of declaring highest dividend in any public sector during 1960-61 and registering its net 
profit on a year to year basis.  As a flagship publ ic sector enterprise, it scored enviable prestige 
and esteem and was looked upon by people with admiration.   
 
5. The inevitable onset of economic reforms in our country unleashed entrepreneurial 
potential of our economy in a more deregulated and competitive atmosphere.  The HMT as a 
public sector enterprise found it hard to cope up w ith the challenges of a reformed economy 
which mandated greater efficiency, prudent use of h uman resources, primacy of competition and 
buoyancy of business activity.  In such a new econo mic setting which required deployment of 
more skills and high degree of competition, the HMT  found itself wanting.  It started declining 
from its much acclaimed position as a profit making company to a loss making enterprise.   
 
6. The Department-related Parliament Standing Commi ttee on Industry studied the HMT 
Ltd. during its visit to Bangalore in January, 2011  and interacted with representatives entrusted 
with the responsibility of running this enterprise.   The Committee was pained to know that the 
HMT which soared high as a public sector enterprise  had to come to such a sorry state of affairs 
due to several factors which include the callous mi smanagement of its affairs and the 
indifference of the Government to accelerate its revival.   
 
7. The vision of the HMT Ltd. sets the target to em erge as an engineering company of 
repute, providing best of products and services wit h contemporary technologies, to suit customer 
needs.  As far as its mission is concerned, it has set itself the goal to serve the country’s strategi c 
sector through development of high technology produ cts and to achieve sustained growth and 
profitability.   
2 

 
 
8. Most of the subsidiaries of the HMT are far from  the aforementioned vision and mission.  
The HMT holding company and its subsidiaries are in  such a sorry state of affairs.  It is now in 
an unenviable position of being referred to Bureau for Reconstruction of Public Sector 
Enterprises.  The Government of India approved a pl an in July 2000 for its turn around by 
restructuring the HMT Ltd. and converting into five  separate subsidiary companies.  The HMT 
Ltd. was considered as a holding company with tract or manufacturing as its core activity.  The 
other subsidiaries are HMT Machine Tools Ltd., HMT Watches Ltd., HMT Chinar Watches Ltd, 
HMT Bearing Ltd. and HMT International Ltd.  The Go vernment holding in the company is 
98.88 per cent.   
 
9. It has got two joint ventures, namely, SUDMO HMT  Process Engineers (I) Ltd. and 
Nigeria Machine Tools Ltd. with the equity particip ation of 50 per cent and 15 per cent, 
respectively.   
 
10. The Committee was given to understand that the HMT suffered decline due to numerous 
factors which include the vertical integration of p lants and assembly ancillaries.  Other reasons 
for its recurrent loss are increasing social overhe ad cost and ageing plant & machinery.  Its net 
worth eroded considerably.  According to the study conducted by Center for Monitoring Indian 
Economy its return on net worth declined from -4.42 in March 2008 to -4.94 in March 2010.   
 
11. The Committee is extremely pained to know that the Government of India adopted 
a casual attitude in not taking measures for modernization of plant and machinery of HMT 
to face the increasingly competitive market.  The C ommittee feels that the management of 
HMT will have to be held accountable for not keepin g the company technologically and 
economically viable.  There are many public sector enterprises which have successfully 
adjusted to a highly commercialized business enviro nment and registered profit.  A 
company like HMT which is engaged in machine tool s ector has a wider market for 
supplying machines which are in growing demand across the economic segment.   
 
 
3 
 

 
 
12. India has a vast and expanding market for machi ne tools.  Its volume is estimated to 
be approximately Rs.8000 crore out of which the HMT  Machine Tools is able to capture 
Rs.200 crore only and rest of its is shared by priv ate players and import from foreign 
countries. 
  
13. Our economy is growing at a reasonably higher r ate.  It is also expanding and 
diversifying.  Therefore, the demand for machine to ols is bound to grow up.  It is in this 
context that concerted efforts have to be made to t ap this vast market by manufacturing 
such tools within our country.  HMT Machine Tools h as to show greater dynamism and 
business competence to increase its share of market for its products.  
 
14. It can be done by employing better skills and m arket management.  The 
Department of Heavy Industry referred the loss maki ng HMT Machine Tools Ltd. and 
HMT Bearings Ltd. to the BIFR.  At a time when the Government of India is 
acknowledging the resilience of public sector enterprises as a major factor for withstanding 
the financial crisis and at a time when the Governm ent is reasonably happy with the 
performance of the PSEs, it is important that speci al and focused attention be given to the 
revival of HMT which can be made robust and forward looking.   
 
15. The summary record of the proceedings of hearing held on 12 June 2008 before the BIFR 
bench consisting of Shri A.K. Goswami, Chairman, BI FR and Shri K. Cherian Varghese, 
Member throw light on the scheme for the revival of  the Hindustan Machine Tools.  The Bench 
while taking note of the general consensus in respe ct of the revival scheme observed the 
following:  
  
 “… there is general consensus in respect of the re habilitation scheme.  … attrition of 
employees on account of unrevised and low salary le vels is an issue which deserves the attention 
of the Government of India.  The Board recognizes t hat the company is not able to afford a wage 
revision with its present financial position but th e issue of competent and technically qualified 
employees leaving the company will make the company less competitive.  The company has to  
4 

 
 
improve its productivity and earn more to pay more.   Banks charged interest rates up to 5% 
above BPLR on the plea that the company was not dec lared sick.  The purpose of the Reserve 
Bank of India guidelines to charge interest at BPLR only from sick companies is to provide relief 
to such units.  Because of the provision of SICA, t he newly formed company could file its 
reference-only after 5 years of its incorporation a lthough the net worth was negative from the 
beginning and consequently the company was sick.  A  very technical and narrow interpretation 
of a sick company under RBI guidelines from the dat e of reference to BIFR and charging high 
rate of interest by banks may not be in the interes t of revival of the company.  The company has 
been honouring the commitments to banks in spite of  its tight financial position by borrowing 
from Government of India.  GOI has made much sacrif ice in respect of the dues of the company.  
In these circumstances the Bench is inclined to ret ain the stipulation in the rehabilitation scheme 
requiring banks to charge interest at BPLR rate only from 1.4.2000.”  
 
16. The Committee noted the following reasons for t he sickness of HMT Machine Tools in 
particular and HMT as a whole.   
• Working capital constraints 
• High interest burden 
• Old plant & machinery not upgraded 
• High costs due to vertical integration  
• Compression of demand since 1996-97 
• High competition from imports due to liberalization 
• Used machines allowed for imports 
• Non-availability of level playing field 
• Surplus manpower in non core areas 
• Non induction of fresh technical talent  
 
17. The Committee takes note of the fact that the r evival package for HMT Ltd. was `880.80 
crore.  The BIFR observed that the revival plan proposals of the Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd. is 
viable.   
 
18.  It is observed that a part time Chairman and acting  Managing Director of the HMT 
Machine Tools Ltd. has been appointed on 1 January 2011 onwards.    
 
5 

 
 
19. With the appointment of a part time Chairman an d acting Managing Director, the 
Machine Tools unit has registered improved performa nce which is certainly heartening.  The 
Committee understands that the following steps have  been taken to bring about a transformation 
in the working culture of the Hindustan Machine Tools.  These are: 
 
I. Change of mindset and attitude of the employees 
II. Aggressive marketing and customer responsiveness 
III. Enforcing financial discipline 
IV. Inculcating Team Spirit 
V. Making the team believe that HMT-MTL can be turned around   
 
20. Out of the five factors outlined above, three o f these concerning change of mindset and 
attitude of the employees, inculcating team spirit and making the team believe that HMT-MTL 
can be turned around are intangibles which are as i mportant as tangible factors such as 
technology, financial discipline and marketing stra tegy.  The fact that some improvement has 
taken place by suitably employing both tangible and  intangible factors prove the point that a lot 
can be done by strategic decision making and guaran teeing independence and autonomy to the 
people entrusted with the responsibility of making viable and profitable.    
 
21. The Committee could see the hopeful trends in t he Order Book position for the Machine 
Tools for the period 2009-10 and 2010-11.   
 
Order Booking 
 
    Rs `Crores      
    2009-10    2010-11 
April-December 102 147 
January-March 64 89 
Total for the year  166 236 
 
22. The figures in the above table are self explana tory. The Order Booking position has 
registered significant increase from `166 crore in 2009 to `236 crore in 2010-11. The Committee 
has been informed through a separate communication that the order booking of the company in  
6 

 
 
the month of March 2011 alone has been `58 crore which, it is said to be, “an all time high  till 
this date”.   
 
23. Similarly, the sales of the Company has been in creasing. While the figure for sales for 
January-March 2009-10 was `49 crore, it was `69 crore for the same period during 2010-11.  
 
24. This increasing trend of high order booking and  sales has generated confidence in those 
who run the Company to pitch for higher annual gros s sales of `340 crores which possibly would 
fetch marginal profit.  
 
25. The Committee warmly welcomes the measures take n by the HMT Machine Tools 
Limited to revitalize it. The hope nursed by the ma nagement of the Company that it would 
achieve a positive turn around due to higher order booking and higher sales augurs well for its 
future. In fact with the growth and expansion of In dian economy there is going to be greater 
demand for machinery. Such demand assumes critical significance in the context of India 
emerging as a global manufacturing hub. The origina l purpose behind the foundation of the 
HMT Machine Ltd. was to provide machines to the div erse sectors of our economy which have a 
great potential to grow. Now that our growth rate i s impressive and manufacturing sector 
substantially contributes to our onward march as a major economic player in the world, it is 
important for the HMT Machine Tools Limited to tap the expanding market.  
 
26. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends t he Government for supporting 
the HMT Machine Tools in every way for its commerci al viability and profitability. It  
compliments  its top management for changing the at titude of the personnel of the 
Company  and inculcating among them the much needed  team spirit and understanding 
that they can once again make it commercially attractive, financially sound, technologically 
up to date and profitable.  The recent initiatives ushered in by the management , it is 
hoped, will go a long way in creating a work cultur e which will help the Company to stand 
on its own strength and make a name for itself thro ugh its quality product and high levels 
of customer satisfaction.  
7 

 
 
27. The Committee after careful perusal of the pape rs submitted to it has understood that the 
subsidiaries of HMT are not able to function with e fficiency and effectiveness due to lack of 
independence and autonomy which are key to the succ ess of any company in the highly 
competitive and globalised environment of our time.   
 
28. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the subsi diaries must be given due 
independence and autonomy.  If all the time these s ubsidiaries remained dependent on 
holding company, their own progress would be retarded by virtue of the fact that these will 
not be able to take faster decision for manufacturing products and doing business.   
 
29. The Committee recommends that the changes that have taken place after the 
appointment of the part time Chairman and acting Ma naging Director must be taken note 
of by the Department of Heavy Industry.  
 
30. The Committee is of the view that one person we ll acclaimed for his or her expertise 
in engineering and technological fields and with ad equate experience of administering 
enterprises may be appointed as CMD for the HMT and  its subsidiaries as a whole.  He 
must be given full responsibility and independence to make decisions for making the HMT 
Machine Tools and other units more competitive and commercially relevant.   
 
31. Except the HMT International, all other subsidi aries of the HMT have not been doing 
well in the field of business and as a result have suffered losses.   
 
32. The Committee was informed that the HMT suffere d sub-optimal performance due to 
following reasons:- 
• 6500 employees were given Voluntary Retirement Sche me during 2000-02 by raising 
`469 crores through external borrowings as 10 year GoIG Bonds resulting in: 
• Interest outgo of `186 crores leading to erosion of working capital.  
• Retention of talent & attraction of new talent cont inues to be a constraint due to non 
revision of pay scales. 
 
8 

 
 
• Investments were not made for upgradation of manufa cturing facilities & product 
technology. 
• Further, in 2003, the age of superannuation was red uced to 58 years resulting in 
accelerated separation of several senior and key executives.  
 
33. However, the Company prepared a plan for turnin g around its performance in 1998.  It 
included restructuring of manpower, organization an d of course restructuring of its debt on 
financial liabilities.  By perusing the literature provided to the Committee, it was understood that 
the turn around of the Company could not be made du e to shortage of working capital, enormous 
liabilities amounting to `374 crores and failure to dispose of non-performing  assets.  Apart from 
these reasons, the Company failed to take up issues  such as product development/diversification, 
technological upgradation and plant modernization o wing to shortage of resources.  In spite of 
the measures taken to revive the Company, its perfo rmance level plummeted.  It is rather painful 
to note that the Company which was doing so well be fore the advent of economic reforms had to 
come to such a sorry state of affairs resulting in its downfall.  One of the predominant factors 
behind the failure of the Company is the absence of  modern technology and machinery.  As a 
public sector enterprise, it had to function within  certain rules and regulations.  In fact, there are  
many PSEs which have proved their worth in spite of  the constraints faced by them.  The 
Committee feels that the utter failure of the HMT to come to terms with the liberalized economic 
environment arrested its productivity and contribut ed to its decline.  The apathy of the 
Government in responding slowly to its problems further compounded its economic woes.   
 
34. The Committee takes heart from the revival plan  which aim at addressing the challenges 
faced by the HMT.  The background paper made availa ble to the Committee outlines the key 
features of the revival plan which include: 
• Upgradation/renewal/modernization of plant and machinery 
• Introduction of new products/processes/technology in line with market requirements 
• Settlement of Overdue long term liabilities on acco unt of the funds borrowed for 
Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) separations along with the interest burden 
 
9 

 
 
• Reduce the large scale attrition of professionals a nd skilled force through implementation 
of revised pay-scales 
• Recruit fresh talent through payment of attractive salaries on par with other PSUs as most 
of the persons recruited had resigned within a year or two on account of low salaries 
• Rationalize manpower, increase outsourcing, vendor development, etc. 
 
35. The Committee understands that the common refra in of all the subsidiaries of the HMT 
are early approval of revival plans by the Governme nt, permission to implement 1997 Pay Scale 
wages and timely payment of salaries to the employe es.  Without going into the details of the 
statistics concerning net worth, profit after tax, turnover and other basic factors which determine 
the resilience of a company in a business environme nt, the Committee strongly feels that most of 
the subsidiaries can be revived and their economic viability assured by giving the leadership role 
of the HMT to a visionary technocrat who can combin e both business acumen and social 
purpose.  It is recommended that in case of HMT Ltd. which ma nufactures tractors the 
possibility of establishing joint ventures for this  purpose may be explored.  In case of HMT 
Bearings Ltd. it is recommended that a strategic pa rtner may be tapped to carry forward 
its business and expand it.  It is also proposed th at infusion of more finance to it may be 
examined.     
 
36. It is rather sad to note that the employees of most  of the subsidiaries are getting pay 
scales which were determined in early 90s.  It is a ll the more shocking to know that Senior 
Managers of the Company are drawing salaries which are less than that of the workers 
who due to accumulation of their annual increments get more salaries than the officers at 
the managerial position.  This is an anomaly which demotivates those who are asked to 
play leadership role in the Company.  The Committee  understand that there are some 
sections of employees who did not draw their pay fo r several years.  They pathetically 
pleaded before the Committee for payment of their s alaries so that at least they would feed 
their families.  In fact, the long pending pay/wage  revision has to be put on fast track 
without which both the Company and employees would face hardships.  In the absence of 
attractive pay scales the Company has lost valuable  human resources to other private 
players.   
10 

 
 
37. The Committee was told that the pay revision co uld not be affected in 1997 except in 
case of the HMT (International) due to the huge los s suffered by all the HMT Companies.  The 
Committee strongly recommends the Government to look into this problem and take measures to 
address it.   
 
38. The Committee also takes note of the fact that the retirement age for the employees of the 
Company is 58 years whereas in many other PSEs it i s 60 years.  Due to the fixation of 
retirement age at 58 years, the Company is in a dis advantageous position to retain its skilled 
work force and Managers beyond that age.  This prob lem has been further compounded by the 
absence of fresh recruitment of new personnel.  All  these issues require serious and focused 
attention from the Department of Heavy Industry and  Government of India.  It is recommended 
that the retirement age may be increased to 60 years.    
 
39. It is painful to note that revival plan is under th e consideration of the Government 
of India for almost half a decade.  The slow pace a t which the Government tries to consider 
the revival plan is indicative of its mindset in ma king our public sector undertakings viable 
from the point of view of business proposition.  Th e Government’s commitment to 
strengthen public sector enterprises does not sound  convincing the way it is treating the 
revival plan of the HMT group of companies.   
 
40. During its presentation before the Committee, t he HMT provided a road map on 
strategies to achieve its targets.  While the HMT ( International) which is a profit making 
subsidiary requested the Government to make it a no dal agency for projects of the 
Ministry of External Affairs, it wanted to appoint representatives in more countries to 
pursue its business activities.  It also desires to  scale up its business two hundred crores in 
two years and focus attention on high value machine  tools/turn key projects.  The 
Committee feels that its future road map and strate gies are achievable.  The success of the 
HMT (International) is indicative of the fact that range of the products of the HMT 
Companies such as machine tools, watches, tractors, bearings, general engineering  
 
11 

 
 
products, industrial commodities software, etc., ha ve a market outside the country.  This 
means if the subsidiaries are made viable and profi table it can get more business abroad.  
Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends for th e revival of the HMT and its 
subsidiaries.   
 
41. The Committee feels that it is worth focusing a ttention on HMT Watches Ltd. which had 
manufacturing units in Bangalore, Tunkur and Ranibagh.  There is yet another subsidiaries HMT 
Chinar Watches, which is located in Srinagar.  Thes e two subsidiaries, HMT Watches and HMT 
Chinar Watches, are engaged in producing mechanical  and Quartz Watches both for ladies and 
gents.  These two subsidiaries also are manufacturi ng special and souvenir watches.  It is rather 
sad to note that most of the products of these Comp anies are sold in CSD canteens and through 
other institutional arrangements.  The public enter prises survey analyze the performance of the 
HMT watches and stated the following:- 
“The Company registered an increase `5.70 crore in total income during 2009-10 which 
went up to `18.27 crore in 2009-10 from `12.57 crore during 2008-09.  The net loss of the 
company increased to `168.35 crore, an increase of `4.29 crore over the previous year’s loss due 
to absence of trade channel, higher interest burden , broken supply chain and also due to 
truncated cash cycle.  Institutional sales contributed 35 per cent of total sales.”  
 
42. In a fiercely competitive market where private players are offering attractive watches to 
the consumers, it is very difficult to promote HMT watches which once enjoyed the confidence 
of the customers across the country.  It has been p roposed that in the present day economic 
environment watch making is no more considered as a  viable proposition as small scale 
industries find it cheaper to get imports from abroad at a lesser cost than the one manufactured in 
India.  The management of HMT Watches Ltd. is of th e opinion that HMT watches still has a 
brand value in the market.  It is hoping that by ma nufacturing only quartz watches it can take 
advantage of the brand image of HMT watches still p ersisting in the mind of the consumer.  The 
Committee cautiously welcomes the hopeful propositi on of the management of the HMT 
watches Ltd .  It, therefore, recommends for the examination of this hopeful proposition and  
 
12 

 
 
accordingly see if HMT watches can be made economic ally viable and attractive for the 
customers in the present day globalised market situ ation.   One possible option is to tap the 
customers in the villages of India by adopting inno vative marketing strategies.  This would mean 
reaching out to them through many other agencies su ch as post offices or some of the public 
sector banks which may display HMT watches in remot e areas through their branches and take a 
commission for doing so.  This would be quite a dif ferent approach in relation to the approach 
involving establishment of showrooms in urban areas  and cities.  Usually it would be very 
difficult to compete with private players who have catered to the customers in towns and cities 
by providing them with new models of watches.   
 
43. The revival and restructuring of the sick publi c sector units receive priority attention of 
the Government.  However, the Committee notes with concern that the inordinate delay on 
the part of the Government in taking up the revival  package will further sink the loss 
making PSEs to a pitiable state of affairs.   The public sector undertakings have to remain 
tuned to the new market situation.  On 27 June 1961 , in a Letter to the Chief Ministers, first 
Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who describ ed the public sector enterprises as the 
commanding heights of economy, had written that, “T he old idea that profit making is a private 
concern and not a public concern has to be discarde d completely.  Our public enterprises have to 
be run with the greatest efficiency and the greates t profit.”  He made those insightful comments 
in the context of the remarkable success achieved by the Hindustan Machine Tools of Bangalore.  
The Department of Heavy Industry, the HMT as a whol e and the Government of India has a 
historic responsibility to once again revive the HM T to its past glory.  All concerned must 
respond to the call of duty to achieve that goal. The Committee recommends that the 
Government of India must expedite the revival proce ss of HMT taking serious note of the 
special concern for the industry and employees on the whole.
