Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The interactions of Committee with various associat ions and banks revealed that 
interest rates charged by banks differ. The Ministr y of Finance should intervene to fix the 
upper limit of rate of interest which must be adher ed to by the banks while extending the 
credit to MSMEs. The Ministry of Finance must ensure its implementation. 
 
(Para 35) 
 
 

-11- 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
Interest rates have been deregulated by RBI. Banks determine their actual lending 
rates on loans and advances with reference to their  Base Rate. Banks have, however, been 
advised that the actual lending rates charged by them should be transparent and consistent.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee observes that while interest rates h ave been de-regulated to 
encourage competition among Banks, the interest rates are almost identical across the 
Banks.  The MSME sector has not benefitted by such de-regulated environment, their 
plight remains the same.  Therefore, the Committee suggests that while RBI 
prescribes base rates, it may also prescribe a cap on interest rate for MSMEs.  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
 
The Committee notes that the burden of insuring the  bank credit through CGTMSE 
ultimately falls upon the entrepreneur who in any c ase pays higher interest rate to Bank. 
The Committee recommends that cost of insuring the credit should be borne by the Bank 
and not by the entrepreneur. In this regard, the Co mmittee would also like to know the 
recommendations of the Working Group under the Chai rmanship of the Executive 
Director, RBI.  
(Para 37) 
 
Action Taken  
 
As per extant guidelines of Credit Guarantee Scheme , the cost of guarantee cover 
has to be paid by the respective Member Lending Ins titutions (MLIs) to Credit Guarantee 
Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE).   H owever, the amount equivalent to 
the guarantee fee and/or the service fee payable by  the eligible lending institution may be 
recovered by the MLI, at its discretion from the el igible borrower whose credit facility is 
covered under Credit Guarantee Scheme. A composite all-in Guarantee fee up to a 
maximum 1% of credit facility sanctioned to be paid  upfront has now been introduced 
w.e.f. January 01, 2013. 
 A Working Group under the Chairmanship of Shri V.K . Sharma, Executive 
Director, RBI, was constituted to review the Credit  Guarantee Fund Scheme for MSEs to 
make it more effective. The Working Group had recom mended that the Government may 
bear the credit guarantee fees for collateral free loans up to Rs. 10 lakh to micro enterprises 
in order to encourage financial inclusion in the se ctor. The Group was of the opinion that 
the micro enterprises should not be burdened with t he cost of guarantee fees and it might 
not be appropriate to ask banks, which are commerci al entities; to bear the guarantee fee as 
any scheme for banks has to be a reasonable busines s proposition for it to be readily 
acceptable. Further, if banks were made to bear the  fee, they would somehow either 
discourage lending to MSEs, especially Micro Enterprises, or somehow  indirectly load  the  
 

-12- 
 
 
same on the customer by charging a higher rate of i nterest on the facility provided thereby 
defeating the very purpose of fostering and developing the MSE sector. 
 
 The above issue was also discussed in the 14 
th  SAC meeting held on November 21, 
2012 and it was decided that as per extant guidelin es banks would provide collateral free 
loans and the guarantee fee would have to be borne by the borrowers or banks or shared by 
both as per the bank’s policies. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 On the issue of bearing the cost of credit guarant ee fee, the Committee is of the 
opinion that either Government or Banks should bear  the cost, atleast in respect of 
Micro Enterprises as part of support to the sector.   
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee also appreciates the concern regardin g shorter repayment period to 
banks. The SMEs face huge pressure of performance a nd work under constant threat of 
defaulting on repayment, which may eventually leads to sickness. 
 
(Para 38) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
As informed by the RBI, credit related matters have  been deregulated and banks are 
free to sanction the credit, including fixing the r epayment periods, as per their commercial 
judgment and the merits of each case keeping in view the loan policies as approved by their 
Board of Directors.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee takes note of the suggestion that the  repayment period may be 
increased up to 15 years and recommends that RBI sh ould take note of such suggestions in 
view of increasing sickness in the sector. The Comm ittee would also expect that RBI 
dilutes NPA norms for micro and small enterprises m ost of whom often suffer constraints 
in cash flow from their respective buyers or face severe vagaries of market. 
 
 
(Para 39) 
 
 
 
 
 

-13- 
 
Action Taken  
 
As indicated above, credit related matters have bee n deregulated and banks are free 
to  sanction  the credit, including  fixing  the  repayment  periods, as  per  their  commercial 
judgment and the merits of each case keeping in view the loan policies as approved by their 
Board of Directors. In this context, IBA has inform ed that repayment period of term loans 
is normally linked to the economic life of the asset covered. 
 
 As regards diluting the NPA Norms, the RBI has inf ormed that guidelines on 
Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Norms are uniformly applicable 
across all sectors, including MSE sector. The 90 da ys delinquency norm for NPAs evolved 
over a period and was brought in through calibrated  process in our efforts to bench mark 
our prudential regulations to the international sta ndards. Further, any delay in recognition 
of NPAs removes pressure on the banks to deal promptly with the problem. As these norms 
have been prescribed with a view to ensuring financ ial soundness of banks, any deviation 
would not be desirable. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation on paras 38 & 39
 
 
 On the one hand it has been stated that the credit  related matters have been 
deregulated but on the other hand, the NPA guidelin es are stated to be uniformally 
applicable.  The Committee finds the reply ambivale nt.  Despite supposed 
deregulation, repayment norms remain almost identic al in all the Banks.  In case of 
NPA too, the Committee is not convinced with intern ational standard   argument at 
the cost of domestic MSMEs.  Given that MSME are at the base of industrial pyramid 
and have to depend on extraneous factors beyond the ir control, the Ministry of 
MSME must take up the issue with Department of Fina ncial Services and Reserve 
Bank of India to relax NPA and other repayment norm s to ease the pressure on 
MSMEs.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
-14- 
 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
 
 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which fi nal replies of the Ministry have 
not been received 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee notes that the number of enterprises who had filed memoranda has 
increased exponentially from about 1.75 lakh in 2007-08 to 2.82 lakh in 2011-12. However, 
the Committee observes reduction in number of regis trations in successive years in case of 
certain States.  The Committee would like to explore the reasons for such reduction. 
(Para 8) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
As per the data on number of Entrepreneurs Memorand um Part-II (EM-II) filed by 
MSMEs a consistent growth is observed in number of filing of EM-II, every year at All 
India Level.  However, it is also noticed that ther e is a variation in number of filing of EM-
II by entrepreneurs in successive years in case of certain States/UTs.  This is because in the 
recent time, the MSMEs have shown consistent growth  of more than 10% every year in 
terms of number of filing of EM-II every year. The number of EM-II filed during 2007-08 
at the district Industries Centres across the count ry has increased from 1.73 lakh to 1.93, 
2.14, 2.38, 2.38 and 3.22 lakh during 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12.   
The filing of memorandum is optional under the MSME D Act, 2006 for micro and 
small (manufacturing & service enterprises) and med ium (service enterprises).   However, 
it is mandatory for the manufacturing medium enterprises.  Ministry of MSME has pursued 
hard with the States to implement online filing of EM.  As a result Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, 
Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, U ttarakhand, Jharkhand, Kerala and 
Assam have already implemented it.  For the rest of the States, the Ministry is still pursuing 
for the same.  As online filing will ease the filin g of EM, the number of EMs filed shall 
improve. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 The Committee is of the view that gradually the re gistration requirement 
should be extended to all SMEs.  To facilitate this , online registration should be 
encouraged with automatic approval after reasonable  time.  Also, the industry 
associations too should share data of their members  with District Industrial Centres 
and encourage their Members to register.  
 
 
 

-15- 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee observes that the said notification d oes not cover the Autonomous 
organizations/Societies/Trusts/ Institutions/ Unive rsities and other Government aided 
organizations under the various Central Government Ministries/ Departments. The 
Committee also wonders if the notification includes  the Constitutional bodies. The 
Committee recommends that the said notification sho uld include such institutions. The 
Committee also recommends that the Central Governme nt should persuade the State 
Governments to adopt similar policies, for which Go vernment can use the National Board 
as a forum where State Governments are also represented by rotation. 
(Para 10) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Under the provision of section 11 of MSMED Act, 200 6, Government of India has 
introduced a Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises Order, 2012.  This 
policy is applicable on Central Ministries, Central  Departments and Central PSUs. The 
Chief Ministers of all the State Governments have b een requested by the Hon’ble Minister, 
Ministry of MSME to formulate similar policy in their States. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee is of the opinion that Autonomous Org anizations, Government 
Societies/Trusts and Universities/Educational Insti tutes too should be covered under 
this Scheme.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Considering the inflation and dynamic market situat ion, the Committee feels that 
definition of MSMEs as provided in the Act may be revised every five years. 
(Para 16) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
To facilitate flexible approach for defined limit o f MSMEs, the Ministry is 
considering to provide it in the notifications only and not in the Act. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee feels that if needed, the Act should be amended to make 
definition flexible.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 

-16- 
 
The Committee notes that the Report of the Working Group on the MSME for the 
12 th  Plan, too recommended    that   the States should encourage ‘online’ filing of 
Memoranda. Considering the consensus on the issue, the Committee expects that necessary 
steps should be taken to resolve the issue expediti ously. The MSME Ministry should 
encourage the Micro and Small Enterprises to register themselves 
 
(Para 19) 
Action Taken  
 
On the initiative and pursuance of Office of Develo pment Commissioner (MSME) 
many States have implemented online filing such as Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Odisha, Uttar 
Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Kerala and Assam. The O/o  
DCMSME is pursuing hard for an early implementation  of online filing of EM by rest of 
the States. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee recommends that registration should b e granted automatically 
after a reasonable period of submission of application. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee recommends to the Ministry to assess whether enjoining the IFCs 
with the provisions of Arbitration and Conciliation  Act, 1996, has actually rendered the 
mechanism ineffective and to devise more effective provisions for IFC. The Committee 
also suggests that methods like supply against Lett ers of Credit etc. should be used more 
regularly to make payment predictable. The Committe e suggests that Ministry should 
explore the possibility if such methods could be made mandatory. 
(Para 20) 
Action Taken  
 
The process of arbitration is a faster approach for  solving of disputes. The same 
case in Civil Courts will take longer period thus c ausing increased suffering for the MSEs 
leading to sickness.  
 
The mode of supply against Letter of Credit by the supplier depends on the contract 
agreed by it with the buyer. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee recommends that to assess the effici ency of Industrial 
Facilitation Councils (IFCs), the Ministry in its A nnual Report should include the 
State-wise figures of new and pending cases with mo re than 90 days in term of 
number and reference. 
 

-17- 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee notes that the Procurement Preference  Policy notified by the 
Government in March 2012 will come to effect from 1 st  April 2015. However the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of MSME work  in close coordination with the 
Directorate General, Supply and Disposal (DGS&D)      and other similar Government 
procurement agencies to iron out initial functional  bottlenecks in implementing the Policy. 
The Ministry must see that tender specifications mu st not be designed to exclude the MSE 
sector. The Committee also notes the exclusion of Medium enterprises from the Policy. 
(Para 22) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry of MSME has been tirelessly communicat ing and coordinating with 
the Central Ministries/ Departments/ CPSUs for effe ctive implementation of the Public 
Procurement Policy. Further, Ministry of MSME is ta king up the grievances/ suggestions 
of MSEs related to tender specification with all the concerned departments/ DGS&D etc. as 
and when it is brought in the notice of Ministry of MSME. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should study the provisions of 
the Public Procurement Bill and highlight the enabl ing provisions of MSME.  The 
NSIC too while extending help to MSMEs, liaise with  DGS&D on their behalf, should 
also provide in its Annual Report State-wise data o f cases in terms of numbers and 
volume with respect to MSME under its programme of Consortia and Tender 
Marketing and Single Point Registration for Government Purchase.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee is in agreement with the suggestion o f the Working Group on 
MSME for 12 th  Plan that ‘Each Ministry/Department and CPSU, etc. , should make a 
specific mention of the compliance with the prefere nce policy in its Annual Report to be 
tabled in Parliament. Progressive Associations of M SEs should be associated with 
monitoring implementation and suggesting appropriate revision of the policies.’ 
(Para 24) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Every Ministry/Department/ CPSU has to report goals  set with respect to 
procurement to be met from MSEs and achievement made thereto in their respective annual 
reports. The suggestions of MSME Associations are c onsidered for coordinating and 
implementing of the policy. The MSE Associations ar e also invited in the revision of the 
policy through Review Committee. 
  

-18- 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Ministry of MSME may compile data on compliance  with the preference 
policy and provide the same to the Committee.  Also , the Ministry of MSME too 
should publish Ministry-wise targets and achievemen ts on Public Procurement Policy 
in its Annual Report.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee recommends that a monitoring mechanis m should be set up to 
effectively monitor 30% procurement from small industries. 
(Para 29) 
Action Taken  
 
The constitution of above mentioned committee is un der consideration in the D/o 
Consumer Affairs. The proposed Terms of Reference, inter-alia include the following: 
(i) to determine the safeguards to be put in place to protect the interest of small traders vis-
à-vis organized retail; 
(ii) to examine the need and the possible mandate f or a Regulatory body/authority for the 
regulation of organized retail trade. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee is of the view that the monitoring or  regulatory mechanism 
should include Ministry of MSME and that changes in  FDI Policy in Multi Brand 
Retail Trade (MBRT) must be discussed in National MSME Board.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Considering the benefits MSEs get in interest rate,  the Committee would like to 
know the coverage of the Performance and Credit rat ing Scheme and steps taken to expand 
the coverage. The Committee suggests that the MSEs should be encouraged to adopt credit 
rating. In view of similar suggestion of the Task F orce, the Committee would like to know 
from the Ministry about Government’s response to th e suggestion of interest rate 
subvention in respect of MSEs. However, the Committ ee again notes that the Scheme 
excludes the Medium enterprises, which goes against  the inherent intent of the MSMED 
Act that considers MSME sector as an organic progression. 
(Para 34) 
Action Taken  
 
The Indian Banks’ Association has informed that cre dit rating is being used by the 
banks in assessment of credit needs of MSME units a nd better rated units are offered finer 
rates of interest for borrowers. Since inception of  the scheme, its performance is 
continuously showing an increasing trend.  For cont inuation of the scheme in 12 th  Plan 
period, EFC Note has  been circulated  among  various Departments.  Inclusion of  Medium 
 

 
-19- 
 
Enterprises under Performance & Credit Rating Scheme has also been proposed in the EFC 
Note. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
 So far the Performance & Credit Rating Scheme excl uding the Medium 
enterprises.  The Ministry in its reply has informe d that inclusion of Medium 
Enterprises has been proposed in EFC Note.  The Com mittee desires that Ministry 
may inform the final outcome of EFC Note. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee also takes note of new concepts like factoring services. The Act 
must provide for such mechanism so as to enable the  MSME units to avail these 
mechanisms for easy access to institutional credit. 
(Para 40) 
Action Taken 
 
 
The Department of Financial Services, Ministry of F inance has informed that an 
EFC Note for Setting up of Credit Guarantee Fund fo r Factoring has been prepared and 
sent to D/o Expenditure to convene EFC meeting. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Ministry of MSME must provide in details of suc h Schemes as and when 
approved alongwith its comments to the Committee.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee takes note of the recommendations of the Task Force, which has 
identified the concerned Ministries and set the tim elines for the implementation of its 
recommendations. The Committee would like to know t he status of implementation of 
these recommendations. In this respect, the Committ ee also took note of the observation 
made by the Task Force which stated “None of these measures will work unless their 
implementation status is monitored regularly at the  highest level. The issues are simply too 
diverse to be handled by a single line Ministry. Th e Task Force accordingly recommends 
the establishment of Prime Minister’s Council on Micro and Small Enterprises in the Prime  
Minister’s Office which may oversee implementation of  these  recommendations on  a half  
yearly basis. The Ministry of MSME shall be the ser vicing arm for the Council.” The 
Committee though shares the apprehensions and conce rn of the Task Force regarding 
implementation of its recommendation; it is convinc ed that the implementation should be 
monitored by a Ministry that is answerable to the P arliament and its Committee, directly 
and  not  a  Task  Force.  The  Ministry  must make use of the available statutory forum like 
 
 

-20- 
 
 
 National MSME Board where concerned Ministries, Ba nkers/ financial institutions, State 
Governments and select associations are represented . Side tracking a Statutory Board shall 
only dilute the eminent force of a law passed by the Parliament 
(Para 42) 
Action Taken 
 
  
 
The Prime Minister’s Task Force on MSMEs made 85 re commendations under 
various areas including credit, marketing, labour, rehabilitation and exit policy, 
infrastructure/ technology/skill development and taxation. Out of the 85 recommendations; 
 
I. action on 39 recommendations have been completed. 
II. action on 24 recommendations completed but follow up to be monitored. 
III. action on 14 recommendations at various stages of implementation and  
IV. 8 recommendations dropped/ delinked as decided in t he 3 rd  meeting of the Steering 
Group held on 1.8.2011. 
 
To monitor implementation of the recommended measur es, a Steering Group under 
the Chairmanship of Principal Secretary was also co nstituted. The Steering Group held its 
three meeting 1 st , 2 nd  and 3 rd  on 06.04.2010, 29.07.2010 and 01.08.2011 respectiv ely. 
Further, based on Task Force recommendations, a Cou ncil for MSME was constituted with 
Hon’ble Prime Minister as Chairman to lay down broa d policy guidelines and review 
development of MSME sector. The Report of PM’s Task  Force on MSMEs and action 
taken thereon was discussed in the 7 th  meeting of the National Board for MSMEs held on 
07.04.2010. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of  the status of  Prime Minister’s Task 
Force’s 24 recommendations whose follow up is to be monitored, 14 recommendations 
on which action are at various stages and 8 recomme ndations that have been dropped 
and reason therefor.  Also, the Committee reiterate s its stand that National Board 
must continue to discuss and monitor the policy cha nges in respect of 
recommendations of the Task Force.  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee believes that the Ministry will give due consideration to the issues 
raised by it in the Report and incorporate the same in the proposed amendments. 
(Para 44) 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry has taken a note of this.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamen tary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred Fifty 
Ninth Report on Review of implementation of Khadi a nd Village Industries Commission 
(KVIC), Act, 1956.

REPORT  
 
BACKGROUND 
 
The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) is a statutory 
body established by an Act of Parliament, 1956, In April 1957, it took over the 
work of former All India Khadi and Village Industries Board. It functions under 
the administrative control of Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2. The statement of objects and reasons of the orig inal KVIC Act, 1956 
states that "with a view to promoting and developing Khadi and Village 
Industries, the Central Govt. constituted a Board called the All India Khadi and 
Village Industries Board and vested it with powers to prepare and organize 
programmes for the production and development of Kh adi and Village 
Industries and to deal with other matters incidenta l thereto.  It has, however, 
been found in actual practice that the work of the 'Board' has been hampered 
by certain procedural and financial difficulties, w hich would be removed if a 
Commission were set up by law.  It is, therefore, p roposed to set up a 
Commission, called All India Khadi and Village Indu stries Commission which 
will be vested with the powers, executive as well a s administrative, for the 
proper development of Khadi and Village Industries.   The bill also provide for 
the All India Khadi and V.I. Board functioning as a n advisory body which will 
advise the Commission generally in the discharge of its duties. “ 
 
3. The Act was amended in 1987 and 2006. The KVIC ( Amendment) Bill, 
2005 was referred to this Committee for examination. The Committee presented 
its Report after due examination that involved inte raction with a range of 
stakeholders.  
 
4. The present KVIC Act has 28 Sections divided in five Chapters and has 
one schedule under Section 2(h) of the Act, enlisti ng the village industries 
under the Act. The Government under Section 26 of t he Act, framed KVIC 
Rules 2006 and the KVIC under Section 27 framed KVIC Regulations, 2007.  
 
 
5. The Amendment of 2005  made the membership of th e KVIC more 
professional and broad-based, it added  more part-t ime members in the  
Commission including  one expert in the field of ma rketing  as improving the 

marketing of Khadi and Village Industry (KVI) produ cts is the most important 
requirements for speeding up the growth of the KVI sector.  
 
6.  Similarly, availability of credit is an importa nt requirement for 
improving the performance of the sector. Therefore,  the amendment included 
the Chairman of the State Bank of India or his nomi nee (not below the rank of 
Deputy Managing Director) as a part-time member of the Commission.. 
 
7. The Act provided for a National KVI Board of uns pecified membership 
to advise the KVIC.  Subsequently, the KVIC Rules 2 006 provided for 51 
Member Board largely consisting of Secretaries and senior executives of 
various departments/agencies of Government of India  and headed by the 
Minister of MSME. 
8. In order to facilitate better coordination with the State Khadi and Village 
Industries Boards established by State Governments,  to obtain regular feed-
back on the problems being faced by the KVI sector in different  zones of the 
country and suggest the measures to resolve difficu lties after reviewing the 
implementation of the programmes at the field level ,  one Zonal Committee in 
each of the six geographical zones of the country w as  provided in the 
Amendment.  
9. The Amendment prescribed for regular meetings of  KVIC, National KVI 
Board and the Zonal Committees.  
10. Also, there were provisions in the Amendment to  give clearer 
demarcation of the roles of the Chairman, Chief Exe cutive Officer and the 
Financial Adviser of the Commission. 
11. The Amendment dealt extensively with the possib le financial resources 
of the KVIC and the extensive control of the Govern ment over Commission’s 
financial and administrative powers. 

12. The Committee in its 177 th  Report on the KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005  
had observed and hoped that  “ it is expected and b elieved that with these 
proposed changes, the KVIC will become more profess ional and relevant in the 
times to come and be better equipped in the dischar ge of its key role in 
facilitating generation of sustainable and wide-spr ead non-farm employment in 
the rural areas of the country.” 
13. In reply to a query whether the objectives of t he Amendment were 
realized in terms of performance of KVI sector.    
14. The Committee was informed that in quantitative  terms the growth of 
KVI sector pre and post Amendment Act, 2006 has imp roved as has been 
indicated below: 
  
• Fund disbursement for the activities of KVI program me 
increased by 159.17% i.e. Rs. 1426.44 crore during the year 
2012-13 against Rs. 550.39 crore in 2005-06 which i ndicates 
annual 22.74% averages growth in the last 7 years.  
 
• Performance of KVI programmes in terms of productio n has 
increased from Rs. 12383.84 crore during 2005-06 to  Rs. 
24024.24 crore during the year 2012-13 which regist ered total 
94% growth. It indicates 13.43% annual averages growth in last 
7 years.  
 
• Employment in Khadi and V.I. programmes has reached  to 
124.76 lakh persons in 2012-13 i.e. it has register ed  50.73% 
growth against the 82.77 lakh persons employment ge nerated 
during 2005-06 which indicates 7.25%  averages grow th in last 
7  years.  
 
15. After having discussions on functioning of the KVIC on different 
occasions, the   Committee agreed to review the implementation of t he KVIC 
Act in view of rapid changes in growth potential in  the KVI sector, emerging 

economic scenario, demographic changes and urbaniza tion and address a few 
structural issues..  
Statutory standing of the KVIC Act 
 
16. In view of the fact that in 1956, the Khadi and  Village Industries was not 
on the Union list of Seventh Schedule of Constituti on and has subsequently 
been included in the Eleventh Schedule for Panchaya ti Raj Institutions ( PRIs), 
the Committee enquired about the  statutory basis o f the KVIC Act, whether it 
was at all desirable to put Khadi & Village Industry in the Eleventh Schedule in 
context of their skills and financial resources needed to support KVI sector.  
 
17. The Committee also sought to know if present Ac t engaged local bodies 
in the bodies created under the Act. The Committee enquired if Government 
proposed to devolve finance to local bodies to impl ement KVI schemes and as 
such what will be the role of KVIC, if such schemes  are delegated to local 
bodies as per the Constitution. The Committee also sought the views if any 
amendment in the Act was required in view of Eleventh Schedule.  
 
18. In its written replies the Ministry submitted t hat though Khadi and 
Village industries was included in the Eleventh Sch edule of the Constitution, 
thereby empowering them to implement the schemes, the Entry 97 of the Union 
List ( List I) of the Seventh Schedule empowered th e Central Government to 
make legislation on the matters not enumerated in e ither the List II ( State List) 
or  the List III ( Concurrent List). Khadi and Vill age Industries was one such 
matter which has neither been mentioned in List II nor in List III. Therefore, 
statutory status of the KVIC Act is justified. 
 
19. The Secretary, M/o MSME in his oral evidence be fore the Committee 
stated: 

 “ Sir, coming to the first issue which is the apparen t conflict or 
reconciliation that may be required between the KVI C Act and the XI 
Schedule, we believe that there is actually no conf lict as such as far as 
the Act is concerned.  In our submission to the Com mittee, we have 
pointed out that under Entry 97 of the Union List o f the VII Schedule, the 
Union can legislate in respect of the khadi and vil lage industries.  Sir, 
our understanding is that in the three Lists, in th e Union List, the State 
List and the Concurrent List, if there is no subjec t which is specifically 
mentioned, because these are the only areas where t he legislation can 
happen, actually XI Schedule does not confer any po wers for legislation, 
one has to see whether a particular legislation can  be made by the 
Union, by the State or by the Union in consultation with the State.  So, we 
believe that legislation can be made under Entry 97 .  So, as such, the 
KVIC Act does not become ultra vires of the Constitution.  However, with 
the coming in force of the XI Schedule, the Constit ution 73 rd  Amendment, 
there is no doubt that the subject of khadi and vil lage industries has been 
mandated also for the Panchayati Raj institutions.  So, one has to see 
that in the functioning of the Central Government, State Government, 
KVIC, KVIC institutions and the Panchayati Raj inst itutions, how the 
provisions in the XI Schedule can be taken into acc ount, what activities 
are such which can be conducted at the level of the  Panchayats and what 
are those activities which might be required by way  of facilitation, 
funding, etc., from other levels of the Government.  In short, what we feel 
in the Ministry is that there is a role for the Panchayati Raj institution.  “ 
 
20. However, the Committee remains unconvinced of the statutory status 
of the KVIC Act. As per the reply of the Secretary and the written reply, 
the Act was framed under Entry 97 of the Union List  that gave the 
residuary powers which rest with the Union in 1956.  However, with 
inclusion of Khadi and Village industries in the El eventh Schedule 
enumerating subjects under the powers and responsib ilities of Panchayati 
Raj Institutions ( PRIs) read with the Article 243 (A), power of law making 
on the subjects enlisted in the said Schedule inclu ding KVI sector, rests 
inter alia  with the State legislature. And as such can not be  covered under 
the residuary powers of the Union in List I. Conver sely, the State 
Government would not have the legislative competenc e in respect of KVI 

sector regardless of Article 243 (A) as residuary p owers are to be vested in 
the Union Government. The Committee therefore recom mends that the 
Ministry may review the statutory position in consu ltation with relevant 
Ministry/agency to give KVIC firm statutory status.  
 
21. Regarding the desirability of keeping KVI secto r in the Eleventh 
Schedule, the Ministry stated that “ considering the fact that the Central Govt. 
has enacted the KVIC Act, 1956 for ensuring massive  promotion and 
development of Khadi and Village Industries in the country, it is not desirable 
to put Khadi and Village Industries in the Eleventh  Schedule, rather it should 
be included in the Union List under Seventh Schedule. ”   
 
22. Regarding the skills and financial strength of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
to implement KVI schemes, the Committee was informed that though the KVIC 
Act did not envisage any role for local bodies, how ever, as per Rule 32 of the 
KVIC Rules, local bodies were also included as the beneficiaries to receive 
grants and subsidies from the KVIC.  Detailing involvement of local bodies, the 
Committee was informed that the representatives of the local bodies were 
included in the District Level Task Force constitut ed to screen proposals for 
PMEGP.   
 
23. Further, in response to  the question regarding  role of KVIC, if KVI  
schemes are to be delegated to local bodies as per the Constitution, the Ministry 
suggested that if the schemes were to be devolved t o the local bodies, it would 
be appropriate to route the funds and schemes to lo cal bodies through KVIC so 
as to ensure proper monitoring and implementation o f the schemes by the local 
bodies.  It was stated that KVIC needed to be strengthened for the purpose. 
 

24. The Committee is of the view that the Government m ust ascertain 
the ways of devolution of funds to Panchayati Raj I nstitutions ( PRIs) and 
monitor and audit their performance in implementing  the Government 
schemes. In this regard the Committee also emphasiz es the need for an 
institutional linkage between KVIC and the State KV IBs supported by 
explicit statutory provisions instead of implicit Rules. 
 
Definitions  
 
25. The Committee sought to review certain definiti ons in Section 2 of the 
Act, in view of changing economic and demographic s cenario and to give 
greater coverage to the KVI programmes. 
 
26. It sought the views on Section 2 (cc) pertainin g to fixed capital 
investment which also includes cost of land unlike definition of MSMEs, 
Section 2(d) pertaining to definition of Khadi whic h does not include poly 
khadi and also excludes innovation of efficient cha rkhas, Section 2(ff) 
regarding need to update the definition of rural ar ea, Section 2 (i) pertaining  to 
per worker fixed capital investment of Rs. 1 lakh.  
 
 
  
 
(i) Poly-Vastra 
 
 
27. Regarding definition of  “Khadi”, it meant any cloth woven on 
handlooms in India from Cotton, Silk or Woolen yarn  handspun in India or 
from a Mixture of any two or all of such yarns.   
 
“Poly-vastra” in the Schedule is defined as any clo th woven on handlooms in 
India from yarn and handspun in India from a Mixtur e of manmade fibre with 

either Cotton, Silk or Wool or with any two or all of them or from Mixture of 
Man-made fibre yarn handspun in India with either C otton, Silk or Woollen 
yarn handspun in India or with any two or all of such yarns. 
 
28. The Committee observed that the definitions of khad i and           
Poly-vastra are limited to cotton, woolen or silk y arns or mixture thereof. 
The definition does not include synthetic yarn. To that extent the definition 
needs to be revised to include Poly-vastra. The def initions include 
handspun fibre and handloom woven cloth. It does no t include innovations 
like E charkhas, which are meant to increase the productivity, which is one 
of the objectives of the KVIC under Section 15 (2) (e). The Committee feels 
that the definition should be flexible enough to in clude technological 
advances which is the mandate of the Commission.  
 
(ii) Village Industry and Rural Area 
 
 
29. The Committee had sought Ministry’s views on th e definitions as 
mentioned in Sections 2(cc), 2 (ff) and 2(h) and no ted that the Ministry too 
agreed that there was a need to change the definiti on of Village Industry and 
Rural Area in the KVIC Act.  
 
30. The Committee notes that the Sections 2 (ff) perta ining to ‘rural 
area’ and 2 (i) regarding village industry acknowle dges that these are 
dynamic concepts and that the Government could chan ge the parameters 
by notifications. However, no notification has been  issued to change these 
definitions, ever since last amendment to the Act i n 2006.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should change the defi nition in consultation 
with the KVIC through notification.  
 

31. The Committee also recommends that like MSME Develo pment Act, 
the definition of  ‘ Fixed per Capita’ investment s hould only include plant 
and machinery and not the cost of land, workshed etc.    
 
32. The Committee takes note of the list of Village in dustry included in 
the Schedule framed under Section 2 ( h). The Commi ttee is of the opinion 
that States should be given flexibility in deciding  the Village industry. This 
will facilitate greater coverage of the Village ind ustry schemes and make 
them more relevant to local traditional crafts, ski lls and employment 
needs. 
 
Demarcation between powers and functions of Commiss ion and the Chief 
Executive Officer  
 
  33. The Committee acknowledged that one of the ob jectives of the 
Amendment was clearer demarcation of the powers and  functions of 
Commission and the Chief Executive Officer.  Howeve r, the ambivalence 
persisted due to Section 4 (1A) regarding Commissio n’s powers of general 
superintendence in day to day affairs and Section 5(1) and (1A) that gave power 
of general superintendence also to CEO.  The Commit tee sought further 
elaboration from the Ministry in this regard in con text of Sections 4 (1A), 5 (1) 
and (1A), Rules 10,11 and 12.  
 
34. The Committee was informed that according to Se ction 4 (1A)  the 
exercise of all powers and discharge of all functio ns under this Act, including 
general superintendence, direction and management o f day-to-day affairs of the 
Commission shall vest in the Commission. Further, a ccording to Section 5 (1), 
the Chief Executive Officer shall exercise such pow ers and discharge such 
functions in respect of general superintendence ove r the affairs of the 
Commission and its day-to-day management, under the  general 

superintendence, direction and management of the Co mmission. Section 5(1A) 
further underscores that the Chief Executive Office r shall exercise such powers 
of general superintendence and management.  
 
35. These Sections read with relevant Rules make th e demarcation clear. As 
per Rule 10, the powers of the Chairman of the KVIC  is limited to the matters 
pertaining to the meetings of the Commission and gi ving directions as to the 
method of carrying out the decisions of the Commission.  Whereas according to 
Rule 11, the Chief Executive Officer is charged wit h duty to deal with the 
meetings of the Commission such as convening the me etings of the 
Commission and drawing up of agenda and maintenance  of minutes of the 
meeting under the direction of the Chairman while Rule 12, particularly Rule 12 
(a) empowers the CEO to coordinate, supervise and c ontrol the works of all the 
departments, establishments, officers and staff of the Commission.  
 
36. The Committee found an anomalous situation exis ts in the Act as 
powers of the Commission under Section 4(1) have be en delegated to the 
CEO under Sections 5 (1), (1A) of the same Act and not through any 
subordinate legislation.    
                          
37. The Committee is of the opinion that the intent of the Act and its 
provisions is abundantly clear. The power of genera l and not specific 
supervision is given to Commission in order to ensu re its administrative 
autonomy required to facilitate its mandate. As the Commission meets once 
a month and by implication can not supervise day-to  day affairs of the 
Commission, the Act itself empowers the CEO to supe rvise the day to day 
affairs. In view of Sections 4(1), 5(1) and (1A) an d Rules 10, 11 and 12 
made by the Central Government under Section 26, th e Committee feels 
that the demarcation is fairly clear that Commissio n is essentially a policy 
making body and powers bestowed on it are incidental.  

 
38. Section 27 of the Act prescribe the Commissions pow ers to frame 
regulations thereby setting broad parameters of adm inistrative policies in 
consonance of its objectives, financial and human r esources. The CEO is 
required to carry out the administration and superv ision as per the broad 
administrative policies determined by the Commissio n through 
Regulations.   The Committee is of the view that ge neral superintendence 
on the part of Commission in its day-to day affairs  as envisaged in Section 
4(1A) is oxymoron. Committee accordingly recommends  that that word “ 
day to day” should be deleted. Similarly, General S uperintendence on the 
part of Chief Executive Officer under Section 5(1) too should b deleted and 
consequential changes be made in the Act. As part o f general 
superintendence, the Commission though may seek inf ormation from the 
CEO on general administrative matters. 
 
Terms and Conditions of service of Chief Executive Officer and Financial 
Advisor  
 
39. Section 13 (2) expects that the terms and condi tions for the Chief 
Executive Officer and the Financial Advisor may be prescribed.  
 
40. The Committee observes that no Rule has been fr amed by the 
Government in this regard. The Committee is of the view that the terms 
and conditions for engagement of these two critical  positions may be 
prescribed immediately. The terms of engagement sho uld clearly specify 
the requirement of previous experience of prospecti ve candidates in the 
Khadi or Village Industries or associated fields. A lso the choice of 
candidates must not be limited to Government by dep utation, instead 

should be open to members of senior management of B anks, financial 
institutions and PSUs. The selection should be made  through an 
independent body like Public Enterprises Selection Board.  
 
Financial Autonomy of the KVIC 
 
  
41. The Committee noted that the Act envisaged fina ncial autonomy for 
KVIC. Considering that Khadi is essentially a finan cially viable vocation,  the 
Committee sought to know if the KVIC had any plan t o attain financial 
autonomy instead of seeking autonomy despite gettin g annual budgetary 
support from the Government.  
 
42.  The Committee was informed that though the KVI C Act envisages 
financial autonomy for KVIC, it was still dependent  on the budgetary support 
because the KVIC is a statutory body created by an Act of the Parliament with 
the social objectives of providing employment opportunities. It is a promotional 
and developmental organization for Khadi and Villag e Industries in the rural 
areas and that the KVIC implements these programmes  as per scheme 
guidelines and pattern of assistance approved by th e Govt. of India. It was 
stated that there is no provision of any income gen eration by the KVIC for 
implementing the programmes, therefore the objectiv e of KVIC is not profit 
motive.  
 
43. As per the Section 17, the Central Government a fter due appropriation 
made by Parliament, pays to Commission in each fina ncial year such sums as 
may be considered necessary for the performance of the functions of the 
Commission under this act. Also, under Section 17 A , the Commission may for 
the purpose of development of Khadi and Village Ind ustries receive gifts, 
grants, donations or benefactions from the Governme nt or any other persons. 
Under Section 21, the Commission has the power to b orrow money against the 

security of funds provided for khadi or village ind ustries or against any other 
asset. As such the KVIC receives fund from the Gove rnment and it does levy 
any fee or charges. 
 
44. The Committee noted the constraints in achieving th e financial 
autonomy and also observed the reluctance in attain ing it. It was stated 
that the KVIC is basically a promotional body and d oes not engage in any 
commercial activities, the question of attainment o f financial sustainability 
in the present set up is too remote.  Instead it was left to the planners of our 
country to consider whether to change the present r ole of KVIC from a 
promotional body to a commercial body. 
 
45. However, the Secretary, M/o MSME in his present ation before the 
Committee did offer that KVIC should leverage its p osition and generate 
resources with the financial institutions or fundin g agencies to generate 
resources to finance its Schemes. However, at prese nt the KVIC generated 
minimal resources on its own and depended predomina ntly on the Government 
for its finances.  
 
“ the other set of issues relates to the financial autonomy of KVIC.  This issue 
had arisen also in one of the earlier meetings and in that as well as in our 
submission before the Committee, we have said that if the KVIC is able to raise 
sufficient resources, it will certainly justify det ermination by KVIC itself of how 
it will utilise those resources. But as things stan d, the KVIC is receiving non-
Plan assistance to the tune of about Rs. 250 crores  every year; Plan assistance, 
for various schemes, the budgeted amount is about R s.1650 crores and its own 
resources are only to the tune of about Rs. 36 crores.  Out of these Rs. 36 crore, 
about Rs. 16 crore  are arising from the bank inter est on funds which the 
Central Government has been giving from time to time.  So, in effect, the overall 
resources generated would work out to be about rupe es 10 crores or so.  So, in 
a budget of over nearly rupees 2,000 crores, the in ternal resources of the KVIC 
which are not linked to the funds which the Government is giving either through 
Plan or non-Plan budgetary support is to the tune of about rupees 10-12 crores.  
In this situation, we have to see what kind of func tional autonomy KVIC can 
actually enjoy because, as mentioned, the bulk of t he resources are for Plan 

schemes and within that the major content is for th e Prime Minister’s 
Employment Generation Programme where the KVIC is t he nodal agency.  So, 
for the Plan scheme, Sir, it is incumbent that the guidelines are followed.  We 
are taking the approval of the Cabinet for these programmes and there are a set 
of guidelines.  There is also a procedure which the  Ministry itself has to follow 
for the release of funds and we are subject to audit, internal audit as well as the 
control of the Ministry of Finance and its represen tatives in the Ministry of 
MSME through the internal finance wing.  So, given that situation, there is very 
little leeway, in my opinion, for allowing a total financial autonomy to the 
KVIC.  However, elsewhere, Sir, you have mentioned that should the KVIC be 
encouraged to have functional autonomy and financia l autonomy.  To that, my 
answer is, ‘certainly yes’, because the Act also pe rmits the KVIC to raise 
resources from elsewhere and this is probably an ar ea which has not been fully 
explored by the KVIC.  Maybe, earlier it was not po ssible for the KVIC to raise 
resources and to receive endowments, but in today’s  context where globally the 
emphasis is on sustainability, green products, envi ronmentally-friendly 
products, in this changed context, there may be pos sibility even for an 
institution like KVIC to position itself and to rec eive funds from sources other 
than the Government.  If that happens, certainly, t he degree of financial and 
functional autonomy which the KVIC can enjoy will be greatly enhanced.   
 
46. The Committee is of the view that the KVIC has neither been given 
the financial autonomy nor was in position to attai n financial autonomy 
despite provisions in the Act.  It has to seek approval from the Government 
at every stage. The Committee is of the view that K VIC should be allowed 
to re-appropriate funds from khadi and Village Indu stry funds, under the 
intimation to the Ministry. KVIC should also be all owed to spend the 
resources generated by it.  
 
47. The Committee is also of the view that the Gove rnment should 
release the Funds in time, but its should be obliga tion of the KVIC of 
keeping the Government informed of the expenditure out of annual 
Budgetary Grants. However, it is essential that KVI C even as a 
promotional organisation for a commercially viable vocation like khadi 
and Village Industries, must leverage itself to generate its own finances.  

 
48. The Committee wonders that if KVIC could access  the funds like 
RIDF. The Ministry may explore if KVIC could avail institutional finances 
from Banks, as a Micro Finance Institution and from  RIDF. The Ministry 
should gradually promote KVIC as specialized resour ce agency and 
financial institution for village industries from b eing a promotional 
organization. Sections 17, 17A and 21 give powers to KVIC to raise funds.  
 
 
49. The Ministry should persuade KVIC to leverage i ts position with 
financial institutions like SIDBI, NABARD, National  Backward Class 
Finance & Development Corporation, National SC Fina nce Corporation, 
National ST Finance Corporation, National Minoritie s Development 
Finance Corporation, Rashtriya Mahila Kosh etc. to raise finances for its 
schemes.  For which the KVIC will have to evolve a sound business model. 
The Committee recommends that Rules 32, 33 and 34 s hould be made 
more substantive.  
 
50. The Committee is of the view that despite prono unced objective of 
the Act, the KVIC may not be able to attain full ad ministrative autonomy 
unless it attains financial autonomy.  It must shed  its reluctance and evolve 
into a self sustaining organization.  
 
51. In this regard the Committee sought details of new Khadi Reform and 
Development Programme( KRDP) with the assistance of ADB.  
 
52. It was informed that Khadi Reform and Developme nt Programme 
(KRDP) was developed after protracted discussion an d suggestion put forth by 
all stake holders of Khadi. The same was placed bef ore CCEA and with the 

direction of CCEA, it is being implemented by KVIC.   KVIC decided that in 
order to assign direct reform assistance to most po tential institutions the views 
of Zonal Committees may be obtained. Accordingly, K VIC has identified the 
first 300 institutions to be supported under direct  reform assistance in 
consultation with the Zonal Committees. 
 
 
53. Under the programme, a Marketing Organization i s being set up as a 
Joint Venture Company between KVIC and a selected p rivate partner with 49% 
and 51% shareholding respectively. On setting up of  the Organization, its role 
would be for brand building, quality control and to  grow the business of KVI 
products in international markets. 
 
54. The Committee may remind that the Khadi as a conce pt evolved 
independent of government support. It was a tool an d symbol of protest 
and not a captive vocation of Government.  To conti nue to make it 
dependent of grants from the Government will defeat the very purpose and 
message of khadi.  
 
National Khadi and Village Industry Board 
 
 
55. The Committee recognized that the Act provided for setting up of a 
National KVI Board. It sought to know the impact of  such Board on the 
functional and financial autonomy of the KVIC consi dering the existence of 
National KVI Board headed by the Minister.  Could s uch a Board, comprising 
largely of Minister and Secretaries of the Governme nt act in an advisory 
capacity.   
 

56. The Committee   noted that Section 16  obliged the KVIC to adhere to 
the directions of the Government whereas Section 11  of the Act required the 
KVIC to ordinarily consult the Board in discharge of its function.  
  
57. In written reply the Committee was informed tha t the Section 10 of the 
KVIC Act deals with the Constitution of the Nationa l Khadi and V.I. Board.  
According to Rule 15 of the KVIC Rules, the Nationa l KVI Board shall consist 
of 51 Members, largely Executives representing the different Departments 
connected with rural development and chaired by the  Minister of MSME 
(formerly ARI).  Considering the large representati on in the Board, it can 
function only as an Advisory Body and it may not be  able to frame policies and 
programmes for the KVIC.   
 
58. Section 16 of the Act deals with the powers of the Central Govt. to give 
direction to the Commission in the discharge of its  functions.   Since the 
directives on behalf of the Central Govt. are being  issued by the Ministry of 
MSME, there will not be any conflict between the ad vice given by the National 
KVI Board and the directives given by the Ministry of MSME as the Chairman 
of the Board is the Minister of MSME itself.  Howev er, Section 16 of the Act 
dilutes the autonomous character of the KVIC to a great extent.   
 
59. The Committee accepts the assertion that Section 16  of the Act does 
dilute the autonomous character of the KVIC to a gr eat extent. The 
Committee also takes note  of an unprecedented arra ngement under 
Sections 10 and 11 where 51 Member National KVI Boa rd chaired by the 
Minister concern and largely consisting of Secretar ies of relevant 
Ministries of Government of India will advise a 13 Member KVIC of which 
10 Members are part-time Members. The Committee won ders if such an 
arrangement exists anywhere in the Government where  a larger body 

headed by the executive Minister renders advice to a smaller Commission 
under the administrative and financial control of that Ministry.  
 
60. The Committee wonders if the Minister, who disc harges executive 
functions could act in advisory capacity to another  body under its 
administrative control. Such an arrangement is furt her complemented by 
Section 16 of the Act which makes directions of the Government obligatory 
upon the KVIC. The situation is indeed paradoxical if not oxymoron. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry must give ti me bound final 
approval to any administrative or financial proposal from the KVIC.  
 
61. Moreover, during the evidence, the Secretary in formed the 
Committee that the National KVI Board has not been meeting regularly as 
mandated in the Act. The Committee takes such state of affairs seriously. A 
statutory Board headed by Minister breaching the st atutory mandate is 
indeed a serious issue. It only highlights the redu ndence of such a 
superfluous arrangement.  
 
62. The Committee recommends that the Government’s powers under 
Section 16 too should be mitigated. Rules should be  framed under this 
Section to limit the powers of Government to give d irection. Powers should 
also be given to KVIC to discuss the issue and appr ise the Government of 
its views.  
 
63. The Committee reiterates that the autonomy of KVIC  is likely to 
remain constricted due to its continued reliance ov er Government for 
finances. It is the mandate given to KVIC to exerci se autonomy and the 
Commission ought to generate resources independent of Government. 

There are provisions in the Act to enable KVIC to g enerate resources 
provided KVIC formulates viable business case.   
  
64. The Committee also takes note of the composition o f the KVIC. The 
objective of the last Amendment of 2005 was to infu se greater 
professionalism to the KVIC. It provided for four e xperts as non-official 
part-time Members of the Commission. The Committee is surprised to note 
that despite having a specialized in-house body Mah atma Gandhi Institute 
for Rural Industrialization (MGIRI), the Act does n ot provide any scope 
for the Institute. The professional mandate of the Institute almost coincides 
with the demands of the KVIC i.e to strengthen rura l industrialization, 
enhance rural employment in rural areas. The Instit ute is designed as a      
“ mechanism that would  provide high quality of sci ence, technology and 
management inputs and support in a comprehensive ma nner to KVI 
sector.” The Committee therefore recommends that th e expert 
representatives  of MGIRI may be included in the Co mmission under 
Section 4(2) (b) and existing part-time non-governm ent experts and also 
government representatives may be involved with the  KVIC as per 
requirement under Section 9 of the Act. This will b ring about a closer 
institutional linkage between KVIC and MGIRI.   
 
Linkage between KVIC and the State Khadi and Village Industries Boards  
 
65. The Committee noted that there are State KVIBs.  However, the Act does 
not prescribe the linkage between KVIC and the KVIB.       
 
66. Regarding the linkage between KVIC and State KV I Board is concerned, 
it is clarified that the relationship between the K VIC and KVI Board is not 
defined anywhere in the KVIC Act or Rules. However,  as per the definition of 
the term" Borrower"  contained in the  KVIC Rules a nd KVIC Loan Rules 

includes a board established under any law for the development of Khadi and 
village industries also. Further, for all practical purposes, KVIC is treating State 
KVI Boards as one its implementing agencies. 
   
67. The Committee sought clarification if there cou ld be an overlap or 
conflict in domains of State KVIBs and the State Directorates of KVIC. 
 
68. It was submitted that as regards the question w hether the State KVI 
Board is different from State KVIC Directorates is concerned, it is clarified that 
though both the organizations are pursuing similar objectives, but they are 
governed by different Acts and functioning independ ently.  The State KVIC 
Directorates are the branch offices of the KVIC ope ned in all the States and 
Union Territories to facilitate the speedy discharg e of the functions of the 
KVIC.  With this arrangement in force, both KVIC an d KVIBs have been 
successfully implementing the KVI programme in fulf illing the objectives of 
the Commission in terms of creating employment oppo rtunities in the country 
in the last several decades  
 
69. The Committee is of the view that given the sho rtage of manpower 
and resources faced by the State Directorates of KV IC and considering 
similar mandate of State KVIBs, the Ministry has no t been able to justify 
the existence of State Directorates. Instead the KV IC must conserve its 
scarce resources for more useful purposes than depu ting them for similar 
assignments as State KVIBs. For this there is a nee d for institutional 
linkage between the KVIC and State KVIBs supported by explicit 
statutory provision. The Zonal Committee could prov ide a forum where 
KVIC and State KVIBs converge to discuss the impact  and shortcomings 
of KVIC schemes.  
 

70. In this regard the Committee also recalled its observations in its 177 th  
Report on the KVIC (Amendment) Bill, 2005 : 
 
“In order to facilitate better coordination with th e State Khadi and Village 
Industries Boards established by State Governments,  obtain regular feed-back 
on the problems being faced by the KVI sector in th e six zones of the country 
and suggest to the Commission measures to resolve d ifficulties after reviewing 
the implementation of the programmes at the field l evel, provision for 
constitution of one Zonal Committee in each of the six geographical zones of 
the country has also been provided in the Bill.” 
 
71. The Committee had further stated in the Report:  
 
“3.7.1    The Committee welcomes the formation of Zonal Commi ttees and 
the measures towards  decentralized  functioning of  KVIC, however, with a 
view to ensuring participation of the real stakehol ders, at least one   
representative of  institutions having not less tha n ten years of   experience 
with khadi and/or village industries with good trac k record of performance 
from  each one of the States in the zones should be  made members of the 
Zonal Committee.   The Committee understands that t he voluntary   
institutions/co-operatives implement the programmes  of the KVIC, 
therefore,   their direct  involvement in the  Zona l Committee would enable 
them to realize the  correct field  position/  corr ect  feed    back  from the 
field and thus would be helpful in decision making – process .    
 3.7.2    The Committee received the suggestion that in many States the 
Chairman of the State Khadi and Village Industries Boards of the States is 
politically appointee with Ministerial rank and it may not be feasible for him 
to attend the meeting of the Zonal Committee.  Acco rdingly, the Central 
Government may decide the representative of the Sta te KVIBs as member of 
the Zonal Committee in consultation with the State Governments.  The 
Committee also agrees with the view point and there fore recommends that  
in place of the Chairman, State KVIB, the represent ative of each of the State 
Khadi and Village Industries Boards of the States o r  the Government of 
each of States in the zone,  as the case may be,  t o be notified by the Central 
Government within 30 days in consultation with Stat e Government 
concerned –member “.   
 
72. To a query regarding role and inputs given by t he Zonal Committees, the 
Ministry informed that the Zonal Committees have di scussed several major 

issues in its meetings. The major issues discussed,  reviewed and recommended 
by the Zonal Committees were pertaining to:- 
i. Position of financial support to the weaker institu tions i.e.  
SC/ST/Minority/OBC, and newly enlisted Khadi institutions. 
 
ii. Review for social security measures extended to the  KVI 
artisans through various Welfare Schemes, Workshed for 
individual as well as group artisans, Artisans Insu rance Scheme 
i.e. Children Education Scholarship, Death claims, etc. 
 
iii. Provide necessary guidance for implementation of KV I 
activities in the Zones. 
 
iv. Extend support/guidance for marketing of KVI produc ts                 
through exhibitions as per Commission’s directions.  
 
73. The Committee sought to know if the Zonal Commi ttees had been fully 
constituted as per the composition prescribed in the Section 12 (A) (1) 
 
74. The Ministry in its response informed the Commi ttee as per the Act, one 
representative of each of the State Khadi and Villa ge Industries Boards of the 
States or, as the case may be, the Government of ea ch State in the Zone, to be 
notified by the Central Government in consultation with the State Government 
concerned and one representative of an institution of repute, working for at least 
ten years in the Khadi or Village Industries sector  and having a good record of 
performance, from each State in the Zone, to be not ified by the Central 
Government, are to be nominated to the Zonal Commit tee. The KVIC had 
requested the Ministry of MSME to accord approval a s well as for notification 
in the Gazette. The same was under process.   
 
75. The Committee expresses serious concern over th e erosion of 
statutory institutions prescribed under the Act. Th e National KVI Board 
does not meet as per the provisions of Act. The Zon al Committee are not 
fully formed despite Committee’s recommendation tha t same should be 

notified within 30 days. The Committee is persuaded  to wonder if these 
bodies are superfluous or have been relegated to redundence. In absence of 
representation of States and khadi institutions, th e Zonal Committee can 
not fulfill its mandate.  In this regard the Commit tee recalls that the initial 
proposal in the Act did not include the khadi insti tution and it was only on 
Committee’s recommendations that the khadi institutions were included in 
the Act. However, despite, provision in the Act, th e Government does not 
comply.

unwieldy size of Zonal Committees the representativ e of the State KVIC 
Directorates should be excluded as the Zonal Deputy  CEO  of the 
Commission is  included in the Zonal Committee. The  Committee 
recommends that Ministry and KVIC should consider the recommendation 
and make necessary changes.  
 
77. The Committee also recommends that the Government s hould set up 
a statutory functional linkage between KVIC and State KVIBs and till such 
time should revitalize the Zonal Committees.  
 
 
78. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry  should 
include the details of the activities/meetings/agen da of the 
boards/committees/other bodies created under this A ct. The Annual 
Report should also include the Rules and Regulation  made under relevant 
Sections of this Act.

1. However, the Committee remains unconvinced of the statutory status 
of the KVIC Act. As per the reply of the Secretary and the written reply, 
the Act was framed under Entry 97 of the Union List  that gave the 
residuary powers which rest with the Union in 1956.  However, with 
inclusion of Khadi and Village industries in the El eventh Schedule 
enumerating subjects under the powers and responsib ilities of Panchayati 
Raj Institutions ( PRIs) read with the Article 243 (A), power of law making 
on the subjects enlisted in the said Schedule inclu ding KVI sector, rests 
inter alia  with the State legislature. And as such can not be  covered under 
the residuary powers of the Union in List I. Conver sely, the State 
Government would not have the legislative competenc e in respect of KVI 
sector regardless of Article 243 (A) as residuary p owers are to be vested in 
the Union Government. The Committee therefore recom mends that the 
Ministry may review the statutory position in consu ltation with relevant 
Ministry/agency to give KVIC firm statutory status.  
(Para 20) 
2. The Committee is of the view that the Government  must ascertain 
the ways of devolution of funds to Panchayati Raj I nstitutions ( PRIs) and 
monitor and audit their performance in implementing  the Government 
schemes. In this regard the Committee also emphasiz es the need for an 
institutional linkage between KVIC and the State KV IBs supported by 
explicit statutory provisions instead of implicit Rules. 
(Para 24)

Poly-vastra are limited to cotton, woolen or silk y arns or mixture thereof.

needs to be revised to include Poly-vastra. The def initions include 
handspun fibre and handloom woven cloth. It does no t include innovations 

like E charkhas, which are meant to increase the productivity, which is one 
of the objectives of the KVIC under Section 15 (2) (e). The Committee feels 
that the definition should be flexible enough to in clude technological 
advances which is the mandate of the Commission.  
(Para 28) 
4. The Committee notes that the Sections 2 (ff) per taining to ‘rural

dynamic concepts and that the Government could chan ge the parameters

definitions, ever since last amendment to the Act i n 2006.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should change the defi nition in consultation 
with the KVIC through notification.  
(Para 30) 
5.  The Committee also recommends that like MSME Develo pment Act,

and machinery and not the cost of land, workshed etc.    
(Para 31)

needs.

Industry having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Twenty-sixth Report 
on Action Taken by the Ministry of Industry on the recommendations/observations 
contained in the 17th Report of the Committee on "Industrialisation of Backward Areas and 
State of Capital Goods Sector".

1. RECOMMENDATION 
Industrial Growth of Backward Areas 
The Ministry of Industry should assume the main responsibility to implement programme 
of industrial· growth in hitherto backward areas. It should draw up detailed blueprints of 
projects in collaboration with the Planning Commission and the State Governments. Detailed 
prescriptions of task for each area should embrace, apart from infrastructural planning such 
measures as the opening of a single window arrangement to cater to the requirements of 
potential entrepreneurs. 
Action Taken 
The primary responsibility for industrial development and development of industrially 
backward areas rests with the State Governments. With the introduction of the New 
Industrial Policy and various measures aimed at liberalisation of the economy there has been 
gradual reduction in intervention by the State. It is in this context that that the role of the 
Union Government is supportive in development of backward areas and the Ministry of 
Industry in the discharge of this responsibility is already implementing the Growth Centre 
Scheme and the Transport Subsidy Scheme for development of backward areas .. This 
recommendation has also been brought to notice of the Planning Commission and the State 
Government so as to enable them to fully addressed themselves to the recommendation. 
Comments/Observations 
The Sub-Committee notes the additional information received from the Ministry of 
Industry on the Committee's recommendation (Annexure-!). It is not convinced with the 
Ministry's reply that primary responsibility for industrial development and development of 
backward areas rests with the State Governments. In the opinion of the Sub-Committee, the 
Central Ministry of Industry has a definite role to play in this regard. The Sub-Committee 
notes that the Central Government are implementing the Growth Centre Scheme and the 
Transport Subsidy Scheme for the development of industrially backward areas, but it is 
unhappy over the pace of implementation of the Growth Centre Scheme. The Sub­
Committee notes with regret that the Growth Centre Scheme which was announced in the 
year 1988 could take off as late as in the year 1994-95 ·and out of the 71 growth centres 
proposed to be set up during the 8th Plan period only 54 were approved. The number of 
growth centres actually set up and in operation must be even less. 
As regards the Transport Subsidy Scheme the Sub-Committee notes that the subsidy 
released was higher than the allocations under the annual plans for the year 1992 and 
thereafter. The Sub-Committee further notes with satisfaction that the Ministry of Industry 
are pursuing for increasing the allocations under this scheme from Rs. 200 crores to Rs. 300 
crores for the 9th Plan period.

3. RECOMMENDATION 
Disinvestment of PSUs shares 
There is a need to formulate clear-cut policies with regard to the role the Union 
Government intend to play in respect of its Public Sector Undertakings, particularly with 
reference to disinvestment of its share holding. 
Action Taken 
The policy of the Government on disinvestment is clearly spelt ,Gfut in the Industrial 
Policy Statement of July, 1991. It states that Government will ensure that public sector plays 
its rightful role in evolving socialistic scenario of the country. The Government will also 
ensure that public sector is run on business lines as envisaged in the Industrial Policy

of part of Government shareholding the controlling stake in the PSUs continues to remain

Government shareholding. The disinvestment policy is decided by the Ministry of Finance

Action Taken 
Office of the DC(SSI) through the field officers of Small Industries Service Institute,

escort services. Further, assistance by way of loans and or grant is also extended to

(iii) Mahila Vikas Nidhi; and (iv) Savings-cum-Credit Scheme for informal banking. 
(i) REFINANCE SCHEME FOR WOMEN ENTREPRENEURS 
The scheme for women entrepreneurs has been formulated with the twin objectives of 
(i) providing training and extension services support to women entrepreneurs through a 
comprehensive package suited to their skill and socio-economic status and (ii) extending 
financial assistance on liberal terms to enable them in set up industrial units in the Small 
Scale Sector. 
(ii) MAHILA UDYAM NIDHI (MUN) SCHEME 
The objectives of the MUN scheme is to provide soft loan (quasi-equity) assistance to 
women entrepreneurs. The scheme till recently operated through the agency of SFCsltwin­
function SID has since been extended to all public and private sector banks as also 
scheduled urban co-operative banks which are eligible for direct refinance assistance from 
SIDBI with a view to further enlarging the reach and covering as many units as possible 
under the scheme. Assistance out of MUN is provided to women entrepreneurs to meet the 
gap in the equity for setting up new industrial projects in Small Scale Sector. 
(iii) MAHILA VIKAS NIDHI (MVN) SCHEME 
While small industrial ventures of individual women entrepreneurs are supported out of 
MUN, a special development fund called Mahila Vikas Nidhi (MVN) was created to extend 
support to specific proposals· for income generating programmes of accredited voluntary 
organisations with strong support amongst poor at the grassroot level and proven track 
record of performance in. managing economic programmes. The basic objectives of this 
programmes is to bring about economic upliftment of women, especially the poor, by 
providing them avenues for taking up self/wage employment activities in the industrial 
sphere. Activities such as setting up of Training-cum-Production Centres, skill upgradation 
programmes, extension of marketing assistance and such other income generating pursuits as 

12 
' would improve the economic status of women are eligible for support under MVN. 
Assistance by way of grant and/or loan is provided out of the fund to accredited voluntary 
organisations for taking up activities which would ensure that the needy women are provided 
with training and employment opportunities. 
(iv) SAVING-CUM-CREDIT SCHEME ON INFORMAL BANKING 
Recognising the fact that the regular banking channel has its own constraints in 
extending small credit to the poor women, the bank has taken the initiative for encouraging

envisages support to well managed NGOs to on lend to the rural women for setting up th~r 
own micro enterprises.

1. REC0!\1!\IENDA TION 
Simplification of labour laws 
The Industry Secretary, Government of Maharashtra, was critical of the present labour 
laws which according to him needed to be simplified. An entrepreneur, particularly who was 
willing to set up a small unit, found the labour laws very difficult to be tackled with. He 
mentioned specifically about the Factories Act which at present was applicable to industries/ 
units employing more than ten persons. He suggested that in order to mitigate the 
difficulties of entrepreneurs and persuading them to set up industries in backward areas it 
was important that industries employing less than fifty persons should be kept out of the 
Factories Act. (Page 42) 
Action Taken 
The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Labour. Ministry of Labour is uf the 
opinion that the Factories Act stipulates minimum standards for safety, health and welfare of 
workers while at work and lays down measures to be taken to ensure protection from bodily 
harm and occupational diseases. Withdrawing the application of this Act or any measure to 
reduce its coverage would be a retrograde measure. The eligibility for getting protection in 
respect of safety and heahh requirements should not be linked with the number of 'Vorkers 
working in an establishment.- Withdrawing the safety and health protection given to· a worker 
under the Factories Act simply for the reason that a number of workers is less than a 
prescribed limit would not at all be proper. 
As· regards simplification of labour legislation, in so far as it relates to reducing the · 
number of returns and registers to be maintained by the concerned units, Labour Ministry is 
in full agreement with the view that such simplification needs to be brought about. On its 
part the Ministry has taken appropriate steps in this regard such as enacting the ''Exemption

been releasing funds of JSP for renewal and replacement of its existing plant and machinery.

counter guarantee to SBI for Rs. 10 crores for meeting working capital requirement.

has been appointed as the Operating Agency for preparing a revival scheme of JSP. The 
revival scheme is expected within 3 months. The dues of retired employees will be taken into 
account in the revival scheme.

finalisation of plan requirement, recruitment in senior posts and manpower rationalisation.

22. RECOMMENDATION 
Implementation of legislation on SSI 
The Small Scale Industries were suffering due to delay in the release of payment by 
large and medium scale industries for purchases made from them in spite of a legislation 
passed by Parliament which provided for prompt payment. The Sub-Committee was 
constrained to express its anguish over the ignorance of legislation and impress upon the 
Government to monitor the implementation of legislation, so passed, in letter and spirit in 
the interest of small scale industries. (Page 198). 
Action Taken 
In order to safeguard the payments due to SSI units against the supply of goods and 
services to the buyers there exists an Act-"The Interest on Delayed Payment to Small Scale 

82 
& Ancillary Undertakings Act, 1993", according to which a buyer is required to make 
payments on or before the date agreed upon between him and the supplier or within a 
period of 30 days from the date of acceptance of services and goods. \\_'herein, if the buyer 
fails to make payment in time, he is liable to pay interest to the supplier on the amount 
from the appointed date or as the case may be at such rate which is 5% points above the 
floor rates for comparable lending. The buyer is also required to specify the amount due 
together with the interest in his annual statement of accounts as remains unpaid to any 
supplier at the end of each accounting year. Moreover, in accordance with the provision of 
the cited Act, amount of interest payable/paid, shall not, for the purpose of computation of 
Income Tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961, be allowed for deduction. 
There are suggestions from different quarters to make the Act more meaningful by 
affecting certain amendments like constitution of District level Tribunals, extending the 
coverage of the Act to NSIC & SSIDCs who are marketing the products of SSI units. These 
suggestions are under consideration.
